It is paid before the bank decides and is not refunded. A monthly due-diligence fee of EUR 20 or 100 follows separate tests (footnotes 4-5), e.g. a beneficial owner's residence.

m-57bb532e.t: Swedbank AS's price list for business clients (section 'Opening accounts', effective as of 01.11.2023, read 5 October 2026): opening an account is free of charge, but a 'fee for enhanced due diligence measures' is paid before the bank decides and is not returned on refusal - EUR 300 for Estonian legal persons with non-residents included as representatives or in the ownership structure, EUR 300 for legal persons from the European Economic Area, EUR 500 for legal persons from other states and for listed activities (payment and e-money institutions, currency exchange, crowdfunding platforms, fast credit, weapons, mining, strategic goods). The fee is not charged again for each further account.

m-54cb2d48.t: Coop Pank AS spells out what the law leaves open - when a consumer has a 'legitimate interest' in a basic payment account in Estonia. Its General Terms and Conditions effective as of 1 October 2025 (clause 4.9) deem it to exist if the consumer works in Estonia or for an Estonian company, studies in Estonia for at least six months, owns property in Estonia whose costs or rent run through the account, or 'has another significant and verifiable link which explains why they need a payment account in Estonia'. On request the consumer must prove that interest and the right to reside in the EU (4.10); the bank answers within 10 banking days of a duly completed application (4.11).

m-529c471a.t: LHV Pank refuses one class of company outright: its page 'Non-residents' (read 5 October 2026) says, under 'Your company is registered in an offshore location or its ownership structure includes companies registered in offshore countries', that 'LHV Pank does not open accounts for these companies'. The page does not say which jurisdictions it counts as offshore. For a company registered abroad that it does consider, LHV asks in addition for notarised articles of association, a notarised list of signatories and a certified registry statement from the last 6 months, translated into Estonian, Russian or English.

m-52380231.t: LHV Pank's published price list for non-residents, as of 5 October 2026: for a company registered in Estonia with non-resident owners — defined as at least 25% owned by legal entities registered outside Estonia or by non-resident private persons, or having a non-resident ultimate beneficiary — account opening EUR 300, monthly fee EUR 30, bank card EUR 2 a month; the fee does not apply to Estonian citizens living abroad. The opening fee is paid with the application and is not refunded if the bank declines. A non-resident private client pays EUR 100 to open and EUR 10 a month if resident in an EU state, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein or Switzerland, and EUR 200 and EUR 20 otherwise.

m-520bed29.t: LHV Pank has no priced business package: its price list (accounts section valid as of 1 May 2026, read 5 October 2026) opens and maintains a company account free of charge, 'except non-residents and business entities related to them'. The non-resident list (valid as of 1 May 2024) charges a legal entity registered in Estonia 'with non-resident owners' - at least 25% held by foreign entities or non-resident private persons, or a non-resident ultimate beneficiary - an account opening application fee of EUR 300, not refunded on refusal, and EUR 30 per month; it does not apply to Estonian citizens living abroad. A company in a high-risk field pays EUR 1,000 to apply.

m-4ae2088d.t: Luminor Bank AS's Payment Terms (Luminori maksetingimused, marked valid from 1 September 2026; copy archived on 12 July 2026, before that date) let the bank amend them unilaterally on at least two months' notice (clause 1.6) and require the client to report an unauthorised or incorrectly executed payment without delay and not later than 13 months from the debit of the account (clause 3.5). The text sets no shorter period for a client that is a legal person, although it treats legal persons separately elsewhere (clause 2.5.5 on opting out of payee verification). Complaints and disputes follow the bank's General Terms (clause 1.4).

m-486fc749.t: LHV Pank's contract with a business customer (General Conditions and Conditions of Payment Services Agreement, both effective 09.10.2025): the agreement comprises the General Conditions, service conditions and the Price List; the bank may amend them on one month's notice - and the Price List and service conditions 'without prior notice, unless it is prohibited by law', with 14 days for the customer to cancel; either party may end the agreement on two months' notice (one month in the 2018 version). A legal person loses the right to contest an incorrectly executed or unauthorised payment order one month after execution, against 13 months for others. Disputes go to the court of the bank's seat.

m-44dc87fe.t: Swedbank AS's page 'Become our customer' (read 5 October 2026) tells a private person who does not live in Estonia and has no Estonian ID card or passport that 'very important pre-condition for opening an account is the connection with Estonia': studying or working in Estonia, owning real estate there, or close relatives there, shown by an original document (employment contract, school certificate, marriage certificate). A person without a residence permit issued for an indefinite period or at least 12 months in Estonia, another EU state, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Great Britain or Switzerland pays EUR 250 in cash for handling the documents; the fee is not returned if the bank refuses.

m-3db2891b.t: Who may query Estonian bank-account data is set by § 63(2) of the Code of Enforcement Procedure (wording of RT I, 07.01.2026, 2, in force 23 February 2026): 'a holder of public authority who needs to use the Enforcement Register to perform a task arising from law' may join if technically able, and must first connect its system to a tool that shows each person the queries made about them - a condition not applied to security authorities. The register is both the channel for electronic seizure of debtors' accounts and for queries on data held by credit and payment institutions (§ 63(1) 3)-4)); its controller is the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs.

m-3affd661.t: Coop Pank AS's General Terms and Conditions effective as of 1 October 2025 set a default change notice of 15 days: amendments to the general terms, service conditions and the price list are made available 'at least 15 (fifteen) days before the amendments take effect', unless law or the service conditions set a longer mandatory period (clause 1.3.3); 'in justified cases' the bank may amend its price lists without advance notice (1.3.5). A client who does not accept may cancel. The client may cancel an open-ended agreement on one month's notice and the bank on two months' (13.7-13.8). The terms contain no clause on non-residents or connection with Estonia for businesses.

m-330e89c9.t: Swedbank's page for opening a business account (read 5 October 2026) gives a remote route for a company whose representative can identify digitally: 'contracts can be signed in the Internet bank by company representatives using Smart ID, Mobile ID or an ID card'; for an application sent on a working day between 8:30 and 16:00 it promises contact within an hour. Where the owners include non-residents or foreign companies, it advises an appointment at the Arter branch; the bank's checklist (26 March 2026) says such an account is not opened directly at the branch and the decision comes within 10 working days after the due diligence fee is paid, if all necessary documents are submitted.

m-324207f3.t: Luminor Bank AS's Terms of the Account Agreement in the Estonian edition marked valid from 01.01.2019 (a file luminor.ee still served on 5 September 2026) say the bank opens the account within 10 settlement days of receiving documents that meet its requirements and tells a natural person of a refusal within the same period; for a legal person there is no duty to notify. The bank 'has the right to decide at its own discretion whether to conclude an account agreement with a person who is not a resident of Estonia'. This is not shown to be the edition in force on 5 October 2026: a search index lists an English edition 'Effective from 01 March 2024' on luminor.ee, not opened (bot check).

m-2f44a2aa.t: AS SEB Pank is to become part of a single Baltic bank. Finantsinspektsioon announced on 22 May 2026 that the European Central Bank has given permission for SEB to merge its Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian subsidiaries into one legal entity to be named SEB Bank AS, with operations in Latvia and Lithuania continued by branches. Per the notice 'the merger of the banks will be completed in early 2027' and the merged bank 'will be the largest credit institution in Estonia'; local supervisors in each country remain responsible for combating money laundering. On 5 October 2026 the bank's Estonian General Terms (valid as of 01.06.2026) still name AS SEB Pank.

m-284f13f8.t: AS LHV Pank's page 'Opening a bank account for a non-resident' (read 5 October 2026) tells a business client: 'Your company must have a clear connection to Estonia' and must prove 'a need to open an account here'; a company registered in Estonia but location-independent is asked for an overview of its activities and clients and, if possible, the business plan. Documents for an Estonian-registered company: the application, passport copies of board members and of beneficial owners holding over 25%, a detailed overview of the ownership structure, and an account statement for the last 12 months. LHV does not open accounts for companies registered offshore or owned through offshore companies.

m-1f03746f.t: AS SEB Pank addresses e-residents on two pages (read 5 October 2026). Private current-account page, section 'For e-residents': 'e-residency and digital ID currently do not enable opening a bank account at AS SEB Pank without going to a bank office. Digital ID does, however, enable you to use the bank's services after opening an account.' Business onboarding FAQ: 'I'm an e-resident. Can I open a business account? Yes, you can. However, as e-residency and digital ID currently do not enable a bank account to be opened online, you must visit a branch in order to do so.' FAQ's main requirements: a clear connection to Estonia, a transparent ownership structure, an understandable business model.

m-1af1fe70.t: Swedbank's checklist of documents for opening a company account (PDF effective 26 March 2026, read 5 October 2026) asks an Estonian legal person only for a document identifying its legal representative(s). An Estonian legal person 'with non-residential connections' adds: a CV of the non-resident legal representative and/or owner, agreements or contracts with Estonian business partners, a business plan or short description, and a document identifying the beneficial owner 'if necessary'. Where the owner is a non-resident company, a register extract not older than 3 months and CVs of non-resident board members are added. The bank 'will take into account the business links with Estonia'.

m-112eb373.t: Since 1 January 2019 § 520(4) of Estonia's Commercial Code no longer names an Estonian bank for paying in share capital. Until then (wording in force from 2011) the founders of an OÜ or AS opened 'a bank account in an Estonian credit institution' in the name of the company being founded; the amendment published RT I, 20.12.2018, 1 put in 'a payment account in a credit institution or payment institution founded in a contracting state of the European Economic Area' or in its branch there. Even before 2019 the expedited procedure allowed a deposit to the registrar's account instead (§ 520(4^1)). The text in force on 5 October 2026 names payment institutions but not e-money institutions.

m-0ac1ec15.t: Swedbank AS charges a 'monthly fee for servicing a client' of EUR 50 (business price list valid from 31 August 2026) to legal persons needing regular enhanced due diligence: those registered in Cyprus, Liechtenstein or outside the European Economic Area (EEA); those with an owner or beneficial owner whose identity document was issued in Cyprus, Liechtenstein or outside the EEA 'and who is not a resident of Estonia' - defined in a footnote as a person without a passport, ID card or other identification document issued by Estonia; those with a company so registered in their structure; and those in listed activities (gambling, currency exchange, fast credit and others). Notice: 30 days.

m-06fa24f1.t: The e-Residency programme's knowledge base (article 'Banks in Estonia', updated 6 October 2025, read 5 October 2026) says Estonian banks 'are less likely to open business accounts for non-residents of Estonia (including e-residents) if their companies are large, involved in manufacturing or wholesale, acting as an intermediary to sell the services of others, only doing business in their home country or outside of the EU', and that 'E-Residency does not grant any rights to open a personal bank account in Estonia'. It advises getting a bank's 'pre-decision' through a service provider before travelling. This is the programme's description of banks' behaviour, not a rule and not the banks' text.

m-040d1c64.t: Before 15 July 2025 Estonia's basic-payment-account right was tied to the bank's own terms. § 710^1(2) of the Law of Obligations Act, in the wording in force from 10 January 2017 to 14 July 2025, obliged a credit institution to conclude a basic payment service contract with a consumer lawfully residing in the EU who had a justified interest 'proceeding from the conditions provided for in subsection 1' - that is, where the person met the law and the bank's general terms. The act published RT I, 08.07.2025, 4 removed that reference, added that proving justified interest must not be unreasonably burdensome (2^1) and barred refusal on the ground of the bank's risk appetite (5^1).

m-01da9f48.t: Swedbank names Cyprus in its fee for higher-risk firms. Its price-list section effective 27 August 2026 (read 5 October 2026) sets a 'Monthly fee for servicing a client' of EUR 50 for a legal person needing regular enhanced due diligence, including one registered in Cyprus, Liechtenstein or outside the EEA, one whose structure includes such a company, and one whose owners or beneficial owners include a person whose identity document was issued there 'and who is not a resident of Estonia' - per the list's note, a person without an identity document issued by Estonia. LHV's non-resident list sets its EU rate for a legal entity registered in an EU state 'except Cyprus, Luxembourg, Malta'.

m-01a32cbb.t: Luminor Bank AS's own pages could not be opened on 5 October 2026: the site answers with a Cloudflare challenge (HTTP 403), which was not bypassed. Second-hand, in a search tool's rendering of luminor.ee documents (not a verbatim extract), the bank may refuse an account agreement if the person has not exhaustively proven a justified interest and connection with Estonia or a legal basis for staying in the EU; the search index ties this to 'Terms and Conditions of Account Agreement Effective from 01 March 2024', a file not opened. The archived Estonian edition valid from 01.01.2019 says only that the bank decides at its own discretion whether to contract with a non-resident of Estonia.

m-fb635528.t: An Estonian e-Residency application's contents are listed in §§ 9 and 17 of Interior Minister Regulation No 20 of 24 July 2025 (text in force from 1 October 2026): a curriculum vitae; a copy of the data page of a travel document or, failing that, of another identity document of the state of citizenship or residence; the purpose of applying, the planned activity and the reasons; social-media accounts; connected Estonian or foreign businesses; any business ban; bank and payment-institution account data of the applicant and of a connected business; use of virtual currency; convictions and pending offence proceedings; visa refusals and entry bans; military or security-service history.

m-fb127c95.t: A citizen of another EU state who actually lives in Estonia is outside e-Residency: the Police and Border Guard Board issues 'an ID card … to a citizen of the European Union residing in Estonia on the basis of the right of residence', valid for up to five years and not valid as a travel document (page read 5 October 2026), and under § 20⁵(1) of the Identity Documents Act an e-resident's card goes only to a foreign citizen without a valid Estonian identity card or residence permit card. That ordinary ID card is one of the Estonian tools the e-Business Register accepts for signing; an EU citizen living elsewhere has no claim to it.

m-f60717f1.t: The e-resident's card gives no right to any service: under § 20^10(1) of Estonia's Identity Documents Act, in force since 1 December 2014 and unchanged on 5 October 2026, a provider of a public or private service may decide to provide a service to an e-resident with the card or to refuse it, may limit the service, and may set additional requirements for access, including additional data and documents or personal appearance at the provider's location. For a public service such limits may be set in two cases: to ensure purposeful use of the card, including preventing offences, or the functioning or safe use of the service (§ 20^10(2)). That a bank is such a private provider is our reading.

m-f517a7b3.t: Regulation No 28 of the Estonian Minister of the Interior of 18 September 2025 (RT I, 23.09.2025, 1), in force since 1 October 2025 and current on 5 October 2026, lists twelve states whose citizens' e-Residency applications are returned without review under § 20⁶(1¹) of the Identity Documents Act, unless an exception in § 2 of the regulation applies: Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Iran, Yemen, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, North Korea, South Sudan, Mali, Nigeria, Syria, Belarus and Russia. It was issued under § 20⁶(1²) of the Act.

m-f491a393.t: An Estonian e-Residency card must be collected in person, because fingerprints are taken at collection: it is not posted, not handed to a representative and not issued by honorary consuls. On 5 October 2026 the programme's list of pick-up locations had no location in Cyprus; it listed Athens (Greece), Tel Aviv (Israel), Cairo (Egypt) and Ankara (Türkiye) among others, and four service offices in Estonia (Tallinn, Tartu, Pärnu, Narva). The programme says a kit not collected within six months of arriving is returned to Estonia and destroyed; the Police and Border Guard Board's FAQ says a longer period can usually be agreed with the pick-up location for good reason.

m-e3ff2198.t: e-Residency was created by the Act amending the Identity Documents Act and the State Fees Act, adopted by the Riigikogu on 21 October 2014 (RT I, 29.10.2014, 1) and in force from 1 December 2014. It added the e-resident's digital identity card to the Identity Documents Act and set the state fee for reviewing an application at EUR 50. The Police and Border Guard Board, which issues the card, describes it as a digital document usable only for identification and digital signature in an electronic environment and states that it 'does not grant the right to reside in Estonia'.

m-e360109a.t: For citizens of Russia and Belarus the e-Residency restriction is older than the 2025 list and is a national measure. On 8 March 2022 the government cabinet took note that the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) would stop taking and processing e-resident digital-ID applications from those of them with no valid card; on 11 March 2022 the PPA's Director General signed order No 1.1-4.11/12 to refuse them first-time cards, per the PPA in Tallinn Administrative Court case 3-22-858 (judgment of 18 May 2023). The rule that a repeat applicant needs an earlier card and permanent economic activity in Estonia dates from 1 October 2025; in May 2025 the help page said only that renewals may take longer.

m-e1901078.t: Bill 905 SE as tabled for its first reading in the Riigikogu (text '905 SE I', filed 18 May 2026; not adopted on 5 October 2026) does not change the amount of the e-Residency state fee. Its § 8 point 1 only replaces, in § 15¹ point 1 and § 272(6) of the State Fees Act, the words for issuing a digital identity card with 'e-identimisvahendi kasutamise õiguse' (the right to use an e-identification means), leaving the EUR 150 of § 272(6) as it is; point 2 repeals § 38(6), the fee waiver for a card issued in a weighty public interest. Both would take effect on 1 March 2028 (§ 9(2)). § 9 also sets 1 September 2028, 15 November 2030, 1 March 2033 and 1 March 2034 for other points.

m-e13086c8.t: The state fee for reviewing an application for an Estonian e-resident's digital identity card is EUR 150 as of 5 October 2026, wherever the card is collected (State Fees Act § 272(6), wording in force since 1 January 2025, introduced by RT I, 20.12.2024, 1). In the version of the Act in force 1 July – 29 December 2024 the same subsection set EUR 100, and EUR 130 at a foreign mission. The fee is not refunded when the application is left unreviewed (§ 15¹ 1)). A renewal is a new application at the same EUR 150.

m-e03fdeb0.t: For citizens of Russia and Belarus the only exception in Estonian Minister of the Interior Regulation No 28 of 18 September 2025 (in force since 1 October 2025) is cumulative: the e-Residency application is not returned without review if the person was issued an e-resident's digital identity card before and has permanent economic activity in Estonia (§ 2(2)). The four wider exceptions of § 2(1) — including three consecutive years of residence in an EEA state, the United Kingdom or Switzerland with a valid residence permit — are expressly closed to Russian and Belarusian citizens.

m-dbeee0c7.t: Vendors' claims, per firms' own pages read on 5 October 2026 (not the authority's figures). Eesti Firma lists 'Company Registration using e-Residency' at EUR 375 and an all-in-one package with legal address and contact person at EUR 700, state fee included and VAT possibly extra; legal address plus contact person alone EUR 400 per year; it says the registry 'usually approves the company within one business day' and that e-Residency 'is usually issued within a few weeks'. Xolo sells its e-Residency company service (Xolo Leap) as a subscription at EUR 59, 99, 139 or 259 per month excluding VAT, virtual office included, and says 'Get your business up and running in days'.

m-d6522702.t: Estonia's state authentication service TARA, which the Information System Authority offers to institutions for adding login methods to their e-services, listed 22 country scopes for cross-border eIDAS login on 5 October 2026, Cyprus among them: its discovery endpoint gave eidas:country: es, de, it, be, lu, hr, lv, pt, lt, nl, cz, sk, mt, dk, at, pl, fr, li, si, bg, cy, se. TARA's technical specification says the supported country codes are to be read from that endpoint. This is login only; it says nothing about signing.

m-d2e5ea89.t: Applications for an e-resident's digital ID from citizens of twelve states are reviewed only under listed exceptions, per the Police and Border Guard Board (page read 5 October 2026), which cites Identity Documents Act § 20^6(1^1) and covers applications submitted after 1 October 2025. Group I - Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Iran, Yemen, DR Congo, North Korea, South Sudan, Mali, Nigeria, Syria: reviewed if, among other grounds, the applicant has lived three years running in the EEA, the UK or Switzerland on a residence permit or has permanent economic activity in Estonia. Group II - Belarus and Russia: only if the applicant already held such an ID and has permanent economic activity in Estonia.

m-cbe59212.t: The state e-Residency programme's article 'Banking basics' (updated 21 April 2026) tells e-residents that access to business banking 'is not guaranteed', that 'e-Residency doesn't give you the right to open a personal bank account in Estonia', and that Estonian banks look for two things: 'a connection to Estonia' (employees, local partners or the Estonian market) and 'a simple ownership structure'. It calls EU/EEA payment institutions and fintechs 'the most commonly used banking option among e-residents'. It dates share-capital payment from any EU/EEA account to Commercial Code changes 'in 2022'; Riigi Teataja shows § 520(4) so worded from 1 January 2019.

m-c5603f44.t: Changing the pick-up location of an Estonian e-Residency card after applying costs a further state fee, as of 5 October 2026: EUR 80 for a document issued through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (an embassy or an embassy mobile pick-up point) and EUR 10 for one issued through the Police and Border Guard Board (a service office or a Board mobile point), under State Fees Act § 272(17). The Board's table applies the amount by the initial location, whatever the new one.

m-c2da87d0.t: For citizens of the ten other listed states (Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Iran, Yemen, DR Congo, North Korea, South Sudan, Mali, Nigeria, Syria) Estonian Interior Minister Regulation No 28 of 18 September 2025 lets an e-Residency application be reviewed if at least one condition is met: at least three consecutive years of residence in an EEA state, the UK or Switzerland immediately before applying, with that state's valid residence permit; permanent economic activity in Estonia; an earlier e-resident card used for its purpose; or being an employee of an Estonian foreign mission, an honorary consul or a contracted export adviser of the foundation set up to guarantee business and housing loans.

m-b86995b8.t: The 30-day limit for an Estonian e-Residency decision comes from § 34(1) of Minister of the Interior Regulation No 20 of 24 July 2025, 'Procedure for the issue and handing over of an identity document' (RT I, 29.07.2025, 1; in force 1 August 2025): the Police and Border Guard Board issues the document or refuses within 30 days after taking into proceedings an application free of deficiencies. Under § 36 the limit may be extended, repeatedly, by up to 30 days at a time, when the grounds for issue or refusal cannot be checked or the applicant's identity verified in time; a refusal is notified within seven working days of the decision (§ 35). Estonian text in force from 1 October 2026.

m-b5a1d25d.t: A founder living outside Estonia can get an Estonian means of digital signature through the e-resident's digital ID. Per the Police and Border Guard Board (pages read 5 October 2026) it may be granted to a foreign national with a justified interest in Estonian e-services who has no Estonian residence permit, right of residence or identity card and whose citizenship is not under application restrictions; the online application needs a copy of the travel document, a photo, a CV and a payment card; state fee EUR 150, not refunded on refusal; decision within 30 days; the card reaches the pick-up location 2-5 weeks later and is collected in person. It serves only to identify and sign.

m-ae32fa8e.t: The Act of 4 June 2025 amending Estonia's Identity Documents Act (RT I, 26.06.2025, 1) also changed e-Residency vetting from 6 July 2025. The Financial Intelligence Unit joined the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), the Security Police and the Tax and Customs Board as a body supervising the use of e-resident cards (§ 20^8(1)) and may process data from the application procedure and on the card's use (§ 20^8(2^1)). The application is now submitted personally in the PPA's self-service (§ 20^7(1^1)); the wording in force until 5 July 2025 let a person file with an Estonian consular officer. Suspension of a card's certificates left the Act on 15 November 2025; revocation remains.

m-adf9e971.t: Recognition of electronic signatures between Member States is a separate rule of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (consolidated version of 18 October 2024), apart from the login duty of Art. 6. Art. 24a(1): qualified electronic signatures based on a qualified certificate issued in one Member State 'shall be recognised' as such 'in all other Member States'. Art. 27(1)–(2): a Member State requiring an advanced electronic signature for an online public-sector service must recognise advanced and qualified signatures 'in at least the formats or using methods defined in the implementing acts'. Whether the Estonian e-Business Register's signing step takes a foreign qualified signature was not tested.

m-aaa5835a.t: The legal basis of Estonian e-Residency is chapter 5² of the Identity Documents Act (Isikut tõendavate dokumentide seadus). The chapter was inserted as §§ 20⁵–20¹¹ by the act published as RT I, 29.10.2014, 1, in force since 1 December 2014; § 20¹² was added from 1 April 2015 (RT I, 23.03.2015, 1). Under § 20⁵(1), in the wording in force since 6 July 2025, the e-resident's digital identity card is a digital document issued to a citizen of a foreign state who holds no valid Estonian identity card or residence permit card and is not applying for one at the same time. Estonian text read, version in force from 1 October 2026 (RT I, 30.06.2026, 53).

m-99fe390a.t: Two dated steps in e-Residency vetting before the 2025 citizenship list. On 29 July 2020 Estonia's National Audit Office published the audit 'Effectiveness of the e-Residency programme', concluding that 'the current ex-ante and ex-post controls do not ensure that the participants of the programme are law-abiding': 48 e-residents with Finnish citizenship had held a valid criminal penalty in Finland when they applied. From 1 April 2021 an amended regulation of the Minister of the Interior makes applicants supply additional data: per the Police and Border Guard Board, on misdemeanour proceedings, prohibitions on business, and their own and related businesses' bank accounts.

m-9575d048.t: The state fee for an e-resident's digital ID application, by the dated versions of § 272(6) of the State Fees Act and the amendment notes under it: EUR 50 from 1 December 2014; EUR 50, or EUR 80 at a foreign mission, from 1 April 2015 (RT I, 23.03.2015, 1); EUR 100 in both cases from 1 February 2016 (RT I, 15.12.2015, 1); EUR 100, or EUR 130 at a foreign mission, from 6 January 2020 (RT I, 31.12.2019, 1); EUR 150 from 1 January 2025 (raised by the Act of 12 June 2024, RT I, 29.06.2024, 3; the separate foreign-mission amount deleted by the Act of 4 December 2024, RT I, 20.12.2024, 1). It is EUR 150 in the version in force on 5 October 2026.

m-901f22ac.t: The state fee for examining an application for an e-resident's digital identity card is EUR 150 as in force on 5 October 2026 (State Fees Act § 272(6), wording of RT I, 20.12.2024, 1, in force from 1 January 2025); the versions of the Act already published for 1 November 2026, 1 January 2027 and 1 July 2027 keep that amount. The fee is not refunded if the application is left unexamined (§ 15¹ p 1), and none is charged where the card is issued on grounds of weighty public interest (§ 38(6)).

m-7ac9931f.t: The Estonian authorities state what e-Residency does not give (pages read 5 October 2026). Police and Border Guard Board: the e-resident's digital ID 'can only be used to identify a person and provide a digital signature in an electronic environment' and 'does not grant the right to reside in Estonia'. The programme: the card 'is not a travel document' and gives no right to enter any country, including Estonia; 'E-Residency does not affect your personal tax residency'; it 'does not guarantee a business banking account' and does not let a person open a personal bank account in Estonia or other European countries.

m-7a7ebac3.t: Every Estonian e-Residency applicant undergoes a background check by the Police and Border Guard Board, which according to the programme assesses compliance with the law, prior and current criminal record and any circumstance that would justify refusing a visa or temporary residence permit or imposing an entry ban, and may ask for information on business activities and public social-media accounts (article updated 21 April 2026). Under § 20⁸(1) of the Identity Documents Act, use of the card is supervised by the Police and Border Guard Board, the Internal Security Service, the Financial Intelligence Unit and the Tax and Customs Board.

m-6ec508c1.t: On 5 October 2026 the unofficial English translations on Riigi Teataja lagged the Estonian texts of three acts used for the founder-abroad questions: the versions in force from 1 October 2026 of the Identity Documents Act (RT I, 30.06.2026, 53), the Income Tax Act (RT I, 09.07.2026, 66) and the Aliens Act (RT I, 30.06.2026, 103) had no translation linked, while their preceding versions (in force until 30 September 2026) did. The current versions of the Social Tax Act, the Commercial Register Act and the State Fees Act each had a linked translation. All acts in this research were read in Estonian.

m-68463875.t: Under § 20¹⁰(1) of the Estonian Identity Documents Act any provider of a public or private service may decide whether to serve a person identified by an e-resident's digital identity card, may refuse or limit the service, or may set additional conditions for access, including asking for further data and documents or personal appearance at the provider's premises (wording in force since 1 December 2014). The card therefore creates no right to a bank account or to any particular e-service.

m-6457d81a.t: An application for Estonian e-Residency is submitted by the applicant personally in the self-service environment of the Police and Border Guard Board (Identity Documents Act § 20⁷(1¹), in force since 6 July 2025); the programme's knowledge base (updated 4 September 2026) and the Board's FAQ add that applications submitted through intermediaries such as legal bureaus or service providers are not accepted. According to the knowledge-base article, the applicant uploads a colour copy of a passport or EU identity card issued by the country of citizenship and valid for at least two more months, a digital photo, a motivation statement and a CV, and pays by Visa or Mastercard.

m-5820d365.t: The Estonian e-Residency programme's own figures for the whole path, as published on 5 October 2026: e-Residency application EUR 150 (review 30 days, card delivery 2–5 weeks, plus travel to a pick-up point); legal address and licensed contact person EUR 200–400 per year (1 day – 1 week); company registration state fee EUR 265 (15 minutes – 1 hour online) — in State Fees Act § 62(2) that is the expedited-procedure fee, the ordinary fee being EUR 200; bank or fintech account EUR 0–200 (1 hour – 1 week); bookkeeping from EUR 50 per month. Its knowledge base (updated 29 October 2025) puts first-year costs at 'Ca €600 (DIY)' and 'Ca €1300 (with accounting support)'.

m-4ab98f4d.t: Vendors' claims, per firms' own pages read on 5 October 2026 (not the authority's figures). Unicount advertises Estonian company formation at EUR 296 including VAT, the EUR 265 state fee included, 'to get your company registered in 1 working day'; its virtual office at EUR 199 per year plus VAT 'is required alongside formation', and accounting plans start at EUR 29 per month plus VAT. 1Office advertises 'a one-time payment of €315' and EUR 15 per month thereafter, including the state fee, a business address in Tallinn and contact-person services, and says registration 'typically takes between one and five working days once all documentation is in order'.

m-4095a41c.t: The Identity Documents Act states the purpose of the e-resident's digital identity card in § 20⁵(2): to promote the development of the Estonian economy, science, education or culture by making it possible to use e-services with an Estonian digital document (wording in force since 1 December 2014, unchanged in the version in force from 1 October 2026). Under § 20⁶(3) 2) the issue of the card may be refused when it is not consistent with that purpose.

m-366349f4.t: Before the listing regulation of 1 October 2025, Estonia's stop on first-time e-Residency for Russian and Belarusian citizens rested not on a published list but on two decisions the Police and Border Guard Board cited in court (Tallinn Administrative Court, 18 May 2023, case 3-22-858): a government cabinet decision of 8 March 2022, which took note that the Board would stop accepting and processing applications from citizens of both states without a valid card, and its Director General's order No 1.1-4.11/12 of 11 March 2022. Refusals were issued under Identity Documents Act § 20⁶(3) 2). Valid cards stayed valid (ERR, 9 March 2022). The statutory ground, § 20⁶(1¹), took effect on 6 July 2025.

m-34b7d224.t: On 15 March 2022 the Estonian Police and Border Guard Board, by decision No 15.3-24/23-1, refused e-resident's digital identity cards to a Russian citizen who had applied on 28 February 2022 and to 227 other applicants, relying on Identity Documents Act § 20⁶(3) 2) (issue not consistent with the card's purpose). The Tallinn Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint on 18 May 2023 (case 3-22-858): the Board has wide discretion, and the card is a benefit made available to a person, not a right, and not a precondition for doing business. The judgment entered into force on 20 June 2023, per Riigi Teataja's register of court decisions.

m-306c5bee.t: The Estonian Police and Border Guard Board explains 'permanent economic activity in Estonia', the condition in the e-Residency exceptions for citizens of listed states (page read 5 October 2026): the applicant owns a company in Estonia or has a direct connection with one, for example as a management board member; the company must be active, generate sales revenue and/or employ staff, and pay taxes to the Estonian state, with annual reports, tax returns and beneficial-ownership information duly filed. A person who once received a positive decision but never collected the card does not count as previously issued one.

m-2aee0010.t: An Estonian e-resident's digital ID issued since 1 May 2018 is valid for five years (Police and Border Guard Board page, read 5 October 2026; Identity Documents Act § 20³(1): a digital identity card is issued with a validity of up to five years, wording in force since 1 May 2018). There is no extension: renewal is a new application through the Board's environment with the 'Renewal applicant' option and a new EUR 150 state fee; the programme advises applying 2–3 months before expiry and says the Board estimates about 10 days on average for renewals where the e-resident's obligations are fulfilled.

m-2181c828.t: E-residents 'can use the e-services of the Estonian Tax and Customs Board under the same conditions as persons holding an Estonian ID-card', and 'the language of tax proceedings is Estonian', per the Board's page for non-residents and e-residents (last updated 4 May 2026). The same page observes that the management board of an e-resident's company 'is usually located in a foreign country and in most cases, the company does not have a permanent establishment in Estonia where documents addressed to the company can be sent', which is why a contact person is needed.

m-1b90732a.t: e-Residency has had statutory citizenship limits since 2025. § 20^6(1^1) of the Identity Documents Act (added by RT I, 26.06.2025, 1; in force 6 July 2025) says an application is returned unreviewed if the applicant is a citizen of a state with a higher money-laundering or terrorist-financing risk or with which Estonia has no justice, security or law-enforcement cooperation, unless an exception set by the minister under (1^2) applies. The Interior Minister's Regulation No 28 of 18 September 2025 (RT I, 23.09.2025, 1), in force 1 October 2025, unamended on 5 October 2026, lists Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Iran, Yemen, DR Congo, North Korea, South Sudan, Mali, Nigeria, Syria, Belarus, Russia.

m-1b0f60c0.t: The Estonian Police and Border Guard Board adds evidence rules to the e-Residency exceptions for citizens of the ten listed states other than Russia and Belarus (page read 5 October 2026): under the three-year EEA, UK or Swiss residence exception 'a valid residence permit must be presented both when applying for an e-resident's digital ID and upon receipt of the digital ID', and the applicant must be ready to prove the three years; under the earlier-card exception the applicant 'must explain and provide evidence' of how the card's use relates to the development of Estonia's economy, science, education or culture. These conditions are the Board's, not the wording of Regulation No 28.

m-1a6aad09.t: Since 6 July 2025 § 20⁶(1¹) of the Estonian Identity Documents Act requires an e-resident's digital identity card application to be returned without review when the applicant is a citizen of a state with a higher money-laundering or terrorist-financing risk, or of a state with which Estonia has no judicial, security or law-enforcement cooperation, unless an exception set under § 20⁶(1²) applies. The list of states and the exceptions are set by a regulation of the minister in charge, agreed with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (§ 20⁶(1²)–(1³), inserted by RT I, 26.06.2025, 1). The first list took effect on 1 October 2025; the police apply the rule to applications submitted after that date.

m-1a44e0b8.t: An e-resident's bank relationship in Estonia hangs on the digital ID staying valid. Finantsinspektsioon's advisory guidelines on preventing money laundering (version valid from 1 May 2024, point 6.3.2) give a credit or financial institution 'the right to cancel the long-term contract serving as a basis for a business relationship extraordinarily and without notice' where issue of the person's e-resident digital identity card is refused, its validity is suspended or it is declared invalid under § 20^6(2) or (3) of the Identity Documents Act. AS SEB Pank's General Terms valid as of 01.06.2026 list the same event among grounds for extraordinary cancellation without notice (clause 118.28).

m-091a442e.t: The Estonian Police and Border Guard Board states that the decision to issue or refuse an e-resident's digital ID is taken within 30 days of the application, and that the card then takes 2–5 weeks to reach the chosen pick-up location unless a mobile pick-up point was chosen (page read 5 October 2026). The programme's own knowledge base says the review 'generally takes 30 calendar days, but PBGB may extend it if necessary' and that most e-residents collect the card within 2–4 months after applying (article updated 4 September 2026).

m-076e97f7.t: Before the list of 1 October 2025, repeat e-Residency applications by Russian citizens were decided one by one. A Russian citizen who held the card in 2019–2024 applied again on 4 June 2024; the Police and Border Guard Board refused him on 12 June under Identity Documents Act § 20⁶(3) 2): in five years he had no link with any Estonian company and, by the logs, had not used the card for three years. The Tallinn Administrative Court dismissed his complaint on 28 February 2025 (case 3-24-1815, in force 1 April 2025), adding that there is no subjective right to the card. The Board told the court it no longer issues cards to first-time Russian applicants and checks repeat ones more thoroughly.

m-043ff108.t: No change to the state fee for an e-resident's digital ID application is enacted for a later date, as far as Riigi Teataja showed on 5 October 2026: the consolidated versions of the State Fees Act already published for 1 November-31 December 2026 (RT I, 11.07.2026, 167) and for 1 January-30 June 2027 (RT I, 11.07.2026, 168) both keep § 272(6) at EUR 150, the amount in force since 1 January 2025. Riigi Teataja's search returns the second of these as the version valid on 2 January 2027; an Act adopted after 11 July 2026 and not yet consolidated would not show in them.

m-01a2c1b4.t: The Government's explanatory memorandum to bill 572 SE (initiated 30 January 2025, adopted 4 June 2025), which created the citizenship-based stop for e-Residency applications, gives the programme's risk record: negative decisions on first applications rose from 2% in 2018 to 8% in 2023; cards revoked after follow-up checks numbered 29 in 2020, 89 in 2021, 224 in 2022 and 267 in 2023; since June 2022 the Police and Border Guard Board runs an automatic follow-up check. It says background checks alone do not reduce risk enough for states with which Estonia has no judicial, security or law-enforcement cooperation, and that existing cards stay valid until expiry or revocation.

m-009a55cc.t: A bill pending in the Riigikogu on 5 October 2026 would end the in-person card pick-up for Estonian e-Residency. Bill 905 SE, amending the Identity Documents Act, was initiated by the Government on 7 May 2026; its first reading was on the plenary agenda of 1 June 2026 and it stood at the second-reading stage, not adopted. Per the Riigikogu's summary, e-residents' identity would be verified remotely by biometrics from March 2027, and from March 2028 a card-free 'e-identification means' would replace the digital ID card, the right to use it granted by the Police and Border Guard Board. The bill's § 9 sets 2 March 2027 and 1 March 2028 for the main provisions.

m-fd60df77.t: An Estonian bank must refuse or end a relationship it cannot vet: § 42 of the AML act (in force 21 July 2026) forbids establishing a business relationship when the bank is unable to apply due diligence or suspects money laundering, and treats a customer's refusal to give information or documents as a fundamental breach obliging the bank to terminate extraordinarily and report to the Financial Intelligence Unit. § 43(2) adds a ground specific to e-residents: the bank may terminate 'extraordinarily and without advance notification' when an e-resident's digital identity card is refused, suspended or declared invalid under § 20^6(2) or (3) of the Identity Documents Act.

m-f9cdd790.t: A cash ceiling will reach Estonian merchants through EU law: Article 80 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 lets persons trading in goods or providing services accept or make a cash payment 'only up to an amount of EUR 10 000', in one operation or several linked ones, and the regulation applies from 10 July 2027 (Article 90). Member States may set lower limits after consulting the European Central Bank; none was found in Estonian law on 5 October 2026. The limit does not apply to payments between natural persons not acting professionally or to payments and deposits at credit institutions, e-money issuers and payment service providers.

m-f2e12e39.t: On 19 February 2019 the management board of Finantsinspektsioon issued a precept prohibiting the Estonian branch of Danske Bank A/S from operating: the bank had to cease its activities in Estonia within eight months of receipt, return all deposits in full and transfer its loan contracts, under a penalty of EUR 100,000 per day for each breach up to 10 per cent of the bank's total net turnover. At the end of 2018 the branch had around 14,700 depositors and 12,300 borrowers in Estonia. The supervisor said it had already forced the branch to end its business serving non-resident customers in 2015, after on-site inspections in 2014.

m-eda54fc3.t: Estonia's AML act (§ 19(1), in force 21 July 2026) requires due diligence when a business relationship is established, for an occasional transaction from EUR 15,000, when earlier data are in doubt and on any suspicion of money laundering. The six measures of § 20(1): identify the customer and verify the data from a reliable independent source; identify the representative and his powers; identify the beneficial owner and understand the ownership and control structure; understand the purpose of the relationship; establish whether the person is politically exposed; monitor the relationship. Measures 1-5 precede the relationship 'unless otherwise provided' (§ 19(5)); § 27 has the exceptions.

m-eaaa7d51.t: A company-formation or virtual-office provider is itself an AML-obliged entity in Estonia: § 2(1) 9) of the AML act (in force 21 July 2026) lists 'providers of trust and company services', which § 8 defines to include founding a company or other legal person and letting an address be used as its seat. § 19(2^4), in force since 15 March 2022, makes such a provider apply due diligence on each occasion it provides the § 8 clause 1 service (foundation, including steps related to a transfer of shareholding). The activity needs an authorisation from the Financial Intelligence Unit (§ 70(1) 2), § 71) - a duty older than the 2017 act: § 52(1) 2) of the previous act already carried it in 2016.

m-e523f558.t: § 2 of Estonia's AML act (RahaPTS, in force 21 July 2026) covers, among others: credit and financial institutions; gambling operators except organisers of commercial lotteries; real-estate brokers; traders in cash deals from EUR 10,000; precious-metal wholesalers; auditors, accountants and tax advisers; providers of trust and company services; pawnbrokers; art dealers (payments from EUR 10,000); notaries, attorneys, bailiffs and bankruptcy trustees in listed transactions. 'Financial institution' (§ 6(2)) includes payment service providers - except payment initiation and account information service providers - e-money institutions and, since 30 December 2024, crypto-asset service providers.

m-e3287404.t: Finantsinspektsioon's own figures for the share of non-residents in Estonian banking, in its annual reports: 19.1% at the end of 2014, 16.2% in 2015, 11.7% in 2017, 7.9% at the end of 2018 and 10.0% at the end of 2019 - called 'non-resident deposits' for 2017 and 2018, non-resident clients or 'non-residents in banking' elsewhere. The 2019 report adds that the share of clients from very high-risk jurisdictions fell from 8.5% to 0.3%, and that deposits of clients from outside the EU were 'exactly 1%' of banking-sector deposits at end-2019 against 11.4% in 2014. Eesti Pank, counting only foreign non-financial companies and households, put the share at a peak of 21% in 2012 and 8.5% by 2017.

m-dd3de9a5.t: A bill widening the data powers of Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit is not law on 5 October 2026. The act amending the AML act and the International Sanctions Act (bill 640, initiated by the Government on 5 May 2025), which concerns the data-processing functions of the Unit's database, was passed by the Riigikogu on 19 June 2025; the President refused to proclaim it on 3 July 2025; on 17 September 2025 the Riigikogu did not re-adopt it unchanged and sent it back for a new procedure. The Riigikogu register shows it under reconsideration, with finance-committee sittings up to 12 May 2026 and no further vote.

m-cede7cc4.t: Finantsinspektsioon names the share of non-resident clients at a bank as a risk indicator in its anti-money-laundering supervision. Its page 'Countering Money Laundering' (last edited 19 March 2019) states that the share of non-residents in the Estonian banking market fell from 20% in 2014 to 7.9% at the end of 2018, and the share of deposits held by offshore clients from 10% to below 1%, and that several banks 'have either ceased or essentially restricted the provision of services to non-residents with non-transparent backgrounds or businesses'. The page does not say whether the 20% and 7.9% are shares of deposits, of clients or of turnover.

m-c3579ec3.t: Estonian law sets no general ceiling on cash payments as of 5 October 2026; sector acts require non-cash settlement in the import, wholesale and export of alcohol and the wholesale of tobacco products. The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act sets thresholds for checks and reports: a trader paid, or paying, at least EUR 10,000 in cash - in one payment or linked payments within a year - becomes an obliged entity and must apply due diligence (§ 2(1) point 5, § 19(2)), and an obliged entity other than a credit institution must report to the Financial Intelligence Unit within two working days any transaction in which more than EUR 32,000 is paid in cash (§ 49(3)).

m-c16501de.t: Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit (Rahapesu Andmebüroo) left the police on 1 January 2021. Under the 2017 wording of § 53 of the AML act it was 'an independent structural unit of the Police and Border Guard Board', its head appointed by the police Director General. The act of 17 June 2020 (RT I, 10.07.2020, 1), reworded before commencement by the act of 12 November 2020 (RT I, 21.11.2020, 1), made it a governmental authority in the area of government of the Ministry of Finance, with its own budget and a head appointed by the Government for five years on the Finance Minister's proposal; § 98^1 transferred functions, staff, files and pending proceedings on that date.

m-bd95c702.t: The make-up of non-residents' deposits changed between 2014 and 2025, in Eesti Pank's year-end table of deposits by customer group (EUR million): non-resident non-financial corporations held 2,026.6 in 2014, 1,262.3 in 2016, 564.9 in 2017, 257.8 in 2018, 131.4 in 2019 and 186.2 in 2025; non-resident households held 561.8 in 2014, 736.4 in 2018, 1,247.6 in 2019, 2,157.3 in 2022 and 3,923.5 in 2025; non-resident financial institutions held 178.0 in 2014, 704.5 in 2017, 2,162.7 in 2021 and 1,437.2 in 2025. By our arithmetic the corporate deposits are down 91% from 2014, and households hold 71% of non-residents' deposits at the end of 2025 against 20% in 2014.

m-bd74eaae.t: Records under Estonia's AML act (§ 47, in force 21 July 2026): identification documents or their copies, registered data and the documents on which the business relationship was founded are kept five years after the relationship ends (Estonian text; the translation adds 'no less than'); transaction documents and the data behind a report to the Financial Intelligence Unit for at least five years after the transaction or report. Copies need not be kept if the person was identified by electronic identification and trust services or the document stays available in a state database. The data are deleted when the term ends; a supervisor's precept may extend retention by at most five more years.

m-bba68a54.t: Estonia's AML act (§ 36(2), in force 21 July 2026) makes enhanced due diligence mandatory in six cases: doubts about the data, the documents or the identification of the beneficial owner; a politically exposed person (exception: § 38(5)); a customer from, resident or seated in a high-risk third country, or the payee's payment provider seated there; a country without effective AML systems per credible sources, or on the EU list of non-cooperative tax jurisdictions (until 31.12.2021: 'a low tax rate territory'); a link to a country with significant corruption or under sanctions, where the § 31(3) scheme is not used; crypto-asset transfers to or from a self-hosted address (since 30.12.2024).

m-b3675e74.t: Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit reports that money can pass to the state without a criminal case: per a notice on its website read on 5 October 2026, 'On 14 August 2026, a ruling of the Tallinn Circuit Court became final following a decision of the Supreme Court, allowing cash linked to suspicions of money laundering to be transferred into state ownership without criminal proceedings.' The statutory route is § 57(7) of the AML act: where the owner is not identified within one year of a restriction, or the possessor gives the property up, the administrative court may permit its transfer to state ownership.

m-af557126.t: The 2020 sanction on Swedbank was Swedish, not Estonian. On 19 March 2020 Sweden's Finansinspektionen gave Swedbank AB a warning and an administrative fine of SEK 4 billion on the findings of two investigations: its governance of money-laundering risk in the Baltic subsidiaries and its Swedish operations. Estonia's Finantsinspektsioon, after its own inspection of April to mid-November 2019, issued a precept to Swedbank AS to bring its anti-money-laundering risk controls into line with the law. Its notice announces no Estonian fine: it says the Prosecutor's Office was investigating and that, double jeopardy not being permitted, it had ended its own misdemeanour investigation in November 2019.

m-adc73ec7.t: In Eesti Pank's monthly table of deposits by residence (EUR million, all customer groups, last updated 24 September 2026; months from December 2017 to August 2026 read), non-residents' deposits were smallest in amount on 30 November 2018, 1,224.1 of 17,631.5, and smallest as a share on 30 April 2019, 1,233.5 of 18,159.2, or 6.8% by our arithmetic. The latest month, 31 August 2026, shows 5,326.2 of 34,524.6 (15.4%), after 5,408.2 of 34,135.2 on 31 July 2026 (15.8%) and 5,552.2 of 33,494.6 at the end of 2025 (16.6%).

m-ac8c29ab.t: Eesti Pank's table 'Stock of deposits by customer group, residence, currency and maturity' (EUR million, all customer groups, currencies and maturities; last updated 24 September 2026) gives non-residents' deposits and the total at year-end: 2012 2,473.9 of 12,610.7; 2013 2,472.1 of 13,650.0; 2014 2,768.8 of 14,878.6; 2015 2,435.1 of 15,535.1; 2016 2,003.2 of 16,333.2; 2017 1,914.6 of 17,066.9; 2018 1,278.3 of 17,720.6; 2019 1,808.5 of 19,857.5; 2020 2,491.1 of 23,917.4; 2021 3,881.9 of 27,882.4; 2022 3,617.7 of 28,060.1; 2023 4,330.0 of 29,452.6; 2024 4,956.1 of 31,996.6; 2025 5,552.2 of 33,494.6.

m-aa76af91.t: Estonia's AML act tells a bank to decide in writing whom it will not serve. § 10 (text of 21 July 2026) defines 'risk appetite' as the exposure the obliged entity is prepared to assume, set by senior management in writing; it must name at least the kinds of persons with whom it wishes to avoid business relationships (§ 10(3)), and the management board of a credit or financial institution also decides whether to deal with persons from outside the EEA (§ 10(4)). The original 2017 text of § 10(4) added 'or with e-residents'; the amendment in force 10 September 2020 (RT I, 10.07.2020, 1) deleted those words. A refusal on this ground is a policy the act makes the bank set, not a statutory ban.

m-a3745fb2.t: Estonia's financial supervisor lists the lack of a link with Estonia among customer-risk indicators for payment services. Annex 1 (money-laundering risks specific to Estonia; repeated in Annex 2 on terrorist financing; both dated 19 November 2018) to Finantsinspektsioon's advisory guidelines 'Organisational solutions and preventive measures for credit and financial institutions to take against money laundering and terrorist financing' — Management Board resolution No 1.1-7/172 of 26 November 2018, shown on its site on 5 October 2026 as effective since 1 March 2019 — names the case where 'the person has no connection with Estonia, but they still want to receive the service in Estonia'.

m-9eea3cbb.t: The Estonian criminal investigation into Swedbank AS ended without charges on 29 February 2024. Swedbank's release of that day says the bank 'has today been informed that the investigation conducted by the State Prosecutor's Office shows that no crime has been committed' and that it concerned 2014-2016; its release of 24 March 2022 had reported the bank served with a suspicion of money laundering. ERR, reporting the Prosecutor General's press conference of 29 February 2024, puts the suspicions at over EUR 100 million and the period at 2011-2016, and says the case was closed as the criminal origin of the money could not be proven, though breaches of anti-money-laundering rules were found.

m-9e8b2b4a.t: Finantsinspektsioon's advisory AML guidelines of 26 November 2018 (on its site as effective since 1 March 2019; read 5 October 2026) name e-residents twice: point 3.2.6.1 has an institution's risk-appetite document determine 'whether and to what extent the obliged entity intends to establish business relationships with entities from states outside the European Economic Area or with e-residents' and by which services and channels; point 6.3.2.1 gives the right to end a business relationship extraordinarily without notice if a person 'is not issued an e-resident's digital identity card, its validity is suspended or it is declared invalid' under § 20⁶(2) or (3) of the Identity Documents Act.

m-9da513bd.t: Besides the EU list of high-risk third countries, Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit publishes its own 'List of Countries with a Higher Risk of Terrorist Financing', an appendix to its Guidelines on the Characteristics of Suspicious Transactions dated 18 September 2024 - still the version linked from its Estonian and English guideline pages on 5 October 2026. It names 32 jurisdictions: 11 on EU or FATF assessments (the United Arab Emirates among them) and 21 on the assessment of national competent authorities, including Turkey, Egypt, Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Uzbekistan and the North Caucasus Federal District of Russia. The document says the list is reviewed once a year.

m-9139a840.t: Under § 20(2) of Estonia's AML act (in force 21 July 2026) an obliged entity, to understand the purpose of a business relationship, must identify 'inter alia, the permanent seat, place of business or place of residence, profession or field of activity, main contracting partners, payment habits', whether the customer acts for another and, for a legal person, its experience. Banks' questionnaires on partners and payments trace to this clause (inference). The act does not require a 'connection with Estonia': the phrase occurs nowhere in its Estonian or English text (full-text search, 5 October 2026); § 10(4) only has a bank's board decide whether to serve persons from non-EEA countries.

m-8d17b10e.t: The Estonian criminal case over Danske Bank's branch that reached court is against individuals. As reported by the public broadcaster ERR, on 17 April 2023 the Prosecutor's Office charged six former employees of the branch's foreign-banking unit with large-scale money laundering in 2007-2015, to the tune of at least USD 1.6 billion and EUR 6 million, citing eight predicate crimes committed in Russia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Switzerland, the United States and Iran; nearly EUR 10 million of property was identified and seized. ERR reported the trial starting in Harju County Court on 13 November 2023. No judgment in that case was found in web searches in English and Estonian on 5 October 2026.

m-896e1894.t: After the Danske Bank case Finantsinspektsioon used its anti-money-laundering powers against the large domestic banks as well, by its own announcements: on 19 March 2020 it issued a precept to Swedbank AS to improve its risk control systems, in an investigation run in parallel with the Swedish supervisor, which fined the parent Swedbank AB four billion kronor; on 25 June 2020 it issued a precept to AS SEB Pank and fined it one million euros for failings in 2017-2019 in customer due diligence and in reporting suspicions to the Financial Intelligence Unit; on 19 October 2023 it fined AS LHV Pank 900,000 euros and issued a precept over correspondent-banking controls.

m-7c56a1f9.t: Share of non-residents in the stock of deposits at banks in Estonia, computed from Eesti Pank's year-end table (all customer groups): 19.6% in 2012, 18.1% in 2013, 18.6% in 2014, 15.7% in 2015, 12.3% in 2016, 11.2% in 2017, 7.2% in 2018, 9.1% in 2019, 10.4% in 2020, 13.9% in 2021, 12.9% in 2022, 14.7% in 2023, 15.5% in 2024 and 16.6% in 2025. The lowest year-end value is 2018; in the monthly series of the same table the low is 6.8% on 30 April 2019. The share then rose in every year but 2022; at the end of 2025 it is above its 2015 level, on a deposit stock 2.2 times as large, and on 31 August 2026 it is 15.4%.

m-7757a289.t: Fines under Estonia's AML act were raised from 1 November 2023 (RT I, 17.03.2023, 2). In the original 2017 text failure to identify a customer (§ 84) cost a legal person 'up to 400 000 euros'. In the text in force on 5 October 2026 the same breach carries up to EUR 1,000,000 or twice the benefit gained, and for an entity under Finantsinspektsioon's supervision up to EUR 5,000,000, twice the benefit, or - for a legal person - up to 10 per cent of the consolidated turnover of the person or its group. The limitation period for these misdemeanours is three years (§ 97(2), from 30 December 2024).

m-6d50f9e2.t: Danske Bank's own press release of 19 September 2018 on the investigation led by the law firm Bruun & Hjejle into its Estonian branch states that around 10,000 customers were identified as belonging to the non-resident portfolio, that the investigation covered around 15,000 customers 'with non-resident characteristics' who made around 9.5 million payments, and that for those 15,000 customers 'the total flow of payments amounted to around EUR 200 billion' over 2007-2015. The bank adds that it is 'not able to provide an accurate estimate of the amount of suspicious transactions'; some 6,200 customers had been analysed by then and 'the vast majority' found suspicious.

m-6518b0e1.t: Estonia's anti-money-laundering statute is the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act (Rahapesu ja terrorismi rahastamise tõkestamise seadus, RahaPTS), passed 26 October 2017, RT I, 17.11.2017, 2, in force from 27 November 2017 (§ 19(3) and §§ 76-80 from 1 September 2018, §§ 81 and 95 from 1 January 2019). The consolidated text in force on 5 October 2026 is RT I, 11.07.2026, 93, in force from 21 July 2026; its header lists 20 amending acts. The two 2026 acts concern savings and loan associations (RT I, 13.02.2026, 1: § 72(2^1), § 118^6) and listed companies (RT I, 11.07.2026, 2: the lower-risk factor of § 34(2) 1) and § 76(3) 3)); §§ 19-22, 31 and 36-43 are untouched.

m-642590a0.t: The European Central Bank withdrew the credit-institution licence of the Estonian bank Versobank AS on 26 March 2018 on a proposal that Finantsinspektsioon filed on 8 February 2018. The stated reason was significant and long-lasting breaches of law, above all in the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, found in repeated inspections in 2015-2017; legal basis § 17(1) clauses 2, 5, 12, 14 and 15 of the Credit Institutions Act. All transactions and payouts were suspended the same day, the Guarantee Fund (Tagatisfond) was notified, and the supervisor applied to court for compulsory dissolution and a liquidator.

m-60290db2.t: Supervision of Estonia's AML act is split by § 64 (in force 21 July 2026). The default supervisor is the Financial Intelligence Unit (Rahapesu Andmebüroo). Finantsinspektsioon supervises the credit and financial institutions under its financial supervision, in all their activities covered by the act. The Bar Association's board supervises attorneys; the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, which may delegate to the Chamber of Notaries, supervises notaries. Applied: a bank or a payment institution licensed by Finantsinspektsioon answers to it, while a company-formation agent, an accountant or a financial institution authorised by the Unit itself (§ 70) answers to the Unit.

m-5b22c1f7.t: To enforce a precept under Estonia's AML act the supervisor may impose a levy (§ 65). For a credit or financial institution that is a legal person: up to EUR 32,000 the first time and up to EUR 100,000 each further time for the same duty, in total not more than the higher of EUR 5,000,000 or 10 per cent of its annual turnover - amounts in the act since 27 November 2017 - or, added from 1 November 2023 (RT I, 17.03.2023, 2), twice the benefit derived from the breach or the harm prevented; for a legal person outside the financial sector up to EUR 32,000. The supervisor may inspect the place of business, examine documents without limitation and demand information without a visit (§ 66).

m-5ac49e0f.t: Versobank's challenge to the loss of its licence failed in both EU courts. The European Central Bank replaced its decision of 26 March 2018 with one of 17 July 2018; on 6 October 2021 the General Court found no need to adjudicate on the first decision (T-351/18) and dismissed the action against the second (T-584/18); the Court of Justice dismissed Versobank AS's appeal on 7 September 2023 (C-803/21 P). The Court confirmed that, although Member States remain competent to apply anti-money-laundering rules, the ECB has exclusive competence to withdraw the authorisation of any credit institution, whatever its size - here on breaches that Finantsinspektsioon had found from 2015 on.

m-50ed3318.t: Versobank AS lost its banking licence by a decision of the European Central Bank of 26 March 2018, on a proposal from Finantsinspektsioon received on 8 February 2018 after inspections had found recurring breaches of anti-money-laundering rules from 2015 and a precept of 8 August 2016 had not been fully complied with. After a review requested by the main shareholder the ECB replaced it with a decision of 17 July 2018, again withdrawing the licence. On 6 October 2021 the General Court found no need to adjudicate on the action against the first decision (T-351/18) and dismissed the action against the second (T-584/18); the Court of Justice dismissed the appeal on 7 September 2023 (C-803/21 P).

m-4e243e8b.t: Estonia's AML act defines a politically exposed person without a domestic/foreign split (§ 9^1, in force 21 July 2026): heads of state and government, ministers, MPs, members of party governing bodies, supreme-court judges, the auditor general, central-bank board members, the Chancellor of Justice (since 24.04.2021), ambassadors, senior officers, board members of state-owned enterprises, heads of international organisations, their family and close associates. § 41 adds senior-management approval, source of wealth and funds and closer monitoring; for a person from or living in an EEA state only where a higher-risk factor exists (§ 38(5)). After office the risk counts for at least 12 months.

m-3e7fbfdb.t: Estonia's AML act holds no national list of high-risk third countries: § 3 clause 18 (in force 21 July 2026) defines the term as a country named in the Commission delegated act under Article 9(2) of Directive (EU) 2015/849. Contact with such a country triggers the six measures of § 39(1): more data on the customer and beneficial owner, the planned relationship, the origin of funds and wealth, the reasons for transactions, senior-management permission and tighter monitoring. § 37(4) adds geographic risk factors: weak AML systems or significant corruption per 'credible sources', sanctions or embargoes (for example by the EU or UN) and support for terrorism (as identified by the EU or UN).

m-3bbe8a04.t: Estonia's AML act lets a bank open an account before due diligence is complete in two cases (§ 27, in force 21 July 2026). An account may be opened before measures 1-3 of § 20(1) if no transaction can be made with the funds until they are applied. A credit institution may also open an account for a company being founded, on personal data verified automatically by the registrar or through a notary, provided the share-capital contribution arrives through an account at a credit institution operating in an EEA state, and the account is not debited before registration and measures 1-5; the representatives must conclude a settlement agreement within six months (§ 27(2), in force 1 February 2023).

m-34baaacb.t: For Danske Bank itself the Estonian-branch case closed in stages. Its company announcement of 13 December 2022 reports 'final coordinated resolutions' with the US Department of Justice, the US SEC and Denmark's Special Crime Unit over the non-resident portfolio of its former Estonian branch: USD 2.06 billion in total (about DKK 15.3 billion) - USD 1,209 million, USD 178.6 million and DKK 4,749 million respectively - with a guilty plea in the United States to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and three years' probation, which the bank confirmed concluded on 15 December 2025. Civil litigation was left out, and a French investigation ended only on 18 September 2024, settled for EUR 6.33 million.

m-2ae2e9dc.t: Swedbank's release of 24 March 2022 says its Estonian subsidiary Swedbank AS 'has now been served with a suspicion of money laundering' for the period 2014-2016, that the maximum fine for the suspected crime is EUR 16 million, and that the criminal investigation grew out of the part of its 2019 inspection that Finantsinspektsioon handed to the Estonian Prosecutor's Office in November 2019.

m-202ae875.t: Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit can freeze money without a court order: under § 57 of the AML act (periods unchanged since the act took effect on 27 November 2017) it may, on suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing, stop a transaction or restrict the disposal of an account or other property by a compliance notice for up to 30 calendar days, and for a further 60 calendar days where the possessor or owner fails to prove the legal origin of the property within the first 30 days or terrorist financing is suspected. Its information requests reach data under banking secrecy (§ 58(2)). An obliged entity reports a suspicion without delay, within two working days at most (§ 49(1)).

m-1708cbdc.t: Estonia's financial supervisor applies the European Banking Authority's guidance on access to accounts as its own advisory guidelines: Finantsinspektsioon's list of AML guidance (page last edited 1 April 2026, read 5 October 2026) names, under 'EBA guidelines adopted as advisory guidelines of Finantsinspektsioon', the 'Guidelines on policies and controls for the effective management of money laundering and terrorist financing (ML/TF) risks when providing access to financial services' and the 'Guidelines on the use of Remote Customer Onboarding Solutions', and says the 'comply or explain' principle applies to them. The page gives neither the dates of adoption nor the EBA reference numbers.

m-149d4628.t: Finantsinspektsioon's guidance treats a missing link to Estonia as a risk signal. Its Advisory Guidelines on preventing money laundering in credit and financial institutions (resolution of 26 November 2018 as amended on 8 April 2024; version valid from 1 May 2024, comply-or-explain, linked from its guidance page on 5 October 2026) keep in Annex 1, among customer risks in payment services, that 'the person has no connection with Estonia, but they still want to receive the service in Estonia'. The 2018 text made the risk-appetite document say whether the institution would deal with non-EEA entities 'or with e-residents'; the 2024 version (point 3.3.6.1) dropped the last three words.

m-110aa7fa.t: Estonia's AML act lists risk-raising factors a bank must weigh (§ 37(2)-(3), in force 21 July 2026). Among them: the customer is a company with nominee shareholders or bearer shares; its ownership structure appears unusual or excessively complex; it is a cash-intensive business or a vehicle holding personal assets; the customer is a third-country national applying for residence rights or citizenship in Estonia in exchange for investment; and the relationship is started without meeting the customer or representative in person and without the § 31 remote-identification safeguard. The bank sets in its rules of procedure whether these factors apply as a whole, in part or as separate grounds.

m-0ed314e3.t: The administrative-confiscation ruling that Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit announced in August 2026 concerned EUR 7,400, per the public broadcaster ERR relaying the Unit (19 August 2026): the Tallinn Circuit Court left unchanged the administrative court's permission to transfer to state ownership 37 damaged 200-euro notes that a person had brought to Eesti Pank for exchange; the court found the person's account of the money's origin contradictory, the person most likely a straw man and the beneficial owner not established. The Unit's head said the cash probably came from a 2017 bank robbery in Libya and that since 2022 nearly EUR 30,000 had gone to the state in five such cases.

m-f6c0825f.t: The company behind the EveryPay online card gateway is now registered as AS LHV Paytech: on 5 October 2026 the e-Business Register showed AS LHV Paytech, registry code 12280690, a public limited company entered on 8 May 2012 with its address at Tartu mnt 2, Tallinn, and listed 'Invalid names: EveryPay AS; Unified Payments Solutions AS; Unified Payments Solutions OÜ'. LHV's payment collection terms valid from 4 September 2024 already name AS LHV Paytech (12280690) as the processor of its online payment service. Swedbank's e-commerce page on the same day still called the card gateway the 'EveryPay technical solution'. The date of the renaming was not read.

m-ee270b36.t: Maksekeskus pays out online card payments late and terminal payments fast, per its own pages read 5 October 2026: the FAQ says payouts of card transactions take place 'with a 7-day delay' (the next banking day if the seventh day is a weekend) and that a card transaction is limited to EUR 1,000 unless raised by exception; the terminal page says sales money reaches the merchant's account 'already on the next business day', to an existing account at any bank in the European Economic Area. Before contracting it expects the shop to show company details, sales terms and a privacy policy, to prove the origin of goods, and to have no unscheduled tax debt to the Estonian Tax and Customs Board.

m-caa8b27c.t: The ECB's payments statistics show the acquiring side for Estonia from 2022, the year the amended reporting regulation (ECB/2020/59) began to apply. Card payments 'received' - reported by acquiring payment service providers resident in Estonia, which by the regulation include Estonian branches of foreign institutions; online and terminal payments together - numbered 345.0 million worth EUR 7,212 million in 2022, 372.9 million and EUR 7,834 million in 2023, 397.2 million and EUR 8,171 million in 2024 and 425.3 million and EUR 8,627 million in 2025. Of the 2025 total, 374.2 million (EUR 7,208 million) are 'received domestic' and 51.1 million (EUR 1,420 million) 'received cross-border'.

m-c8f71ccd.t: LHV's payment-acquiring page (read 5 October 2026) does state a settlement time for card payments: 'Money transferred to your account the next day, 7 days a week'. The same page publishes, as of that date: bank links - no monthly fee and EUR 0.05 per transaction (six months free for new clients); terminal rental EUR 12.50-20 per month, free for the first three months for business clients not yet using an LHV terminal, VAT added; card payment transaction fee 'set by agreement according to transaction volume'. The page does not say whether the account credited must be an LHV account for card payments; for bank links it says each payment is credited to the corporate account in LHV.

m-c6f04c35.t: Under § 65 of Estonia's Public Transport Act (wording in force 1 April 2026 - 31 January 2027, read 5 October 2026) a taxi driver whose rides are not ordered and priced through an information-society service must switch on a taximeter and give the passenger a printer-printed receipt showing the carrier's name and registry code, the number plate, date, start and end time, distance, prices used and the total; serving a passenger with a broken taximeter or printer is forbidden, and the passenger may refuse to pay if these duties are breached. For app-ordered rides the carrier gives a ride summary in a reproducible written form. The act has no rule on which means of payment a taxi must accept.

m-bf8bca31.t: PayPal publishes no in-person card product for Estonia as of 5 October 2026: the business menu of paypal.com/ee offers Online Checkout, Invoicing, Payment Links, Payouts and Recurring Payments, and four guessed point-of-sale addresses under /ee/business return 'Lehte ei leitud' (page not found).
