The only face-to-face item in the Estonian fee table is QR-code transactions. Withdrawing a business balance to a bank account is free when no currency conversion is involved (3% to a US bank account). The fee page gives no payout time; the user agreement (7 September 2026) says PayPal aims to send the withdrawal instruction to its bank by the end of the next Luxembourg business day.

m-b8d61e2c.t: Outline (i), same online shop - stage 3, cards to first payout, as of 5 October 2026. Stripe accepts an Estonian company if the people behind it live in a Stripe-supported country, takes only a passport from a person living outside Estonia, contracts through its Irish entities under Irish law, lists 1.5% + EUR 0.25 for standard EEA cards, and settles after 7 calendar days at first, then 3 business days. Local checkouts add bank payments: Montonio (cards through Adyen; Core plan EUR 14.99 a month, 1.29% + EUR 0.20 for EU consumer cards; payout T+2) and Maksekeskus (Luminor as acquirer, 1.35% + EUR 0.15 plus EUR 10 a month, card payouts after 7 days, Estonian law). PayPal: 3.4% + EUR 0.35.

m-b534aa22.t: Dated entries in Finantsinspektsioon's report for 2017 on who may process and acquire payments in Estonia: Maksekeskus AS received a full payment-institution authorisation on 21 August 2017, replacing its exemption for money remittance, and on 9 October 2017 the authorisation to provide cross-border services in Finland, Latvia and Lithuania; Wallester AS was authorised as a payment institution on 18 December 2017; and the Danish payment institution Nets Denmark A/S appears with the date 20 November 2017 in the table 'Establishment of Branches of Foreign Companies in Estonia'.

m-b419ef8b.t: Swedbank's price-list section 'Servicing payment cards (for merchants)', effective 11 April 2025 (read 5 October 2026), gives the commission on the transaction amount as 'as agreed' but prints a phone-terminal transaction at 0.99% + EUR 0.02 and a smart-terminal transaction at 1.45%. Monthly terminal rent, plus VAT, three-month minimum: stationary terminal or card reader EUR 13, 'stationary, mobile terminal' and stationary Bluetooth terminal EUR 18, mobile terminal EUR 19.50, cash-register terminal EUR 45. The e-commerce table below it (no date printed): agreement and monthly fees free, commission 'as agreed', payment initiation EUR 0.10 per transaction.

m-a22594a8.t: Coop Pank does not acquire card payments itself. Its page 'Collection of payments at the point of sale' (read 5 October 2026) offers the service 'in cooperation with our partner Nets Denmark A/S Estonia branch': the merchant applies through the bank, then Nets contacts it, draws up the price offer ('depends on the volume of card payments') and answers contract and technical questions. The bank's own conditions are that card receipts must arrive in a Coop Pank current account and that the service is for sole proprietors and legal entities registered in Estonia. A company first registered less than 6 months ago may use up to three terminals free for three months.

m-9d09bb05.t: AS LHV Pank offers both terminals and an e-commerce solution, and publishes almost none of the transaction prices. Its price list (section 'Servicing of payment cards', valid as of 1 December 2022, read 5 October 2026) gives: agreement signing free; payment card service fee, monthly terminal rental and monthly e-commerce terminal fee 'upon agreement'; chargeback processing EUR 25; EUR 50 if the merchant ends the agreement within six months. The product page quotes terminal rental of EUR 12.50-20 per month plus VAT with a six-month minimum, short-term rental EUR 25 plus VAT, installation within five working days and terminal support by Nets Estonia.

m-9c5fdd7b.t: SEB publishes its e-commerce card prices, unlike LHV and Swedbank: on 5 October 2026 its e-commerce page listed an online card payment service fee per transaction of 1.35% (minimum EUR 0.13) for a card issued within the European Economic Area and 2.55% (minimum EUR 0.13) for a card issued outside it, EUR 0.10 commission per PayPal payment, no fee for concluding the agreement and no monthly agreement fee; the payment initiation (bank payment) fee is 'according to agreement'. The service 'is provided through the bank's partner's payment gateway platform EveryPay'. For terminals the price list gives only 'transaction processing fee as per contract'.

m-994acf97.t: Wise does not currently onboard new merchants for card acceptance: its Estonian page 'Accept card payments' carries the notice 'This feature to accept card payments is currently unavailable to new Wise Business customers' (read 5 October 2026). The prices still published there for businesses registered in the EEA are 1% for any consumer card issued in the EEA and 2.9% for a consumer card from outside the EEA or for any business card, with no monthly fee and no payout fee; payments are taken through payment links, invoices and QR codes and paid into the Wise account. The product is online only - Wise offers no terminal.

m-986347e6.t: EveryPay is a gateway, not a contract party for acquiring: its support article 'Start Accepting Payments' (11 March 2026, read 5 October 2026) tells a merchant to 'contact your acquiring bank directly'; 'supported acquiring banks include' LHV, SEB and Swedbank. The support site names no operating company; the e-Business Register lists EveryPay AS as a former name of AS LHV Paytech (registry code 12280690, registered 8 May 2012, Tartu mnt 2, Tallinn - the address of LHV), and EveryPay's support telephone is the one LHV gives for its online payment collection support. AS LHV Paytech is in none of Finantsinspektsioon's lists of Estonian payment or e-money institutions read the same day.

m-984d9ebb.t: By its own account, one company sits behind card processing for Estonia's banks. Nets Estonia AS (registry code 10452335) describes itself (nets.eu/etee, read 5 October 2026) as founded in 1993 by Estonian banks as the Bank Card Center, now part of the Nets group, 'the dominating provider of payment processing solutions for finance institutions in Estonia', the 'national standard setting body for the payment cards processing' and 'responsible for certification of all the card payment solutions that are in use in Estonia'. Services: processing of issuing and acquiring, switching of POS and ATM transactions, rent, sale and maintenance of POS terminals. Undated page; no authority figure found.

m-94472a98.t: The ECB series 'POS transactions with cards issued by resident PSPs at domestic terminals acquired by non-resident PSPs' shows for Estonia 61.5 million transactions worth EUR 1,120 million in 2022, 87.0 million and EUR 1,539 million in 2023, 133.1 million and EUR 2,322 million in 2024 and 147.3 million and EUR 2,568 million in 2025. It is counted on the issuing side: Estonian issuers report the acquirer as non-resident, and resident acquirers' own reports do not mirror it. In the other direction, resident acquirers took 12.9 million POS transactions worth EUR 395 million on foreign-issued cards at terminals outside Estonia in 2025 (5.0 million and EUR 208 million in 2022).

m-86b5c20e.t: Montonio changed its card processor from Stripe to Adyen: its help article of 1 April 2026 (read 5 October 2026) says merchants were told of 'the switch from Stripe to Adyen' and that migration of the existing merchant base would begin in November 2025. By the same article, under Stripe a merchant filled in Stripe's sign-up form and gave documents for Stripe's verification, payouts came from 'Stripe Payments Europe Ltd', and a daily payout reached the bank 3 or more business days after the transaction; under Adyen no outside verification follows once the card service is activated, payouts come from Montonio on a T+2 business-day basis, and card fees are deducted from payouts, not invoiced.

m-72390070.t: SEB Estonia's merchant terms leave the 'technical partner' for its card terminals unnamed, but its terminal page (read 5 October 2026) links 'Technical instructions on our partner's website' to nets.eu/etee - the terminal manuals of Nets Estonia AS (registry code 10452335) - and posts usage videos for Worldline Yoximo and Yomani terminals. The page therefore points to Nets Estonia as the partner behind SEB's terminals; neither the page nor the terms say who processes SEB's card transactions.

m-6fb200ce.t: ECB payments statistics show a growing volume of in-store card payments in Estonia being acquired from abroad. POS transactions made with cards issued by Estonian-resident providers at terminals located in Estonia but 'acquired by non-resident PSPs' numbered 61.5 million in 2022, 87.0 million in 2023, 133.1 million in 2024 and 147.3 million in 2025, worth EUR 1,120 million, EUR 1,539 million, EUR 2,322 million and EUR 2,568 million (series PTT.A.EE.W1.W2.TRSO.1.2222.N.PN and .EUR, annual, read 5 October 2026). The series is blank before 2022; their share of all in-store card payments is not computed here, and the ECB does not name the acquirers.

m-639e24a8.t: Nets Denmark A/S operates in Estonia through a branch, Nets Denmark A/S Eesti filiaal (registry code 12951516, Viru väljak 2, Tallinn), listed by Finantsinspektsioon on 5 October 2026 among 'Branches of foreign payment institutions' with a single service: issuing of payment instruments and acquiring of payment transactions. Nets Denmark A/S is also listed as a cross-border provider with the right received on 17 October 2017. It is one of only two foreign payment-institution branches in the register (the other is Banqup SA Eesti filiaal, home state Belgium).

m-62f6dd69.t: Adyen lists Estonia both online and in person as of 5 October 2026: 'Estonia' is an entry in the Location filter of its public price page, and its documentation page 'Locations and languages' names Estonia among the European countries where 'In-person payments with Adyen is available' (Estonian is a terminal interface language), adding that its mobile solutions 'do not yet support all of the countries' listed. Adyen publishes no Estonian-locale site and no separate terms for Estonia; its general Terms and Conditions for agreements entered into on or after 1 November 2023 define Adyen as Adyen N.V. 'and/or where relevant, one or more of its local affiliates' and are governed by Dutch law.

m-5e6c7dad.t: The ECB's payments statistics are collected under Regulation (EU) No 1409/2013 (ECB/2013/43); Regulation (EU) 2020/2011 (ECB/2020/59) of 1 December 2020 replaced its annexes and applies from 1 January 2022. Since then sent card payments are reported by the issuing payment service provider and received ones by the acquiring provider (cards with only an e-money function excluded), and a card payment is 'cross-border' as defined in Article 2(8) of Regulation (EU) 2015/751: issuer and acquirer in different Member States, or a card issued in a Member State other than that of the point of sale. The 2013 text had only the payer's and the payee's providers being in different countries.

m-5311c863.t: SumUp's own help centre for Estonia gives a slower payout to a bank than its price page suggests. The articles on payouts (read 5 October 2026) say a payout 'takes 2-3 business days' to arrive from the day SumUp makes it when sent straight to the merchant's bank account, and arrives in one day when sent to the SumUp business account and its card; the merchant chooses a daily (not on weekends or public holidays), weekly or monthly frequency for bank payouts, while payouts to the SumUp Business Card are always next-day. SumUp's fee is deducted before the payout.

m-4fffa198.t: Coop Pank's pages (read 5 October 2026) present card acceptance as a partner service: at the point of sale 'in cooperation with our partner Nets Denmark A/S Estonia branch', to which the bank refers contract and technical questions and which draws up a quote that 'depends on the volume of card payments'; online 'in cooperation with Montonio'. The service is for sole proprietors and legal entities registered in Estonia; takings must go to a Coop Pank account and accrue on working days net of fees. A company first registered less than 6 months ago gets up to three terminals rent-free for three months, repayable if the contract ends within a year. The pages do not name the contract party.

m-4ac7339e.t: Estonian sector acts forbid cash in two wholesale trades (Estonian texts read 5 October 2026). Alcohol Act § 20(1): on import, wholesale and export of alcohol the alcohol is paid for by non-cash settlement, except alcohol meant for use on board internationally operated vessels and aircraft (§ 20(2)); breach is a misdemeanour under § 61 - up to 300 fine units, or up to EUR 5,000 for a legal person. Tobacco Act § 20: wholesale of tobacco products and related products is settled without cash (wording in force since 19 January 2018). Neither provision covers retail sale.

m-4525e62c.t: Two readings of the same statistics give very different shares of terminal payments in Estonia on Estonian-issued cards acquired from outside Estonia in 2025. Issuer side: 147.3 million (ECB) of 397.0 million (Eesti Pank), about 37% (18% in 2022, 34% in 2024). Acquirer side: the ECB's series for resident acquirers appear doubled from 2022 (the one for foreign cards is exactly twice Eesti Pank's own count); halved, 356.1 million were acquired by resident providers, leaving about 41 million, or 10% (15% in 2022, 13% in 2024). Resident providers include Estonian branches of foreign institutions, which issuers may report as non-resident. Neither share is published; both are estimates.

m-3dd07a41.t: LHV's Estonian terminal terms (valid from 22 August 2016, read 5 October 2026) keep the merchant's money within the bank's reach after the contract ends: the merchant answers for chargebacks for 6 months after expiry (clause 13.6), and on termination by either party the bank may suspend payouts for up to 6 months and set them off against the merchant's debts (13.7). The bank may end the contract without notice if more than 1% of transactions in 24 hours are cancelled or charged back, or if no transaction is made within 1 month (13.5.8, 13.5.11). LHV's price list (section valid from 1 December 2022) charges EUR 25 for handling a chargeback and EUR 50 for termination within 6 months.

m-3bb65ad4.t: Viva.com entered Estonia in 2026: its announcement of 14 May 2026 says it 'has extended its European operations to Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia and Slovenia, bringing its total footprint to 29 countries', and an Estonian site (viva.com/en-ee) with in-person, online and account products was live on 5 October 2026. The terms linked from the Estonian terms portal ('Effective from 30.9.2026') are agreed with VIVABANK BANKING S.A., a credit institution supervised by the Bank of Greece providing payment services 'across EEA countries under freedom of services regime'; clause 8.1 applies the laws of Greece.

m-38f3be37.t: Estonia has one sector-wide cash-register duty that reaches shops, cafes and restaurants: under § 44 of the Alcohol Act (Alkoholiseadus; the section in force since 15 April 2004, act wording in force 1-31 October 2026 read on 5 October 2026) retail sale of alcoholic beverages in a shop and in a catering establishment is permitted if the place of business has a cash register, through which all retail sales of alcohol must be recorded. Failing to record a retail alcohol sale in the cash register is a misdemeanour under § 62: up to 200 fine units, or up to EUR 3,000 for a legal person. The act does not describe the device or require a fiscal memory.

m-349fbb66.t: Swedbank AS (registry code 10060701) appears in Finantsinspektsioon's register on 5 October 2026 as a payment agent of a cross-border provider: it represents American Express Payments Europe, S.L. for the service 'issuing of payment instruments and acquiring of payment transactions'. The entry was last changed on 17 September 2026. Separately, Swedbank Pay AB (Sweden, 559465-5366) is listed as a cross-border payment service provider with the right received on 21 March 2025 for issuing/acquiring and execution of payment transactions.

m-30e88ab2.t: Montonio does not acquire cards itself: its help centre (article dated 17 June 2026, read 5 October 2026) says it supports Mastercard, Visa, Maestro, American Express, Apple Pay and Google Pay 'through the international online payment service provider Adyen' and that 'Montonio has contracted Adyen to provide payment processing services'. Card funds first reach the shop's card-payment balance and are paid out daily with a two-business-day buffer (T+2), weekly on Mondays or monthly on the first day, as the merchant selects; card fees are deducted before the payout, while bank-payment, shipping and subscription fees are invoiced monthly.

m-27f2f383.t: Coop Pank outsources online acceptance as well: its 'E-commerce' page (read 5 October 2026) offers the payment solution 'in cooperation with Montonio' - bank payments, card payments, Apple Pay, Google Pay and payment links - and pays VAT-liable business clients a 'merchant bonus' of up to 100% of the cost of using Montonio, paid quarterly at up to 2% a year of the average account balance, if at least 60% of the company's turnover is received at Coop Pank and no more than 30% of that is moved to its accounts in other banks. The bank's own product is the bank link for payments from Coop Pank accounts: subscription is free, and under its Business plan payments via the link carry no fees.

m-27e4afa6.t: Stripe does not tie the payouts of an Estonian account to a bank in Estonia. Its payout documentation, viewed for Estonia on 5 October 2026, says bank accounts 'generally must be located in a country where the settlement currency is an official currency', asks for an IBAN, and lists for Stripe accounts in Estonia that EUR 'can be paid out to banks in these countries': 32 named countries, among them Estonia, Cyprus, Belgium, Lithuania, Ireland, Germany, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Under 'Supported bank account types' it accepts 'virtual bank accounts (such as N26, Revolut, and Wise)', adding that 'you might see higher payout failures for these accounts'.

m-218d1344.t: Other fixed merchant fees in Swedbank Estonia's price list (section effective as of 11.04.2025, unchanged in the complete price list valid from 31 August 2026; read 5 October 2026): replacement of a card terminal at the client's request EUR 21 plus VAT; amendment of the card servicing contract EUR 15; early return of a rented terminal - the sum of the rent still payable; failure to return a terminal on time - the cost of the terminal; purchase of a smart terminal EUR 140 plus VAT, the seller named as Hansab AS. For the separate payment initiation product: agreement fee free, EUR 0.10 per transaction, authentication fee EUR 0.11 plus VAT.

m-1c787cf5.t: Outline (ii), same café - stage 3, terminal and settlement, prices as of 5 October 2026. Banks: Swedbank phone terminal 0.99% + EUR 0.02 or smart terminal 1.45%, rent EUR 13-45 a month plus VAT; SEB and LHV: by contract; Coop Pank: through Nets. Maksekeskus: 0.95% + EUR 0.02, rent EUR 13, paid next business day. SumUp: 1.69% with no monthly fee, or EUR 19 a month and 0.89% (1.69% on foreign, business, premium cards); 2-3 business days to a bank. myPOS: 1.45% + EUR 0.05 for EEA consumer cards, paid at once to a myPOS account. Viva: 1.69% for EEA consumer cards and a monthly account plan. Stripe Terminal is in preview for Estonia; PayPal, Wise, Montonio and Paysera publish no terminal.

m-1bc4c287.t: Estonian banks carry a statutory card-side duty for crises. § 87-1 of the Credit Institutions Act, added on 15 July 2025 (RT I, 08.07.2025, 4), requires them to enable offline card-based payments on conditions set by Eesti Pank when a failure of the communications network or of card acceptance or processing systems makes card payment impossible or materially hinders it. Until 30 September 2026 it applied 'in an emergency' to credit institutions and Estonian branches of foreign ones meeting the conditions of § 3(2) of the act; since 1 October 2026 (RT I, 30.06.2026, 1, § 220) it applies 'during a crisis situation' to every credit institution and Estonian branch. It lays no duty on merchants.

m-174b8600.t: Adyen's mobile in-person products do not all cover Estonia. Its documentation table of countries for Mobile solutions (read 5 October 2026) marks the row 'EU' as supported '(excl. GR)' for Tap to Pay on Android, the Android card reader and the iOS card reader, but for Tap to Pay on iPhone lists country codes one by one - AT, BE, BG, CH, CY, CZ, DE, DK, ES, FI, FR, HR, HU, IE, IS, IT, LI, LU, MT, NL, NO, PL, PT, RO, SE, SI, SK - and EE is not among them (nor are LT and LV). Payment terminals proper are covered: Estonia is in the list of countries where 'In-person payments with Adyen is available'.

m-0d09ba9f.t: Before reference year 2022 the acquiring side of Estonian card payments is found in the ECB's terminal-based dataset PTT. POS transactions at terminals in Estonia acquired by payment service providers resident in Estonia, in millions (read 5 October 2026): with cards issued by resident providers 228.9 (2014), 243.8 (2015), 259.8 (2016), 278.8 (2017), 296.6 (2018), 318.4 (2019), 307.6 (2020), 320.8 (2021); with cards issued by non-resident providers 12.4, 13.7, 10.6, 15.6, 18.1, 21.6, no value for 2020, and 15.6 in 2021. In 2022, the first year of the revised reporting, the two series read 595.8 and 59.3, not reconciled with the 310.1 million 'received domestic' card payments of dataset PCP.

m-0ce0302b.t: myPOS settles into its own e-money account rather than to a bank: the Estonian site (read 5 October 2026) promises 'Payout in seconds at no additional cost' and 'Instant settlement of received card payments', and explains that funds from a terminal, online checkout or payment link 'will be instantly deposited' into the myPOS account. Moving the money on to a bank is an outgoing transfer priced in the tariff. Sign-up and verification are done 'entirely online'; the Legal Agreement says customer due diligence 'may include' the collection and verification of identification documents, without publishing a list for companies or sole proprietors.

m-094e60dd.t: Wise's notice that card acceptance 'is currently unavailable to new Wise Business customers' appeared between 21 May and 20 June 2026 on the page read in the web archive: the German-locale page wise.com/de/business/accept-card-payments/ carries no such notice in the snapshot of 21 May 2026 and carries it ('steht für Neukunden von Wise Business derzeit nicht zur Verfügung') in the snapshots of 20 June, 24 July and 14 September 2026. The archive holds no snapshot of the Estonian-locale page, so the bracket comes from another EEA locale; the Estonian page showed the notice on 5 October 2026.

m-08350b12.t: In the ECB's card payment series for Estonia, payments with Estonian-issued cards shift towards 'cross-border': payments 'sent domestic' were 338.5 million in 2021, 302.4 million in 2022, 298.6 million in 2023, 264.4 million in 2024 and 259.3 million in 2025, while 'sent cross-border' were 44.8 million in 2021, 126.8 million in 2022, 162.2 million in 2023, 226.2 million in 2024 and 261.3 million in 2025 (series PCP.A.EE.W2.W0.CP0.1… and PCP.A.EE.W1.W0.CP0.1…, read 5 October 2026). The jump between 2021 and 2022 falls on the first reference year of the ECB's revised reporting (Regulation (EU) 2020/2011), so it may be a break in the series rather than a change in behaviour.

m-f5e85715.t: A café that sells alcohol must have a cash register: Estonia's Alcohol Act § 44 (wording in force since 15 April 2004; consolidated text in force on 5 October 2026) permits retail sale of alcoholic drinks in a shop or a catering establishment only if a cash register is located at the place of business, through which every transaction in the retail sale of alcoholic drinks must be recorded. Not recording such a sale in the cash register is a misdemeanour: a fine of up to 200 fine units, for a legal person up to EUR 3,000 (§ 62). The act speaks of a cash register and sets no fiscal-memory or certification requirement. §§ 44 and 62 are unchanged in the text in force from 1 November 2026.

m-ef96b403.t: Besides licensed and passported firms, Finantsinspektsioon's register of payment institutions listed on 5 October 2026 a group of 12 active 'Persons with notification obligation providing services excluded from the scope of Payment Institutions and E-money Institutions Act': AllePal OÜ, AS Alexela, Coop Pank AS, Edenred Corporate Payment, Facebook Payments International Limited, Neste Eesti Aktsiaselts, Ridango AS, Stebby OÜ, Swaper Platform OÜ, TKM Finants AS, xChange AS and Yaga OÜ. These hold no payment licence; the register shows them as having notified an excluded service.

m-ebc47445.t: State fee for a virtual-currency licence application in Estonia, by the dated versions of § 269 of the State Fees Act: EUR 345, one rate for every licence under the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act, in the versions in force from 1 January 2015 into 2020; EUR 3,300 from 10 March 2020 (RT I, 31.12.2019, 2); EUR 10,000, plus EUR 4,000 for an application to amend a licence, from 15 March 2022 (RT I, 12.03.2022, 2). Both virtual-currency items were repealed from 30 December 2024 by the Markets in Crypto-Assets Act (RT I, 21.06.2024, 3), from when that Act applies to new crypto-asset service providers; the version in force on 5 October 2026 shows them as repealed.

m-e1736d4b.t: The licence of Ühisarveldused AS (registry code 14192799), third-largest Estonian payment institution by volume in 2024-2025, was withdrawn by Finantsinspektsioon on 18 August 2025 for material breaches of the rules governing its activity and of anti-money-laundering requirements. Tallinn Administrative Court suspended the decision provisionally on 8 September 2025 (at first until 22 September); by a ruling announced on 19 May 2026, open to appeal within 15 days, it lifted the interim relief, leaving the company without a valid licence from that ruling. On 5 October 2026 the supervisor's register lists it among closed institutions; per the May 2026 notice the main proceedings continue.

m-dd792488.t: Estonia's 2020 tightening of virtual-currency licensing: the Act amending the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act and the State Fees Act, adopted 11 December 2019 (RT I, 31.12.2019, 2), in force from 10 March 2020. It merged exchange and wallet providers into 'virtual currency service providers', required the applicant's registered seat, management board and place of business to be in Estonia (or an Estonian-registered branch of a foreign company), a payment account with an EEA credit, e-money or payment institution serving Estonia, and share capital of at least EUR 12,000 paid in money; the application fee became EUR 3,300. Existing holders had to comply by 1 July 2020.

m-dc3a1564.t: Payment institutions authorised by Finantsinspektsioon before its current yearbook series, per its own reports: 10 at the end of 2013 (four under a special licence with lighter requirements and a cap on payment volume), 12 at the end of 2014 (five such), 12 at the end of 2015 (five), 13 in 2017 (four), 13 in 2018 (three), 12 at the end of 2019 (two), plus one branch of a foreign payment institution in 2019. In 2019 the supervisor withdrew three payment-institution authorisations 'because of serious breaches in their compliance with legal requirements'. The first e-money institution authorisation recorded in the reports read is that of inHouse Pay AS, on 9 September 2019.

m-d86a9c6d.t: Estonia's food supervision fee is set by statute. Under Food Act §§ 49^1-49^4 (text in force on 5 October 2026) a business that has notified or holds a licence pays an hourly fee for official controls: for the time spent on the supervision act but for no more than eight hours per act, counted to the half hour, travel time excluded (§ 49^3(3)); the minister sets the hourly rate for each year (§ 49^3(5)). For 2026 it is EUR 40.84 (regulation No 103 of 10 December 2025, RT I, 11.12.2025, 5, in force 1 January - 31 December 2026). The Board issues the payment decision by the seventh day of the month after the control, and the business pays within 28 days of receiving it (§ 49^4(1), (3)).

m-d3df08f4.t: Of the Estonian-licensed institutions in Finantsinspektsioon's register on 5 October 2026, seven hold the service 'issuing of payment instruments and acquiring of payment transactions' in their licence scope: the payment institutions Adson AS (licence of 24 August 2020), Maksekeskus AS (21 August 2017), Paywerk AS (11 April 2022) and Wallester AS (18 December 2017), and the e-money institutions inHouse Pay AS, IPF Digital AS and Monemon AS. The register's service name joins issuing and acquiring in one item, so it does not show which of the seven actually acquire card payments for merchants.

m-d3293f83.t: MakeCommerce is the trade name of Maksekeskus AS (registry code 12268475, Liivalaia 45, Tallinn), which Finantsinspektsioon lists among Estonian payment institutions (entry last changed 21 January 2026, read 5 October 2026). Its General Terms in force from 25 March 2024 are a collection mandate: the merchant authorises Maksekeskus to receive transaction amounts from payers on its behalf and pass them on. Card acquiring is not done by Maksekeskus: clause 3.2.4 names Luminor Bank AS (11315936) as the acquirer and applies Luminor's general terms. The contract is under Estonian law, disputes go to Harju County Court, and ordinary termination needs two months' notice.

m-c7f68850.t: Payment and e-money institutions holding a licence from Finantsinspektsioon, at year-end per its yearbooks: payment institutions 12 in 2020 (two under an exemption), 15 in 2021 (four exempt), 16 in 2022 (four exempt), 16 in 2023, 14 in 2024, 12 in 2025 (two exempt); e-money institutions 2 in 2020, 2021 and 2022, 3 in 2023, 2024 and 2025. On 5 October 2026 the supervisor's register lists nine Estonian payment institutions, two more 'with an exception', two branches of foreign payment institutions (Banqup SA and Nets Denmark A/S) and four Estonian e-money institutions (inHouse Pay AS, IPF Digital AS, Lightspark Payments Europe AS, Monemon AS).

m-c5ab54c8.t: The 2022 tightening: the Act amending the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act and other Acts, adopted on 23 February 2022 (RT I, 12.03.2022, 2), in force from 15 March 2022, set the share capital of a virtual currency service provider at no less than EUR 100,000, or EUR 250,000 where it provides the virtual currency transfer service, added own-funds requirements checked by an auditor, and gave existing licence holders until 15 June 2022 to comply, failing which the Financial Intelligence Unit revokes the licence. The unit reported that by 15 June 2022 amendments had been applied for on 135 authorisations, 94 providers had surrendered theirs and it had revoked 18 in 2022.

m-bd7d43cf.t: Montonio, the Tallinn-founded checkout provider, does not hold an Estonian payment licence: its site (read 5 October 2026) states that the payment initiation service is provided by Montonio Finance UAB, a Lithuanian company (registry code 305205122) holding payment institution licence No LB002007 issued by the Bank of Lithuania. Finantsinspektsioon's register lists 'Montonio Finance, UAB' among providers of cross-border payment services and does not list any Montonio company among the nine Estonian payment institutions shown on 5 October 2026. The Estonian company Montonio Finance OÜ (registry code 14557628, Tallinn) appears on the site as copyright holder.

m-bc276886.t: Finantsinspektsioon's register shows twelve Estonian payment-institution authorisations ended between 2018 and 2026 (decision dates, read 5 October 2026): Grape Tax-Free OÜ 26.02.2018; Meieni OÜ's exemption 20.12.2018; AS Talveaed 29.04.2019; GFC Good Finance Company AS 27.05.2019; PayHub AS 08.07.2019; TransferFast OÜ 20.04.2020; Crumblo OÜ 08.07.2022; Coop Finants AS 01.04.2024; AS Pocopay 12.06.2024; OÜ MyFinancier 09.06.2025; AS Creditinfo Eesti 16.06.2025; Ühisarveldused AS 18.08.2025. Three earlier ones are also listed (Tavid AS 2015, IIZI Kindlustusmaakler 2015, Eurex Capital OÜ 2017). The register gives dates, not reasons.

m-bba8ddc3.t: Outline (ii), same café - stage 2, notices before opening, as of 5 October 2026. Food: an ordinary café needs no activity licence; it files a free notice of economic activities with the Agriculture and Food Board, may operate after notifying, keeps a written self-check plan, and is inspected afterwards at EUR 40.84 an hour (2026). Alcohol: serving it takes a second notice, for catering, filed through eesti.ee or a notary, and a cash register on the premises recording every alcohol sale (Alcohol Act § 44); the city government supervises retail sale and the council may restrict it. Staff: each employee's start of work is entered in the employment register no later than the moment work begins.

m-b33ac82d.t: The Agriculture and Food Board's page for food businesses (read 5 October 2026) says a notified business 'may operate after notifying' and is inspected afterwards, while a licensed one is inspected before the licence is issued and may operate only after it. Notifying and applying are free; they are 'most conveniently' filed in the ministry's client portal and may also go through eesti.ee, by post or e-mail to the Board's regional office, or a notary. Supervision that follows is charged by the hour: EUR 40.84 in 2026, set by ministerial regulation No 103 of 10 December 2025 (RT I, 11.12.2025, 5). A written self-check plan need not be filed with a notice but must exist and be available.

m-a9772616.t: No Montonio company is among the Estonian payment or e-money institutions in Finantsinspektsioon's register (read 5 October 2026). The register lists Montonio Finance, UAB (Lithuania; registry code 305205122 per GLEIF) among providers of cross-border payment services, with the right received on 23 November 2020 and amended by a decision of 28 March 2023. The notified services are issuing of payment instruments and acquiring, execution of payment transactions, credit-funded payment transactions, money remittance, payment initiation and account information.

m-a0d57869.t: Valid Estonian virtual-currency licences fell from hundreds to dozens in five years, per the Financial Intelligence Unit: 641 when it began its clean-up in mid-2021; 381 on 31 December 2021 (in 2021 it withdrew 329 and issued 86); 37 on 4 December 2025; 36 at the start of 2026. 1 July 2026 was the deadline in § 48(4) of Estonia's Markets in Crypto-Assets Act (RT I, 21.06.2024, 3) for such providers to comply; a joint notice of 30 June 2026 said the unit 'will consequently cancel on 1 July the register data' of the remaining licences (no confirmation found by 5 October 2026). Finantsinspektsioon's register then lists one Estonian crypto-asset service provider, Lightspark Payments Europe AS.

m-96634131.t: Passport entries in Finantsinspektsioon's register of supervised entities, counted on 5 October 2026: 338 active 'Providers of cross-border payment services' and 14 payment agents of such providers on the payment-institution side; 267 active 'Providers of cross-border e-money services' (266 distinct names) and 34 distributors of such providers on the e-money side. The 'Closed' filter held 339 former cross-border payment service providers and 177 former cross-border e-money providers. The lists carry no date of their own. An entry shows only the home country, the date the right was received and the services notified; the register does not show whether the firm does any business in Estonia.

m-94971e69.t: On 5 October 2026 Finantsinspektsioon's public register of supervised entities listed, under payment institutions with the filter 'Active': 9 Estonian payment institutions (Adson AS, Crowdestate AS, Maaelu Edendamise Hoiu-laenuühistu, Maksekeskus AS, Meieni OÜ, Modena Payments OÜ, Paywerk AS, TavexWise AS, Wallester AS), 2 Estonian payment institutions with an exemption (Kambja Hoiu-Laenuühistu, OÜ Krediidiregister), 2 branches of foreign payment institutions (Banqup SA Eesti filiaal, Nets Denmark A/S Eesti filiaal) and 4 payment agents.

m-8ea56ae3.t: Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit counted the virtual-currency licences it issued in 2017-2019 from the Register of Economic Activities: for exchanging virtual currency for money 4 (2017), 612 (2018) and 666 (2019), 1,282 in all; for wallet services 2, 525 and 638, 1,165 in all; held by 4, 617 and 687 unique enterprises, 1,308 in all. The first licences were issued in late autumn 2017 under the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act of 2017. Between 1 March and 31 July 2020 the unit declared 1,296 licences void, concerning 705 enterprises, leaving 611 licences on 1 August 2020.

m-88b22784.t: The Bank of Lithuania's public record for Montonio Finance, UAB (company code 305205122; read in the web-archive snapshot of 17 February 2026, the live site answering with a Cloudflare check on 5 October 2026) shows authorisation code LB002007 and a payment institution licence valid from 5 November 2020. Payment initiation and account information services are listed from 5 November 2020; execution of payment transactions, 'issuing of payment instruments and/or acquiring of payment' and money remittance from 9 February 2023, with services in other Member States without a branch. The entity is thus licensed for acquiring, while Montonio's help page says card processing is contracted to Adyen.

m-668b776b.t: A café in Estonia does not need a food licence in the ordinary case; it notifies. Food Act § 7(1) requires a notice of economic activities to the Agriculture and Food Board (Põllumajandus- ja Toiduamet) for handling food in an establishment under Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, with no state fee (§ 7(7)); an activity licence (§ 8) is reserved for listed cases such as establishments needing approval, retail handling of food of animal origin supplied to other retailers, and catering in kindergartens, schools, hospitals, care homes, prisons and the Defence Forces. The Board's page lists 'toitlustamine' (catering, including serving hot drinks) among activities to be notified.

m-4de87332.t: Two Estonian payment institutions lost their licences in spring 2019 for breaches of the payment-institutions act and the anti-money-laundering act. On 29 April 2019 Finantsinspektsioon withdrew the licences of AS Talveaed, whose business model 'focused on providing payment services to foreign resident clients' and which had served such clients on at least 49 occasions despite a January 2018 ban; its market share grew to 45% in 2016, per the supervisor. On 27 May 2019 it withdrew the licence of GFC Good Finance Company AS for 'serious breaches of the law', including own funds long below the legal minimum; Tallinn Circuit Court upheld that withdrawal on 23 November 2023, per the supervisor.

m-45d9a753.t: Finantsinspektsioon's public lists of firms notified for cross-border services into Estonia (read 5 October 2026) carry the entities behind most providers studied. Among 427 entries (422 distinct names) for cross-border banking services: Adyen N.V., PayPal (Europe) S.à r.l. et Cie, S.C.A., Revolut Bank UAB and VIVABANK SINGLE MEMBER BANKING S.A (entry last changed 14 May 2026). Among 267 for cross-border e-money services: Stripe Technology Europe, Limited, SumUp EU Payments UAB, myPOS Limited and UAB 'Paysera LT'. Among 338 for cross-border payment services: Wise Europe SA, Montonio Finance, UAB and Nets Denmark A/S. Stripe Payments Europe, Limited is on none of the three.

m-3ab5b122.t: A café that serves alcohol files a second notice. Alcohol Act § 23(1) requires a notice of economic activities for selling alcohol in three fields of activity - retail trade, wholesale trade and catering - stating the place or places of business and the kinds of alcohol handled (§ 23(2)); the notice can be filed only through the Estonian information gateway (eesti.ee) or a notary (§ 23(3)). No notice is filed for selling alcohol at a public event (§ 23(1^1)). The local government - in Tallinn the city - supervises retail sale of alcoholic drinks on its territory (§ 49(4)) and its council may restrict it (§ 42).

m-36861292.t: As of 5 October 2026 Finantsinspektsioon's public lists ('Active') show 9 Estonian payment institutions, 2 payment institutions with an exemption (Kambja Hoiu-Laenuühistu, OÜ Krediidiregister), 4 Estonian e-money institutions (inHouse Pay AS, IPF Digital AS, Lightspark Payments Europe AS, Monemon AS), 2 branches of foreign payment institutions (Banqup SA Eesti filiaal, Nets Denmark A/S Eesti filiaal), 4 payment agents, 12 persons with a notification obligation, and 338 providers of cross-border payment services. Neither Montonio Finance OÜ nor AS LHV Paytech (EveryPay) is in any Estonian list; Montonio Finance, UAB is among the cross-border providers (entry last changed 28 March 2023).

m-2fd7609b.t: Maksekeskus AS (registry code 12268475, Tallinn; the operator of MakeCommerce) is an Estonian payment institution. Finantsinspektsioon's register shows: a money-remittance licence of 21 August 2013, replaced on 21 August 2017 by a licence for issuing payment instruments and acquiring payment transactions, execution of payment transactions and credit-funded payment transactions; a payment initiation licence of 18 May 2020; an account information licence of 27 September 2021; branches in Latvia (decision of 3 May 2021) and Lithuania (decision of 15 December 2025). Read 5 October 2026.

m-11aec103.t: Since 1 October 2026 a non-bank payment provider can be a provider of a vital service in Estonia. § 7-1(1) of the Payment Institutions and E-money Institutions Act, added by the Crisis Situation and National Defence Act (Kriisiolukorra ja riigikaitse seadus, adopted 2 June 2026, RT I, 30.06.2026, 1), covers a payment institution, an e-money institution or the Estonian branch of a foreign one whose payments or cash payouts in Estonia exceed one per cent of the corresponding total of Estonian credit, payment and e-money institutions and which Eesti Pank assesses as having a significant effect on payments in Estonia. On 5 October 2026 Eesti Pank's page named only five banks as such providers.

m-0f20e475.t: Finantsinspektsioon's register records foreign providers' passported right to acquire payment transactions in Estonia with the date the right was received (read 5 October 2026), among them: Worldline Financial Services (Europe) S.A., Luxembourg, 26.04.2012; UAB Paysera LT, Lithuania, 23.10.2012; Worldline SA, Belgium, 07.03.2016; Nets Denmark A/S, 17.10.2017; Stripe Technology Europe Limited, Ireland, 25.03.2019; SumUp EU Payments UAB, Lithuania, 18.10.2019; Montonio Finance UAB, Lithuania, 23.11.2020; myPOS Limited, Ireland, 20.09.2022; Swedbank Pay AB, Sweden, 21.03.2025. Of the nine only Nets also has an Estonian branch. An entry shows a notified right, not activity or volume.

m-0747d9cc.t: Two dated readings from Finantsinspektsioon show how small and how changed the Estonian-licensed payment sector is. Its overview for the first quarter of 2019 counted 13 payment institutions, three of them under an exemption, which intermediated EUR 183 million in 1.8 million payments in that quarter (EUR 196 million in the fourth quarter of 2018). Its register shows no Estonian e-money institution, active or closed, licensed before 9 September 2019. On 5 October 2026 the register listed 11 payment institutions (two under an exemption) and 4 e-money institutions, and the supervisor's review put their 2025 payments at EUR 1.8 billion in 28.1 million payments for the whole year.

m-0336cd0e.t: Estonia's licensing act for non-bank payment firms is the Payment Institutions and E-money Institutions Act (adopted 17 December 2009, in force 22 January 2010). A company needs an activity licence to act as a payment or e-money institution; Finantsinspektsioon grants and revokes it (§ 14(1), (3)); licences have no term and are not transferable (§ 14(4)). By Finantsinspektsioon's decision chapters 3, 4, 6 and 8 of the act do not apply to a payment institution if its average monthly payment volume over 12 months is at most EUR 3 million, it earns less than half its income from payments and it provides none of the services of § 3(1) points 6-8 (§ 11(2)); such a firm may not passport (§ 11(6)).

m-fc45e173.t: LHV's Estonian terminal terms (valid from 22 August 2016) forbid the merchant to set minimum or maximum transaction amounts (clause 4.10.1) and to collect from the card user 'any additional charge whatsoever' when a transaction is made, 'if applying additional charges is prohibited under the legislation of the country where the Bank is registered at and/or under the rules of International Card Organisations' (4.10.2). The contract thus refers the surcharge question to Estonian law and scheme rules rather than deciding it.

m-f38f8dc5.t: Since 1 January 2025 cash payments at physical points of sale in Estonia are rounded to the nearest five cents: up if the final price ends in 3, 4, 8 or 9 cents, down if it ends in 1, 2, 6 or 7 (§ 5-1 of the Act on the Introduction of the Euro and the Settlement of Cash Payments in Euros, inserted by RT I, 30.05.2024, 2). Card and other non-cash payments are not rounded, nor is a final price below three cents. The rule binds every trader and applies to payments by consumers, sole proprietors and representatives of legal persons; the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority supervises it (§§ 5-3 to 5-5).

m-f1ca7442.t: Price indication in Estonia is governed by §§ 7-8 of the Consumer Protection Act: when offering and selling goods a trader must make known to the consumer the selling price and the unit price - unless the regulation under § 7(8) provides otherwise for the unit price - in writing, clearly legible, unambiguous and easily noticeable (§ 7(1), (4)); the selling price is the final price the consumer pays (§ 7(2)); for a service the trader gives the final price or, where it cannot be fixed in advance, its components and basis of calculation, and displays a price list at the place of service or otherwise (§ 8). A price-reduction notice must show the earlier price (§ 7(6-1), since 28 May 2022).

m-ccb146e5.t: LHV's terminal contract in Estonia is with the bank itself: the 'Terms and conditions of the agreement for the servicing of payment cards', valid from 22 August 2016 and still the version served on 5 October 2026 in both Estonian and English, govern relations between AS LHV Pank and the merchant under Estonian law (clause 1.4). The merchant's account must be at LHV Pank (2.2.7). A separate 'Processor', designated by the bank, handles the transactions; the bank's product page sends terminal support calls to Nets Estonia.

m-b681dfd0.t: Adyen publishes two sets of general terms split by the date of the merchant agreement (both read 5 October 2026). For agreements entered into on or after 1 November 2023 ('Last update 1 November 2023'): Dutch law, and all disputes 'finally settled' by ICC arbitration in Amsterdam, in English, before one or three arbitrators. For agreements entered into before 1 November 2023 ('Effective from: March 7th, 2023'): Dutch law and 'the exclusive jurisdiction of the competent courts of Amsterdam'. Both exclude the Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. A merchant signing in 2026 therefore gets arbitration, not the Amsterdam courts; neither set has terms specific to Estonia.

m-b5e76848.t: Paysera serves Estonian clients from Lithuania, with a local company that is not the contract party: the footer of paysera.ee (read 5 October 2026) says Paysera EE OÜ provides call-centre, marketing, business-development and administrative support, and that 'all payment and e-money services agreements with Estonian clients are concluded and the corresponding services are provided in Estonia by Paysera LT UAB' (Lithuanian code 300060819; e-money institution licence No. 1 of 27 September 2012, Bank of Lithuania). The General Payment Services Agreement for Business Clients (in force 12 September 2025) applies the law of the country of the licensed Paysera company that registered the client.

m-ab450749.t: Swedbank's Estonian terminal terms (valid from 1 September 2025) contain no standing reserve or deposit clause. Instead the bank may, without the merchant's consent, withhold from card turnover or debit from the merchant's accounts disputed or non-compliant transaction amounts, fees and card-scheme fines (clause 5.3); demand funds within 10 Business Days and block accounts up to the claim (5.4); and, for disputed or suspect transactions, suspend payouts until the scheme's chargeback deadlines (5.6). Either party may terminate on 1 month's written notice (9.5); the bank may end it at once on listed grounds, e.g. no transactions for 2 months (9.7.2). Unilateral changes: 1 month's notice (8.1).

m-a5a0c44f.t: Nets contracts Estonian merchants directly as acquirer. Its 'Acquiring - Terms and Conditions 2021' for the Baltics (read 5 October 2026) say Nets operates in Estonia through Nets Denmark A/S Eesti filiaal, registration no. 12951516, under the supervision of the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority; the agreement is subject to Estonian law, disputes go to Harju County Court, and the Estonian version prevails. Either party may terminate on thirty days' written notice (11.2). On its risk assessment Nets may demand a bank guarantee, withhold settlement in whole or in part, or extend the settlement period (2.7.3). Prices and the settlement period are left to the agreement form and price list.

m-942b7fff.t: At SEB in Estonia the terminal contract is with the bank itself: the 'Terms and Conditions of the Merchant Agreement for Card Transactions' valid from 1 July 2023 (marked 'In force' in SEB's index on 5 October 2026) define the Bank as AS SEB Pank and are governed by Estonian law (clause 111). The bank 'generally pays' the merchant on the calendar day after the transaction record is forwarded and no later than within two settlement days (81). Either party may cancel on one month's written notice (94); the bank may suspend or cancel without notice on listed grounds, including no transactions for two months (95.5). Terminal installation and repair are done by an unnamed 'technical partner'.

m-85a4b5a0.t: SumUp's Estonian Payment Terms (in force from 7 February 2022, read 5 October 2026) sit under Estonian contract law but take their payment-services rules from Lithuania: the merchant, as a payment service user who is not a consumer, is informed of the exception in Article 3(7) of the Law on Payments of the Republic of Lithuania and agrees that the terms may depart from that law - among others from Article 13 (content of the framework contract) and Articles 37, 39, 41, 44, 51 and 52. Supervision is by the Bank of Lithuania, whose licence page (web-archive snapshot of 27 November 2025) shows e-money institution licence No. 56 of 27 August 2019 for SumUp EU Payments UAB.

m-8151b77f.t: myPOS sells to Estonian merchants through a localised site (mypos.com/en-ee, 'Eesti' in its country list) and contracts them, like merchants elsewhere in the EEA, through myPOS Limited, an Irish e-money institution (Central Bank of Ireland licence C475122, company no. 700880). The Legal Agreement downloaded from the Estonian terms page on 5 October 2026 is 'Effective as of: 17.07.2023', is governed by the laws of Ireland 'subject to your local mandatory rights', with the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts in Dublin, and states that the Irish Deposit Guarantee Scheme does not apply to the myPOS account. The English version prevails over any translation.

m-80fac2be.t: Estonian law obliges a merchant to accept cash, not cards. Under § 2(2) of the Act on the Introduction of the Euro and the Settlement of Cash Payments in Euros, persons other than Eesti Pank and credit institutions must accept up to 50 valid euro coins at a time and banknotes without limit, 'unless there is an agreement to use another means of payment' (wording in force since 1 March 2016). Refusal is a misdemeanour under § 74 of the Consumer Protection Act: up to 200 fine units, or up to EUR 40,000 for a legal person. No provision requiring a merchant to accept cards or other electronic payments was found in these two acts or in the payment chapters of the Law of Obligations Act.

m-7e8acc4f.t: For online card payments Swedbank AS is itself the contracting acquirer ('Service Provider means Swedbank AS, registration number 10060701'), while the technical gateway is EveryPay: the bank's e-shop page names 'EveryPay technical solution' for the card acquiring service. Under the Terms and Conditions for Online Card Acquiring valid from 1 September 2025 the default payout is within 5 Business Days after receipt of transaction data (clause 3.2), and if turnover exceeds the planned monthly amount the bank may lengthen the settlement period, refuse the excess or 'require collateral' (2.4). Governing law: that of the bank's country of registration (10.1). Read 5 October 2026.

m-677f8aa5.t: Estonia's general receipt rule is a consumer-law duty and prescribes no device. Under § 4(4) of the Consumer Protection Act (wording in force from 1 September 2025, RT I, 08.07.2025, 71) a trader must give the consumer a document proving the purchase when goods or services are paid for immediately; it must state at least the trader's name and address, the date, and each item's name, price and the amount paid (§ 4(4-1)). A paper document is given on request, and by default for a cash purchase without a loyalty card giving electronic access; it is not required where the consumer expressly agreed to receive it by e-mail or another channel (§ 4(4-2), (5-1)).

m-4c401d45.t: Maksekeskus keeps seven editions of its General Terms online (12.06.2017 to 25.03.2024). The 2017-2020 editions (12-15 pages) never mention a terminal, PCI DSS or an acquirer; card refunds go to an unnamed 'partner bank'. The edition of 31.10.2022 (21 pages, 16 sections) adds a section on card payments and terminal use, PCI DSS, a ban on surcharging card payments unless law requires it or Maksekeskus consents under scheme rules, termination where sanctions apply, and two named acquirers - LHV Pank AS and Luminor Bank AS. The edition of 25.03.2024 (24 pages) names Luminor alone and replaces the transport section with Tarne+. All state Estonian law and Finantsinspektsioon's supervision.

m-425b0ef2.t: Under LHV's Estonian terminal terms (valid from 22 August 2016) the bank pays sales revenue to the merchant's LHV account within 1 Banking Day of receiving settlement data from the processor, or within 2 if the agreement is under 3 months old or the merchant's settled total does not exceed EUR 10,000 (clause 7.1). The bank may require a Security Deposit, a pledged term deposit at LHV (15.1). On termination by either party the merchant is deemed to pledge funds at LHV equal to 10% of its average monthly transactions over the past six months (15.3). Either party may terminate on 30 calendar days' written notice (13.2); leaving within 6 months may cost a fee (13.3), EUR 50 in LHV's price list.

m-3e5b51b7.t: Swedbank Estonia keeps old versions of its terminal terms online. The version valid from 1 December 2014 paid within 3 Business Days, forbade any minimum or maximum transaction amount and said nothing on interchange or surcharging. The version valid from 9 June 2016 - the day Articles 7-10 of Regulation (EU) 2015/751 (unblending, honour-all-cards) began to apply; the terms do not cite it - pays within 2 Business Days unless otherwise agreed, says commission includes interchange and scheme fees shown in monthly 'IFR reports' if the merchant chooses them, forbids surcharging where law or scheme rules prohibit it, and names minimum and maximum amounts as forbidden only for non-EU cards.

m-323430e4.t: PayPal's user agreement for Estonia ('Last updated on 7 September 2026', read 5 October 2026) is a contract with PayPal (Europe) S.à r.l. et Cie, S.C.A. (R.C.S. Luxembourg B 118 349), licensed in Luxembourg as a credit institution and supervised by the CSSF (register number B00000351); it lists Estonia among the countries of residence it covers. It 'is governed by the laws of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg'; a user acting as a business submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Luxembourg City. The balance is electronic money, not a deposit, and is outside the Luxembourg deposit-guarantee scheme.

m-23d80b3e.t: The contracting party under Swedbank's Estonian terminal agreement is the bank itself: the Terms and Conditions for Payment Cards Servicing valid from 1 September 2025 define the Bank as Swedbank AS, registry code 10060701, Liivalaia 34, Tallinn. Unless otherwise agreed, the bank pays the transaction amount less commission to the merchant's account not later than within 2 Business Days after receiving the batch, except where it is entitled to suspend payment (clause 3.3). It may use third-party service providers (5.2), and the relations are governed by the law of the bank's country of registration (10.2). Read 5 October 2026.

m-1baed472.t: SumUp advertises to Estonian merchants 'järgmise päeva väljamaksed' - payouts by the next business day (price page read 5 October 2026). Its Payment Terms (in force from 7 February 2022) say: after SumUp has received the funds it pays the amount owed into the merchant's SumUp wallet, from which payouts may be routed automatically to a linked bank account; transfers to bank accounts 'may take up to 3-5 business days depending on the provider'; SumUp may at any time, at its discretion, withhold payouts temporarily and build a reserve; opening the account may involve a credit check and a request for documents. The wallet is e-money, 'not a bank account', outside any compensation scheme.

m-13914614.t: SEB Estonia's index of merchant-agreement terms lists five versions: 16.02.2015-12.01.2018, 13.01.2018-14.12.2021, 15.12.2021-09.10.2022, 10.10.2022-30.06.2023 and from 01.07.2023. The 2015 text forbade minimum and maximum amounts and said nothing on surcharging, interchange or strong authentication. The version valid from 13 January 2018 - the day Estonia's PSD2 amendments entered into force - added a ban on taking an additional fee for card use 'if this is forbidden by legislation' (9.2), a duty to apply strong authentication (23), and a clause that the processing fee includes the issuer's commission and the scheme fee, whose rates the bank publishes on its website (37).

m-0dde47dd.t: Wise's card acceptance is a separate contract - 'Customer Terms for Acquiring Payments Services' with Wise Europe SA ('Last updated: 26 September 2025', read 5 October 2026) - in which Wise 'is acting as a payment facilitator' working with 'a third-party merchant acquirer ("Processor")'. A customer reaching USD 1,000,000 a year on Visa or Mastercard must contract directly with the Processor on its standard terms 'as set out on' adyen.com. Wise pays only funds it has received from the scheme, may hold a rolling reserve, and asks before contracting about finances, activities, shareholders, beneficial owners, registered office and licences. Belgian law; courts of Belgium.

m-0a47c1d5.t: For online card acceptance SEB in Estonia is also the contracting party, on older terms than for terminals: the 'Terms and conditions of e-commerce service agreement' valid from 13 January 2018 are 'In force' on 5 October 2026 (the only earlier version dates from 18 February 2015). The bank pays the merchant within five settlement days of receiving the transaction notice (clause 23) and withholds chargebacks from payouts or debits the account (25). Either party may cancel on one month's notice (32); the bank may suspend or cancel at once on listed grounds, including no transactions within two months (33.4). The product page says the service runs on the 'payment gateway platform EveryPay'.

m-09750ca1.t: SumUp runs an Estonian site (sumup.com/et-ee) and contracts Estonian merchants through SumUp EU Payments UAB, a Lithuanian e-money institution (Bank of Lithuania licence no. 56 issued 27 August 2019, company code 305074395, Vilnius). Unlike the other pan-European providers read on 5 October 2026, its Estonian General Terms ('Kehtivad 07.02.2022', in force from 7 February 2022) choose Estonian law and give Estonian courts exclusive jurisdiction; the Payment Terms of the same date are supplementary terms of that contract, yet their clause on wallet transfers refers to grounds in 'the legal acts of the Republic of Lithuania'.

m-01b5c5b0.t: For a user in Estonia the Stripe Services Agreement (Estonian-locale page, 'Last modified: September 28, 2026', read 5 October 2026) names the same parties as for the other EEA states: its table of contracting entities lists Estonia among the 'Countries in the European Economic Area' served by Stripe Payments Europe, Limited, with Stripe Technology Europe, Limited as an additional party where the financial-services or other service terms say so. The regional terms for EEA users make the laws of Ireland the governing law, send disputes to ICC arbitration held in Dublin, and give the courts of Ireland exclusive jurisdiction over claims not subject to arbitration.

m-fec59926.t: Luminor, the bank combining the Baltic operations of DNB and Nordea, started on 1 October 2017. From 2 January 2019 it operates as one Estonian-registered bank, Luminor Bank AS, with branches in Latvia and Lithuania: per the bank's own notice the cross-border merger agreement was signed on 29 March 2018, the European Central Bank gave final approval on 28 June 2018, and on completion all assets and liabilities of Luminor Latvia and Luminor Lithuania passed to Luminor Bank AS, so that deposits at those branches are covered by the Estonian Guarantee Fund from 2 January 2019. Finantsinspektsioon's 2019 report says the head office 'has been in Estonia since the start of 2019'.

m-f1f5dadb.t: Maksekeskus AS (registry code 12268475), second by payment volume among Estonian payment and e-money institutions in 2025 (23%, per Finantsinspektsioon), belongs to a bank. By a contract of 31 January 2022 Luminor Bank AS (11315936) agreed to buy 99% of its shares from Eesti Post AS (55.6468%), Maksekeskus Holding OÜ (29.7887%), Olsson & Nielsen Nordic OÜ (12.0292%) and a natural person (2.5353%); the Competition Authority cleared the concentration by decision no. 5-5/2022-009 of 28 March 2022, which says Maksekeskus earned about 85% of its 2021 revenue in Estonia. On 5 October 2026 the e-Business Register shows Luminor Bank AS as its sole shareholder.

m-e8bf8891.t: In its Luminor/Maksekeskus decision of 28 March 2022 the Estonian Competition Authority measured payment solutions (credit included) offered to web shops in Estonia two ways. On Eesti Pank's data - 38,331,300 e-purchases worth EUR 1,474.0 million in 2021 - the merging parties held under 20% by number and under 25% by value. Its own study of 2021 volumes provided or intermediated by banks operating in Estonia found that 'the main part (about 80%)' came from six nationwide banks and the parties had under 20%; the decision calls this a narrow selection. Largest competitors named by the notifying party: Swedbank AS, AS SEB Pank, AS LHV Pank, Montonio Finance OÜ and Paysera LT UAB.

m-e4322b13.t: Bank market shares in Estonia before and after the reshuffle of 2017-2019, per Finantsinspektsioon. By loans to the non-financial sector at 31 December 2013: Swedbank 39.75%, SEB Pank 23.81%, Nordea's Estonian branch 17.81%, Danske Bank's Estonian branch 7.96%, DNB Pank 3.71%, Bigbank 1.96%, LHV Pank 1.26% - the four largest together 89%. By assets at the end of 2019, with the end of 2018 in brackets: Luminor 37% (15%), Swedbank 29% (40%), SEB 18% (24%), LHV 8.1% (6.3%), foreign branches 2.8% (8.4%), Coop 1.6% (1.7%). The chart's note says the shares changed significantly from 2018 because Luminor's Latvian and Lithuanian branches were added to the Estonian banking sector.

m-d7d65138.t: ECB payments statistics (dataset PCP, read 5 October 2026): card payments sent, i.e. made with cards issued by payment service providers resident in Estonia, numbered 226.6 million in 2013, 264.1 million in 2015, 340.4 million in 2018, 370.8 million in 2019, 357.8 million in 2020, 429.2 million in 2022, 490.7 million in 2024 and 520.6 million in 2025 (series PCP.A.EE.W0.W0.CP0.1._T._T.PCS_ALL._Z._X._Z.N.PN). Their value was EUR 3,740 million in 2013, EUR 4,692 million in 2015, EUR 7,012 million in 2019, EUR 6,814 million in 2020, EUR 9,340 million in 2022 and EUR 12,200 million in 2025 (same key ending .EUR).

m-ce837fc7.t: Card payments at physical points of sale in Estonia made with cards issued in Estonia, summed from Eesti Pank's monthly table 'Card transactions' (updated 24 September 2026): 243.8 million payments worth EUR 3,880 million in 2015; 318.4 million and EUR 5,294 million in 2019; 320.8 million and EUR 5,940 million in 2021; 397.0 million and EUR 7,588 million in 2025; 272.0 million and EUR 5,297 million in January-August 2026. Cards issued abroad added 37.3 million payments worth EUR 993 million at Estonian points of sale in 2025 (13.7 million and EUR 505 million in 2015).

m-c10c3022.t: ECB structural indicators put the share of the five largest credit institutions in the total assets of credit institutions in Estonia (CR5) at 89.7% in 2013, 89.9% in 2014, 88.6% in 2015, 88.0% in 2016, 90.3% in 2017, 91.0% in 2018, 93.0% in 2019, 93.7% in 2020, 93.0% in 2021, 90.8% in 2022, 89.6% in 2023, 89.9% in 2024 and 89.0% in 2025 (series SSI.A.EE.122C.S10.X.A1.Z0Z.Z, read 5 October 2026). The Herfindahl index for total assets in the same dataset was 0.2483 in 2013, reached its highest value of 2013-2025 in 2018 (0.2698) and stood at 0.2030 in 2025 (SSI.A.EE.122C.H10.X.A1.Z0Z.Z); before 2011 it had been higher still (0.4067 in 2001).

m-a944f902.t: Deposit market shares in Estonia, per Finantsinspektsioon's market overviews (Estonian editions). End of 2018, with end of 2017 in brackets: Swedbank 49% (46%), SEB Pank 25% (22%), Luminor Bank 10% (10%), LHV Pank 8% (9%), Coop Pank 2% (2%), Danske Bank's Estonian branch 1% (3%). End of 2025, with end of 2024 in brackets: Swedbank 39% (40%), LHV Pank 21% (19%), SEB Pank 19% (20%), Bigbank 7% (6%), Coop Pank 6% (6%), Luminor Bank 3% (4%), Inbank 2% (2%), others 3%. Companies' deposits at the end of 2025: Swedbank 37%, LHV Pank 27%, SEB Pank 23%, Coop Pank 6%, Luminor Bank 3%. Bank loans at the end of 2025: Swedbank 35%, SEB Pank 24%, LHV Pank 14%, Luminor Bank 11%, Coop Pank 7%.

m-a5764cc3.t: The ECB counts 50,297 POS terminals provided by payment service providers resident in Estonia at the end of 2025: 49,311 in Estonia and 986 in other EEA countries; all but one accept contactless payments. Earlier year-ends, in Estonia: 28,761 (2014), 31,601 (2015), 35,482 (2017), 35,886 (2019), 37,797 (2021), 43,432 (2023), 48,041 (2024); abroad: 83 (2015), 187 (2021), 305 (2023), 898 (2024). Eesti Pank's table shows 52,869 at end-2025 because it adds 2,572 e-commerce terminals to 37,333 POS terminals and 12,964 cash-register systems. The ECB's ATM series (695 at end-2021, 364 at end-2025) is not a count of all ATMs: Eesti Pank counts 660 at end-2025, 364 of them with a payment function.

m-a4936be2.t: ECB payments statistics (dataset PCN, annual, read 5 October 2026) give the number of cards issued by payment service providers resident in Estonia at year-end: 1,797,405 (2013), 1,820,812 (2014), 1,835,297 (2015), 1,842,332 (2016), 1,862,332 (2017), 1,883,448 (2018), 1,880,568 (2019), 1,872,894 (2020), 1,898,006 (2021), 1,970,625 (2022), 2,011,700 (2023), 2,141,673 (2024), 2,176,308 (2025) — series PCN.A.EE.PCS_ALL._T.PN, total cards irrespective of the number of functions. Debit cards (PCN.A.EE.PCS_ALL.11.PN): 1,442,843 in 2013, 1,753,104 in 2025; credit cards (…13.PN): 347,944 in 2013, 328,704 in 2025, with 2018-2020 blank.

m-96a98d2f.t: A change of owner of Luminor Bank, the fourth-largest lender among banks in Estonia at the end of 2025, is signed but not completed as of 5 October 2026: OTP Bank Plc. (Hungary) announced on 20 July 2026 that it had signed a share purchase agreement to acquire 100% of Luminor Holding, the parent of Luminor Bank, from a consortium of private equity funds managed by Blackstone and from DNB Bank, and that 'Completion of the transaction is subject to obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals'. The announcement puts Luminor's total assets at EUR 15.9 billion and its profit after tax at EUR 158 million in 2025. DNB Bank ASA announced the sale of its shareholding the same day.

m-82e57a6b.t: Finantsinspektsioon's yearbooks give the number of credit institutions operating in Estonia at year-end: 15 at the end of 2019 (the 2020 yearbook's 'one fewer than a year earlier'); 14 at end-2020, of which five were branches of foreign banks; 15 at end-2021, of which six branches; 13 at end-2022, of which four branches; 9 banks with an Estonian licence plus 4 branches at end-2023; 9 plus 5 at end-2024; 8 plus 6 at end-2025. On 5 October 2026 the supervisor's register lists eight licensed credit institutions (Inbank, LHV Pank, SEB Pank, Bigbank, Coop Pank, Holm Bank, Luminor Bank, Swedbank) and five branches (Citadele, Finora Bank, Nordea, OP Corporate Bank, TF Bank).

m-816c3288.t: Finantsinspektsioon's half-yearly review 'The Estonian financial services market as at 31 December 2025' (page edited 14 May 2026) puts numbers on the licensed non-bank sector: payment and e-money institutions intermediated payments of EUR 1.8 billion in 2025 (EUR 1.2 billion in 2024) in 28.1 million payments (19.4 million). Shares of volume at end-2025, end-2024 in brackets: Wallester 62% (49%), Maksekeskus 23% (29%), Ühisarveldused 7% (9%), Meieni 3% (7%), TavexWise 2% (2%), Adson 1% (1%), other 2% (3%); by number Wallester 58% and Maksekeskus 37%. For scale it cites Eesti Pank: domestic payments at banks were EUR 238 billion in 2025.

m-7faa695c.t: Estonian payment cards are almost all Mastercard on the debit side. On 30 June 2026 Eesti Pank counted 2,175,057 cards in issue (21.3% non-active): 1,765,162 debit cards, of which 1,720,412 Mastercard and 43,896 Visa, and 409,895 credit cards, of which 290,177 Mastercard and 39,673 Visa; 2,173,586 cards were contactless. On 31 March 2015 there were 1,820,475 cards, with debit split 1,141,476 Mastercard and 328,966 Visa.

m-7dd2cdb8.t: Online card payments on Estonian-issued cards, summed from Eesti Pank's monthly table 'Card transactions': 'e-commerce card transactions' in Estonia grew from 0.2 million worth EUR 22 million in 2015 to 3.6 million and EUR 81 million in 2019, 17.7 million and EUR 268 million in 2021 and 34.5 million and EUR 671 million in 2025; those abroad from 5.9 million and EUR 295 million in 2015 to 42.4 million and EUR 2,038 million in 2025. In 2025 e-commerce was 15.2% of the number and 24.3% of the value of all purchases on Estonian cards (POS and e-commerce, Estonia and abroad).

m-7d6b7436.t: Eesti Pank's page 'The payments market' (first published 1 November 2018 per its metadata; read 5 October 2026) sums up the non-bank sector in one sentence: 'Some payment services are also provided by payment institutions, but the volume of payments that they intermediate is very small next to those of the credit institutions.' It gives no figures and names no acquirers. Its page on continuity of banking services lists five credit institutions as providers of vital services - Swedbank AS, AS SEB Pank, Luminor Bank AS, AS LHV Pank, Coop Pank AS - and no payment institution, although since 1 October 2026 the law makes a payment or e-money institution with over 1% of Estonian payments eligible.

m-62a33411.t: AS TBB pank left the market in 2025: on 14 April 2025 Finantsinspektsioon gave it permission to terminate its services voluntarily, which revoked its operating licence and allowed voluntary winding-up; the notice of 15 April 2025 puts its market share at 0.003% of deposits and 0.02% of loans and says 'There are from today eight credit institutions operating in Estonia with a licence issued by Finantsinspektsioon'. By a precept announced on 4 March 2024, citing major deficiencies in money-laundering prevention, the supervisor had barred it from 19 February 2024 from cross-border payment services for non-resident legal entities or those with a non-resident beneficial owner.

m-5cbcd757.t: Finantsinspektsioon's yearbooks give the banks at the start of the period: 'As at 31 December 2013, there were 8 locally authorised credit institutions and 7 branches of foreign credit institutions operating in Estonia', with four more branches (UniCredit Finance, Bank DNB, Siemens Financial Services, Bankas Snoras) in liquidation; the same 8 and 7 are given for 31 December 2014. Estonian bank licences after that, per its reports: Cofi AS (later Inbank AS) in 2015 and Holm Bank AS in the first half of 2019. For end-2018 the 2019 market overview's key-figure box gives 16 banking market participants (15 at end-2019, six of them branches); the 2015-2017 reports read state no year-end total.

m-5226ceb4.t: Eesti Pank's table 'Number of ATMs, POSs and POS terminals' (last updated 23 July 2026) counts 57,602 point-of-sale terminals on 30 June 2026 - 41,610 POS terminals, 13,200 cash-register systems and 2,792 e-commerce 'terminals' - at 31,479 points of sale accepting cards. Year-end terminal totals: 32,400 (2015), 36,064 (2018), 38,895 (2020), 46,111 (2022), 51,688 (2024), 52,869 (2025). Points of sale: 20,773 (2015), 27,244 (2020), 32,702 (2023), 29,840 (2024), 29,634 (2025). The components step between 31 March and 30 June 2024 (points of sale 32,830 to 30,398; e-commerce 5,766 to 2,729) with no note in the table. ATMs: 801 at end-2015, 660 at end-2025, 668 on 30 June 2026.

m-47374740.t: EveryPay, the gateway behind Estonian banks' online card acceptance, belongs to LHV. AS LHV Group announced on 4 March 2022 a contract to acquire 100% of EveryPay AS for EUR 8 million, paid in new LHV Group shares and subject to its general meeting of 30 March 2022. It stated: 'About 70% of Estonian online card transactions and approximately 50% of those in the Baltics, are currently made through EveryPay' - over 15 million payments a year worth over EUR 800 million; the buyer's own 2022 figures, method not given. On 5 October 2026 the e-Business Register shows the company (registry code 12280690) as AS LHV Paytech, former name EveryPay AS, with AS LHV Group as sole shareholder.

m-3a8e30cf.t: Banks' physical network in Estonia shrank by two thirds over the period: the ECB's structural financial indicators count 163 offices of credit institutions in Estonia at the end of 2012, 140 in 2013, 107 in 2015, 91 in 2018, 74 in 2020, 62 in 2023 and 53 in 2025 (series SSI.A.EE.122C.N40.1.A1.Z0Z.Z, read 5 October 2026), while staff rose from 4,861 in 2013 to 6,146 in 2025 (SSI.A.EE.122C.N30.1.A1.Z0Z.Z). In the same dataset the total assets of branches of banks from other EU states fell from EUR 6,382 million at the end of 2016 to EUR 2,654 million in 2017 and EUR 1,071 million in 2019 (SSI.A.EE.122C.T11.1.L0.Z01.E).

m-32da507a.t: The Estonian branch of Danske Bank A/S ended in 2019: Finantsinspektsioon's annual report for 2019 lists 'Danske Bank A/S Estonia branch — Terminating the operations of the branch' with the date 02.12.2019 (the date of its management-board decision or of the notification forwarded), and says the branch's portfolio of loans to private clients was acquired by AS LHV Pank. The same table records the end of the Estonian branches of Svenska Handelsbanken AB (23.09.2019) and Scania Finans AB (10.12.2019); the 2020 yearbook says the Handelsbanken branch 'ceased its activities' during 2020.

m-1d9476d1.t: The e-Business Register (read 5 October 2026) shows who owns the two Estonian card-payment intermediaries. Maksekeskus AS (12268475): share capital EUR 631,089; shareholder row 'Luminor Bank AS' (11315936) with a contribution of EUR 631,089, dated 6 June 2025 - the bank its merchant terms name as card acquirer. AS LHV Paytech (12280690, formerly EveryPay AS): share capital EUR 1,679,422; shareholder row 'AS LHV Group' (11098261) with a contribution of EUR 1,679,422, dated 18 June 2026. The register notes that it shows holders of more than 10% of votes from the Estonian Central Register of Securities and that this information 'has an informative meaning'.

m-fff3dda4.t: myPOS's full tariff for Estonia (mypos.com/en-ee/pricing-and-fees/fees, read 5 October 2026) prices the step its 'instant settlement' leaves out: moving money from the myPOS e-money account to a bank costs EUR 4.00 per SEPA transfer and EUR 4.00 per SEPA Instant transfer as of that date; an international transfer 0.25% (minimum EUR 9.00, SHA) or 1% (minimum EUR 14.90, OUR). The account with IBAN, incoming transfers and the monthly and annual service fees are 'free of charge'. Two fees described as not standard apply after 10 consecutive months without transactions and two months' notice: an inactivity fee of EUR 15.00 and a 'No Acquiring Fee' of EUR 30.00.

m-f9e6806e.t: Paysera's Estonian fee pages (read 5 October 2026) price online card payments by the merchant's last 30 days: for cards issued in the EU from 1.45% (0-50 transactions or up to EUR 2,500) down to 1.25% (501-750 transactions or EUR 25,001-37,500), and for cards issued outside the EU from 2.90% down to 2.50%, minimum EUR 0.15 per payment; above that a special offer. Its newer 'Checkout Modern', open to businesses registered in Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, charges 0% on Baltic bank transfers made by payment initiation and cards 'from 1.25%', with no monthly fee. Paysera's point-of-sale tariff covers QR-code payments (0.70% falling to 0.20%), not card terminals.

m-ebea7133.t: LHV's indicative table also shows a 'processing fee' (töötlemistasu) per card type, which the page says derives from the price lists of card organisations and processors, with a second column dated from 24 April 2026. For EEA-issued Visa consumer debit cards the undated column gives 0.0150% + EUR 0.0418 at a terminal and 0.0250% + EUR 0.0418 in e-commerce; the column from 24 April 2026 gives 0.0779% + EUR 0.053136 and 0.0961% + EUR 0.11301. For EEA-issued Mastercard cards: 0.0100% + EUR 0.053155 for all cards and channels, and from 24 April 2026 0.01% + EUR 0.045 (consumer, terminal) and 0.164% + EUR 0.072796 (consumer, e-commerce). Read 5 October 2026. LHV's merchant fee is by agreement.

m-e99d5086.t: No enacted amendment changes the two state fees of the e-Residency path through mid-2027. In the versions of the Estonian State Fees Act already published for 1 November 2026, 1 January 2027 and 1 July 2027 (RT I, 11.07.2026, 167–169), § 272(6) still sets EUR 150 for review of an application for an e-resident's digital identity card (in force since 1 January 2025, RT I, 20.12.2024, 1) and § 62(2) still sets EUR 200 for entering a private limited company in the commercial register, EUR 265 on an expedited-procedure application (in force since 1 January 2022, RT I, 08.12.2021, 1). Compared on 5 October 2026 with the version in force 1 August–30 October 2026.
