m-e848b6f9.t: In-person acceptance through Stripe is not generally available in Estonia: Stripe's Terminal availability page (read 5 October 2026) lists EE under 'Available in (Preview)', not among the countries where Terminal 'is available'; EE is not among the preview countries marked as Tap to Pay only. The Estonian price page nevertheless publishes Terminal prices as of 5 October 2026: 1.4% + EUR 0.10 per successful charge for EEA cards and 2.9% + EUR 0.10 for non-EEA cards, plus EUR 0.10 per authorisation for Tap to Pay; the BBPOS WisePad 3 reader is listed at EUR 59.00 and the Stripe Reader S710 at EUR 259.00, both excluding VAT.

m-d1b76e8b.t: LHV's product page for payment collection in Estonia (read 5 October 2026, undated) shows monthly terminal rent of EUR 12.5 to EUR 20 plus VAT by device (LAN EUR 12.5, GSM EUR 19, Bluetooth EUR 20, cash-register-integrated EUR 13.5), first three months free for a business not yet using an LHV terminal, shortest rental 6 months; short-term rent (up to six months, GSM only) EUR 25 plus VAT. The bank's formal price list (section valid from 1 December 2022) gives both the terminal's monthly fee and the card servicing fee as 'by agreement'; the product page says the card fee depends on transaction volume. Bank links: no monthly fee, EUR 0.05 per transaction, first 6 months free for new customers.

m-8efa298b.t: Viva.com's Estonian price page (read 5 October 2026) publishes a 'price pack for Domestic & European Economic Area Consumer Cards' as of that date: in person 1.69% per transaction, minimum fee EUR 0.03; online 2.19% + EUR 0.24, the same over the phone. For domestic and EEA commercial cards, UK and international cards interchange and scheme fees are passed through, plus a Viva acquiring fee of 1.16% in person or 2.06% + EUR 0.24 online; Amex 2.75% in person and 2.95% + EUR 0.24 online, plus 0.40% if the card was issued outside the EEA. A refund costs the acceptance fee + EUR 0.30; 3-D Secure EUR 0.03 per attempt online; with certain e-commerce plugins a 0.35% surcharge 'may apply'.

m-87624e9b.t: Swedbank's published business price list in Estonia (section 'Servicing payment cards (for merchants)', effective as of 11.04.2025 and repeated unchanged in the complete price list valid from 31 August 2026; read 5 October 2026) gives the commission on a terminal transaction as 'as agreed', with two fixed tariffs: phone terminal transaction 0.99% + EUR 0.02, smart terminal transaction 1.45%. Monthly terminal rent, VAT added: stationary EUR 13, mobile EUR 19.50, 'stationary, mobile terminal' EUR 18, stationary with Bluetooth EUR 18, cash-register terminal EUR 45, card reader EUR 13. Minimum rental 3 months; installation within 5 banking days of signing is free, within 2 banking days EUR 84.

m-8699c1c9.t: SEB Estonia publishes fixed monthly fees for some terminals and leaves terminal transaction pricing to the contract (pages read 5 October 2026, undated). POS on Phone application: EUR 5 a month; touchscreen mobile terminal and mobile POS terminal: EUR 18 a month, each 'plus individual pricing for transactions'; stationary terminal and integrated cash system: 'applied individually'. New customers get up to 2 terminals free for 1 year. Payment card servicing: subscription free, transaction processing fee 'as per contract', installation by the next banking day EUR 75. SEB bank link: subscription minimum EUR 65, transaction fee 1% of the value, min EUR 0.13, max EUR 3.20; amendment EUR 15.

m-84b3313d.t: Stripe's price page for Estonia (stripe.com/en-ee/pricing, read 5 October 2026) lists for online card payments, as of that date: 1.5% + EUR 0.25 for 'standard European Economic Area cards', 2.8% + EUR 0.25 for 'premium European Economic Area cards', 2.5% + EUR 0.25 for UK cards and 3.15% + EUR 0.25 for international cards, plus 2% if currency conversion is required. SEPA Direct Debit is EUR 0.35. A dispute costs EUR 20.00 when received and a further EUR 20.00 when countered manually, the second returned if the dispute is won. For standard pricing the page states 'No setup fees, monthly fees, or hidden fees'; what counts as 'premium' is defined in a linked support article, not on the page.

m-8357d3e7.t: Revolut's Estonian payment-acceptance price page, as archived on 18 October 2025, listed for Visa and Mastercard: domestic consumer cards 1% + EUR 0.20 online and 0.8% + EUR 0.02 in person; domestic commercial cards and all international cards 2.8% + EUR 0.20 online and 2.6% + EUR 0.02 in person; no set-up or maintenance fee, the monthly fee 'included with Revolut Business plans'; Revolut Reader EUR 49 + VAT; chargeback EUR 15, refunded if the business wins. It advertised '24-hour settlement'. The plans page archived the same day showed Basic from EUR 10, Grow from EUR 30 and Scale from EUR 90 per month. The prices on 5 October 2026 were not read (security check).

m-820cb29a.t: Montonio's price page for Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania (read 5 October 2026) sells monthly plans as of that date, all fees stated without VAT: Starter EUR 11.99 per month with cards at 1.49% + EUR 0.25 and bank payments at EUR 0.20; Core EUR 14.99 and Core Flex EUR 39.99 per month with cards at 1.29% + EUR 0.20 and bank payments at EUR 0.05. The card price is for EU-issued consumer cards; EU-issued commercial cards cost 2.39% + EUR 0.20, UK-issued 2.50% + EUR 0.20, non-EU consumer 2.99% + EUR 0.20 and non-EU commercial 3.60% + EUR 0.20; a card dispute EUR 20; refunds free. Shopify shops have a separate tariff. The product is online only (checkout, payment links); no terminal is offered.

m-5ebefbd9.t: Stripe defines the two card classes of its EEA price list in a support article (metadata date 3 October 2026, read 5 October 2026): 'standard' domestic cards are consumer cards issued by Visa, Mastercard and Cartes Bancaires and all cards issued by American Express, Discover, Diners Club, Maestro and UnionPay; 'premium' domestic cards are 'commercial, corporate, or business cards issued by Visa, Mastercard, and Cartes Bancaires'. Stripe classifies a card 'based on information from card networks at the point of capture'. On the Estonian price page as of 5 October 2026 this is the difference between 1.5% + EUR 0.25 and 2.8% + EUR 0.25 per online payment.

m-58b4524e.t: Stripe's payout documentation (read 5 October 2026) gives Estonia an initial settlement timing of 7 calendar days and a default settlement timing of 3 business days for card payments, counted from the capture of the payment; it adds that after the first live payment the initial payout is typically scheduled 'within 7-14 days, depending on your industry, country of operation, and risk level', and that risk criteria may keep an account from moving to the default timing. SEPA Direct Debit payments settle in 6 business days.

m-5682bac8.t: Maksekeskus (MakeCommerce) publishes this Estonian price list, read 5 October 2026, VAT to be added: Baltic and Finnish bank payments 0.9% + EUR 0.05; online card payments (Mastercard, Visa, Apple Pay, Google Pay) 1.35% + EUR 0.15 plus a monthly fee of EUR 10; in person on a standard terminal 0.95% + EUR 0.02 with rent of EUR 13 per month, the same rate without rent on the phone app MakeCommerce POS; a card chargeback EUR 20; refunds and payment links free. Clients who joined up to 31 May 2025 keep the agreed or then-current prices; terminal contracts signed before 7 May 2026 keep the list in force at application, shown as 1.5% + EUR 0.05 with a EUR 19 minimum monthly fee (none for the app).

m-53c8e55f.t: The account behind Viva.com's Estonian plans carries a Greek IBAN and its own charges, per the Estonian price page (read 5 October 2026): an 'Account with IBAN (GR) with unlimited free incoming transfers' costs EUR 10.00 a month, or there is no monthly fee and each incoming transfer is charged - EUR 0.50 up to EUR 5,000, EUR 2.00 up to EUR 10,000, EUR 3.00 up to EUR 20,000 and EUR 4.00 above; an outgoing SEPA credit transfer or SEPA instant credit transfer costs EUR 0.25; a physical debit card costs EUR 2.99 a month, the digital business debit card is free; 'Daily Sales Clearance' is listed as free. These come on top of the monthly payment plan.

m-33b5d85b.t: SumUp's Estonian price page (read 5 October 2026) offers two plans as of that date. Pay-as-you-go: EUR 0 per month and 1.69% per in-person transaction for all cards, American Express and premium cards included. Payments Plus: EUR 19 per month and 0.89% per in-person debit or credit card transaction, with 1.69% for foreign, business and premium cards such as Amex; the page says the plan pays off from EUR 2,800 of monthly transactions. Online payments through Payment Links, Bookings and other digital products cost 1.69% on either plan. No set-up fee, hardware rental or monthly minimum; readers are sold from EUR 34 (Solo Lite), EUR 79 (Solo) and EUR 169 (Terminal), excluding VAT.

m-282ac6f9.t: SEB in Estonia publishes fixed rates for online card acceptance on its e-commerce product page (read 5 October 2026, undated): 1.35% per transaction, minimum EUR 0.13, for a card issued within the European Economic Area, and 2.55%, minimum EUR 0.13, for a card issued outside it; EUR 0.10 per PayPal payment; no fee for concluding the agreement and no monthly fee. The payment initiation fee is 'according to agreement' and an individual offer is available on request. The page does not say whether VAT is added, nor whether the card rates include interchange and scheme fees.

m-20ffc6c9.t: For an online shop Swedbank Estonia publishes (business price list read 5 October 2026): e-commerce payments platform — agreement fee free, monthly fee free, commission on a card transaction 'as agreed', and EUR 0.10 per transaction for payment initiation 'from Swedbank and from other financial institutions'; amendment of the agreement EUR 15. Its product page lists the banks reachable through payment initiation: Swedbank, SEB, Luminor and Citadele in all three Baltic states, LHV and Coop in Estonia, and Artea, Urbo and Revolut Bank in Lithuania.

m-1f4a35cf.t: Viva.com's Estonian price page (read 5 October 2026) adds a monthly subscription for the viva.com account to its transaction fees: omnichannel plans Zero at EUR 0.00 (minimum monthly charge EUR 4.99), Default EUR 4.99, Standard EUR 13.99, Premium EUR 19.99, differing in terminal IDs, websites, users and free outgoing SEPA transfers (4, 15, 30); each is marked 'Real time settlement: yes', and the account is listed as an 'Account with IBAN (GR)'. The terms effective 30 September 2026 say acquired amounts are credited to the user's Viva.com account 'as per the Payout Schedule, as published on www.viva.com', which Viva may amend unilaterally (clause 9.1) and extend in listed cases (clause 9.2).

m-178bba36.t: myPOS's Estonian price page (read 5 October 2026) charges no monthly fee for merchants under EUR 10,000 of monthly card turnover and prices per transaction as of that date. Card present (terminal): domestic and EEA consumer cards 1.45% + EUR 0.05; American Express 2.45% + EUR 0.05; all other consumer and commercial cards 2.85% + EUR 0.05. Card not present (online): domestic and EEA consumer cards 1.30% + EUR 0.20; American Express 2.50% + EUR 0.20; all other cards 2.90% + EUR 0.20; mail and telephone orders the online fee + 0.5%; UK-issued cards count as non-EEA online. Above EUR 10,000 a custom quote is offered. The merchant account with IBAN and a business Mastercard are listed as free.

m-07cf4a29.t: PayPal's merchant fee page for Estonia ('Last Updated: 7, September 2026', read 5 October 2026) applies one table to accounts of residents of 13 markets including Estonia. Receiving a commercial transaction costs 3.4% + fixed fee (EUR 0.35 for euro); a card-funded payment from a payer without a PayPal account 1.9% + fixed fee; QR-code transactions 0.9% + EUR 0.10 from EUR 10.01 and 1.4% + EUR 0.05 up to EUR 10.00. 'Domestic' means sender and receiver both in the EEA; for other senders an additional 1.29% (UK) or 1.99% (all other markets) applies. Advanced Credit and Debit Card Payments: 1.9% + fixed fee (EUR 0.35) blended, or interchange + 1.9% + fixed fee; American Express 3.5%.

m-0378a6f4.t: Adyen's public price page (read 5 October 2026) prices Visa, Mastercard and Maestro as a fixed processing fee plus 'Interchange+ + 0.60%'; the tooltip says interchange fees are variable and 'Interchange++ pricing passes these fees directly to you'. The processing fee is shown in the locale's currency: USD 0.13 on the global page, GBP 0.11 on en_GB, EUR 0.11 on the four euro-locale pages read (de_DE, nl_NL, fr_FR, it_IT); there is no Estonian locale, so EUR 0.11 is the euro-locale figure, not one stated for Estonia. The page states: 'We do not have monthly fees, set-up fees, integration fees or closure fees. We do have a minimum invoice depending on industry or business model.'

m-fa0bd9dc.t: Art. 6(1) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS, consolidated version of 18 October 2024) obliges a Member State whose public-sector online service requires electronic identification to recognise an eID means issued in another Member State for cross-border authentication if (a) its scheme is on the Commission's published list, (b) its assurance level is substantial or high and at least the level the service requires, and (c) the public body itself uses level substantial or high for that service; recognition 'shall take place no later than 12 months after the Commission publishes the list'. Art. 6 covers authentication only; electronic signatures fall under its Arts 24a and 27.

m-f757f0eb.t: Stripe accepts companies registered in Estonia through e-Residency, with a residence condition on the people behind them: its support article (read 5 October 2026) says 'the place of residency for individuals associated with your account needs to be located in one of the countries currently supported by Stripe'. Stripe's country list read the same day includes Estonia and Cyprus. A person based in an unsupported country is told he 'may be able to' set the business up as a US company through Stripe Atlas. Stripe's document page adds that when a person linked to the account (representative or owner) lives in a country other than the account's, a valid passport is the only accepted form of ID.

m-dd599f6a.t: Under § 22 of Estonia's AML act (in force 21 July 2026) a legal person is identified by name, registry code and registration date, and the names and powers of its board members, on the basis of the registry card or registration certificate of the relevant register or an equivalent document. Where the bank itself has access to the commercial register or to the relevant foreign register, submission of these documents 'does not need to be demanded from the customer'. The representative of a foreign legal person must, at the bank's request, produce a document proving his or her powers that is notarised and legalised or apostilled, unless an international agreement provides otherwise.

m-d4a8000c.t: SumUp's Estonian help centre (read 5 October 2026) says identity must be verified before payments are accepted: the user scans an identity document and sends a face photo, and verification 'may take several days'. Further documents may be asked by e-mail. For a natural person: an official identity document, proof of home address not older than 6 months, proof of business activity (sales invoices, public web pages) and other business documents. For a legal person: proof of business activity, documents naming every natural person who directly owns 25% or more, their identity documents, and other business documents such as registry code, founding documents, articles or a power of attorney.

m-d1b7ff89.t: Stripe's verification-document page (data served for Estonia, read 5 October 2026) lists as company documents: articles of association (Põhikiri), commercial register extract (Äriregistri registrikaart), tax certificate (Maksuandmete tõend) and VAT registration; as proof of address: bank statement, government letter, residence registration, utility or waste bill; and as proof of ownership or directorship: annual report, articles of incorporation (Asutamisleping), certificate of corporate status (Äriregistri väljavõte), registration document, partnership agreement, the beneficial-owner register and Stripe's own attestation templates. The data do not separate companies from sole proprietors.

m-ba9bc56d.t: Estonia's AML act defines the beneficial owner (§ 9, wording of RT I, 10.07.2020, 1, in force 20 July 2020 and unchanged on 5 October 2026) as the natural person who has the final dominant influence over a person through ownership or other control, or in whose interests a transaction is made. If that test gives no answer, it is the natural person whose direct and indirect shareholding in the company together 'exceeds 25 per cent', bearer shares included; failing that, the senior managing official. The 2017 wording spoke of '25 per cent plus one share or an ownership interest of more than 25 per cent'.

m-b337ebd2.t: For an Estonian account Stripe lists four acceptable identity documents - Juhiluba (driver's licence), ID-kaart (identity card), Pass (passport) and Elamisluba (residence permit) - and compares the ownership and control information a company submits with the national registry, naming for Estonia the Centre of Registers (rik.ee). Where the details differ from the registry, Stripe says this 'may be reported to your national registry of business'; where the business cannot be found there, Stripe asks for a confirmation in the Dashboard, and the ability to receive payouts 'will be paused if you are unable to submit this confirmation' (pages read 5 October 2026).

m-addf7426.t: For an e-resident, § 31(4) of Estonia's AML act (wording in force since 1 July 2024) says that where a bank identifies a person remotely with the e-resident's digital identity document, 'another document mentioned in subsection 3 of § 21 … must be used simultaneously' - that list includes a valid foreign travel document and a driving licence meeting § 4(1) of the Identity Documents Act. Until 30 June 2024 it made every foreign national add an identity document issued by the foreign state. Where the customer lives or is seated in a high-risk third country or a jurisdiction that funds or supports terrorism (§ 37(4) 4)), only the eIDAS-notified scheme or qualified trust service may be used.

m-9219215b.t: § 31 of Estonia's AML act (remote identification by banks) in three versions. Original (in force 27 November 2017): 'information technology means' were mandatory when a relationship was opened without presence with an e-resident or a person from or living in a non-EEA country, and with an EEA person whose outgoing payments exceeded EUR 15,000 a month (legal person 25,000); only an Estonian digital ID or an eIDAS scheme of level 'high' qualified. From 10 September 2020 (RT I, 10.07.2020, 1) the e-resident trigger was dropped. From 1 July 2024 (RT I, 21.06.2024, 3) the trigger is residence or seat outside the EEA, no longer origin, or the thresholds; 'substantial' level is accepted.

m-8775fba5.t: Estonia's AML act (RahaPTS § 21, in force 21 July 2026) has a natural person identified on one of: an Estonian identity document listed in § 2(2) of the Identity Documents Act, a valid travel document issued in a foreign country, a driving licence meeting § 4(1) of that Act, or a birth certificate for a child under seven. The bank keeps the name, the personal identification code or - where the person has none - date of birth and place of residence, the data on the right of representation and the contact details. If the original is not available, a notarised or officially certified copy or other credible independent information may be used, with at least two different sources.

m-511239f6.t: Finantsinspektsioon's advisory guidelines on preventing money laundering in credit and financial institutions, in the version valid from 1 May 2024 (comply-or-explain), say when the data taken at identification must be verified face-to-face or by video identification (point 4.3.1.14): if the customer is from a country outside the European Economic Area or has their residence or place of business there, or if outgoing payments exceed EUR 15,000 per calendar month for a natural person or EUR 25,000 for a legal entity, whatever the person's origin. Below those sums an EEA customer may be verified from two reliable sources instead.

m-4db6328b.t: Remote identification by an Estonian bank or financial institution is governed by § 31 of the AML act as rewritten from 1 July 2024 (RT I, 21.06.2024, 3). When the customer is not met in person and either lives or is seated outside the European Economic Area, or outgoing payments exceed EUR 15,000 a month (natural person) or EUR 25,000 (legal person), the institution must use an eIDAS-notified electronic identification scheme of assurance level substantial or high, or a qualified trust service; if that is not possible, another means that secures correct data, recorded image, video and audio of sufficient quality, and failure of the procedure if the connection breaks (§ 31(3^1)).

m-2404eab4.t: From 28 May 2018 to mid-2024 remote onboarding by Estonian banks ran under Minister of Finance regulation No 25 of 23.05.2018 (RT I, 25.05.2018, 17). It required high-assurance e-identification, a questionnaire and a mandatory real-time interview recorded with sound and image, kept for five years after the relationship ends. Its § 10 had the questionnaire establish 'the connection of the person's economic or family interests with Estonia' and, for a legal person, its economic links with Estonia, EEA states and third countries; an e-resident had to show the data page of a foreign travel document on camera. Repealed by RT I, 05.07.2024, 3: in force 8 July 2024, applied from 1 July 2024.

m-109be171.t: Cyprus has an eID scheme notified under the eIDAS Regulation: 'Cyprus National eID' with the eID means IDMe.cy, level of assurance High. It entered the list of notified schemes published in the Official Journal of the EU on 26 February 2024 (notice C/2024/1719) and still stands in the list as republished on 12 August 2026 (C/2026/4428), the latest in the EU repository on 5 October 2026. The European Commission's page for the scheme (last updated 28 February 2024) adds the earlier steps: pre-notified 11 July 2023, opinion of the Cooperation Network of 6 December 2023 (Opinion No 5/2023).

m-e98e780c.t: Estonian Government Regulation No 42 of 8 April 2022 (version in force since 21 May 2023) covers every Russian citizen applying for any visa (§ 2(1²)) or a temporary residence permit for study, employment or enterprise (§ 2(1¹)), and every Belarusian citizen applying for a visa for short-term employment, start-up entrepreneurship, remote work or enterprise or a residence permit for employment or enterprise (§ 2(1)). Extending a permit for employment or enterprise is outside it (§ 2(3)); § 2(6) excepts from the visa ban, among others, a visit to a spouse or direct-line relative living in Estonia as its citizen or long-term resident, and persons with EU free-movement rights.

m-c3d9ab02.t: Estonian law exempts start-ups from the EUR 65,000 investment and business-plan requirements of the residence permit for enterprise (Aliens Act § 192(2¹) 2), (6¹), in force since 18 January 2017) and provides a short- or long-stay visa for start-up entrepreneurship (§ 62⁴). A start-up is a business unit of a company registered in Estonia that is starting up and aims to develop and launch an innovative, repeatable business model with great global growth potential that contributes significantly to Estonia's business environment. Per the Police and Border Guard Board, an expert committee of the Ministry of the Interior evaluates the company within 10 working days of a complete application.

m-b06944d1.t: A second enterprise route needs no residence in Estonia. Under Aliens Act § 197³(1) (text in force 1 October–31 December 2026) a large investor is an alien who has made a direct investment of at least EUR 1,000,000 in a company in the Estonian commercial register that invests mainly in the Estonian economy, or in an investment fund investing mainly in such companies; the investment must last for the permit's term (§ 197³(2)). § 197⁴ lifts the conditions of actual residence and of registering a residence in the population register; § 115 point 17 takes the permit out of the immigration quota. The Police and Border Guard Board's page gives a reply in 90 days and a permit of up to 5 years.

m-aade8c2e.t: The restrictions on Russian and Belarusian citizens' business migration to Estonia in force on 5 October 2026 rest on Government Regulation No 42 of 8 April 2022, 'Imposition of a sanction of the Government of the Republic in connection with the aggression of the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus in Ukraine' (RT I, 08.04.2022, 3; in force 9 April 2022; last amended version in force since 21 May 2023, RT I, 20.05.2023, 4), issued under § 27(1) of the International Sanctions Act. It restricts granting visas, short-term employment and temporary residence permits for employment, study or enterprise.

m-9c64468f.t: Separately from the residence-permit sanction, Estonian Government Order No 247 of 8 September 2022 (RT III, 10.09.2022, 2), issued under § 17(1) 1) of the State Borders Act and in force since 19 September 2022, restricts crossing of the external border to enter Estonia by Russian citizens holding a valid short-stay visa. It was in force on 5 October 2026 as amended by Order No 14 of 22 January 2026 (in force 25 January 2026). Point 2 lists exceptions, among them visiting a spouse or direct relative living in Estonia who is an Estonian citizen or long-term resident, EU free-movement rights, transit to the state of residence and humanitarian grounds.

m-795879bd.t: The EUR 65,000 investment requirement of Estonia's residence permit for enterprise does not apply where the company has been in the Estonian commercial register for less than 12 months and starts up with state or private backing — an investment or loan from the state or from a private fund manager licensed by Finantsinspektsioon, or a grant from a state support measure (Aliens Act § 192(2¹) 1), wording in force since 1 January 2026, RT I, 17.04.2025, 2; text read as in force on 5 October 2026). Unlike a start-up, such a company is not freed from the business-plan description of § 192(5): the waiver in § 192(6¹) names start-ups only.

m-781bf81f.t: The ordinary residence permit for enterprise counts against Estonia's annual immigration quota, which may not exceed 0.1% of the permanent population (Aliens Act § 113(2); text in force 1 October–31 December 2026). § 115 leaves outside the count, among others, citizens of the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom (points 8, 9, 9¹), an alien granted a residence permit for enterprise in connection with start-up entrepreneurship (point 16) and a large investor (point 17); the shareholder route of § 192(2) is not on that list. Since 1 September 2026 the quota is set by Government regulation (§ 114(1), RT I, 21.05.2026, 1).

m-4fffba6b.t: The version of the Estonian Aliens Act already published for 1 January 2027 (RT I, 30.06.2026, 104) leaves the founder-migration rules as they stand on 5 October 2026: §§ 62⁴ (start-up visa), 62⁵ (remote-work visa), 192 (residence permit for enterprise, EUR 65,000 and EUR 16,000) and 197³ (large investor, EUR 1,000,000) are word for word the same as in the version in force 1 October–31 December 2026. In § 115, the list of persons outside the immigration quota, only point 19 changes: a residence permit for employment in a field with labour shortage under § 181(8) replaces the short-term employment permit of § 176² (RT I, 21.05.2026, 1).

m-4dc61c94.t: A holder of Estonia's residence permit for enterprise need not keep EUR 65,000 invested for ever: one year after the permit is granted, and on its extension, one of two tests may be met instead — the company's sales revenue is at least EUR 200,000 a year, or the social tax paid monthly in Estonia for persons working in the company at least equals the social tax payable monthly in Estonia on remuneration of five times Estonia's average gross wage for the year (Aliens Act § 192(7), § 194(2); text in force 1 October–31 December 2026). Where several aliens hold permits through one company, the test applies to each of them separately (§ 194(3)).

m-3c3e585a.t: A third-country national wishing to live in Estonia as a company owner needs a temporary residence permit for enterprise; citizens of EU states, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland do not (Police and Border Guard Board page, 5 October 2026). Under Aliens Act § 192(2) a shareholder must have at least EUR 65,000 invested in the share capital of an Estonian company and spent on real estate, machinery or equipment booked as fixed assets in Estonia; a sole proprietor needs EUR 16,000 (§ 192(3)). § 192(2¹) lifts the amount for start-ups and for companies under 12 months old started with state or licensed-fund backing. The page gives a reply within 90 days and a permit of up to 5 years.

m-3b4634d8.t: Estonia's 'digital nomad visa' is the visa for remote work of Aliens Act § 62⁵, in force since 1 July 2020: a short- or long-stay visa for an alien whose work does not depend on location and who continues working for an employer registered abroad, doing business for a company registered abroad in which he or she has a holding, or serving clients mainly abroad. It gives a temporary stay, not a residence permit. The programme page states a minimum income of 'EUR 4,500 net/monthly' and a stay of up to one year (read 5 October 2026); the Police and Border Guard Board asks for proof of income for the six months before the application.

m-13f65c91.t: The money test of Estonia's remote-work ('digital nomad') visa is fixed by § 15(7) of Minister of the Interior Regulation No 82 of 18 December 2015 as a rate of sufficient funds per day of stay: 0.60 times the subsistence level since 1 January 2026 (amendment RT I, 25.04.2025, 5), 0.75 times until 31 December 2025. With the subsistence level at EUR 220 a month in 2026 (2026 State Budget Act § 2(5) 5)) that is EUR 132 a day, EUR 3,960 for 30 days; at EUR 200 in 2025 it was EUR 150 a day, EUR 4,500 for 30 days — the figure the e-Residency programme page still showed on 5 October 2026. The regulation does not say net or gross.

m-fd71ca60.t: Two dates circulate for the start of instant payments in Estonia. Eesti Pank's page on the payments market says 'The first Estonian banks joined the instant payment system in 2018', and its page on RT1 says that system, run by EBA Clearing, 'started work in November 2017'. The European Payments Council's participant register dates AS SEB Pank's readiness for SEPA Instant Credit Transfer to 21 November 2017, the scheme's first day, and Swedbank's and LHV Pank's to autumn 2018. So 2017 is the date of the first Estonian participant and 2018 the year the other two largest banks followed.

m-f8273ee0.t: Eurosystem central banks, Eesti Pank among them, do not hold client funds for payment or e-money institutions. Decision (EU) 2025/222 of the European Central Bank of 27 January 2025 (ECB/2025/2), applying from 9 April 2025, states in Article 3(1): 'Eurosystem central banks shall not offer or provide safeguarding accounts to NB-PSPs or to crypto-asset service providers.' Accounts that non-bank providers hold in central-bank-operated payment systems serve settlement and are capped by a maximum holding amount (Article 4). The date from which non-bank providers may request access to TARGET was moved from 16 June 2025 to 6 October 2025 by Decision (EU) 2025/1148 of 2 June 2025 (ECB/2025/18).

m-ce9e63b4.t: Taken together, bank-link and payment-initiation payments by Estonian households were 43.4 million worth EUR 2,387 million in 2025 - 8.8% of the number and 23.7% of the value of household card payments that year (492.2 million, EUR 10,072 million). Against online card purchases alone the picture reverses: Estonian-issued cards made 34.5 million e-commerce transactions worth EUR 671 million in Estonia in 2025. In August 2026 Eesti Pank's table of 'transactions initiated by banklink and open banking' showed 3.87 million transactions worth EUR 431 million for all customer groups.

m-9879ce3d.t: SEPA migration in Estonia happened on 1 February 2014, the deadline of Regulation (EU) No 260/2012. Per Eesti Pank: from that date only the IBAN is officially used; it closed its retail payment system ESTA on 31 January 2014 and interbank payments moved to STEP2, with five settlement cycles a day instead of ten. The domestic direct debit gave way to the 'e-invoice standing order'. Its SEPA page (read 5 October 2026) says 'The banks operating in Estonia do not offer direct debit services'; its FAQ of early 2014 is narrower: banks do not let companies collect by SEPA direct debit within Estonia, while a bill abroad can be paid by cross-border SEPA direct debit from an Estonian account.

m-60450468.t: Bank links against cards in Eesti Pank's statistics (payments sent by households, summed by year): 'bank link payment orders' rose from 14.7 million worth EUR 385 million in 2015 to a peak of 29.8 million and EUR 1,083 million in 2021, then fell to 14.5 million and EUR 657 million in 2025. A new row, 'payment initiated with another service provider', starts in 2022 with 13.1 million payments worth EUR 840 million and reached 28.9 million and EUR 1,730 million in 2025. Household card payments in the same table were 257.1 million (EUR 4,210 million) in 2015 and 492.2 million (EUR 10,072 million) in 2025.

m-5a4aa20b.t: Eesti Pank's Payments Review of March 2026 (Maksete Ülevaade) puts instant payments at 87% of the monthly number of domestic payments in December 2025 (88% a year earlier) and 93% of cross-border ones (89%); the review charts this share only for payments made in the RT1 and STEP2 systems (Figure 6.1), i.e. among interbank transfers, not card payments. Contactless payments were 82% of payments with Estonian bank cards in Estonia in the fourth quarter of 2025 (78%), and 33% of point-of-sale payments in Estonia with Estonian banks' cards were made by digital wallet (28%). Point-of-sale payments with Estonian-issued cards averaged 1,172 thousand a day in 2025, 1,088 thousand of them in Estonia.

m-45587147.t: For non-bank providers in the euro area, Estonia included, the EU duty to offer instant payments comes later than for banks. Under Article 5a of Regulation (EU) No 260/2012 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/886, the duty falls on providers that offer their users ordinary credit transfers: in the euro area they had to receive instant credit transfers in euro by 9 January 2025 and send them by 9 October 2025, while payment institutions and e-money institutions located in the euro area must offer both by 9 April 2027 (Article 5a(8)). Charges for instant transfers may not exceed those for other credit transfers of the corresponding type (Article 5b, euro area: from 9 January 2025).

m-36a5115a.t: Since 18 July 2025 Estonian payment and e-money institutions not operating under an exemption have a statutory route into settlement systems: the act of 18 June 2025 (RT I, 08.07.2025, 5) lets them be system members once Finantsinspektsioon has recognised their compliance (Payment and Settlement Systems Act § 6(3-1); Payment Institutions and E-money Institutions Act §§ 63-9, 63-10). The supervisor decides within two months of receiving all documents, at most four months after the application. The act also lets client funds be kept at Eesti Pank under its rules (§§ 79(1), 80(1)), but ECB Decision (EU) 2025/222 bars Eurosystem central banks from offering such safeguarding accounts.

m-3104f4d0.t: The European Payments Council's register of SEPA Instant Credit Transfer participants listed eight Estonian payment service providers on 5 October 2026, with these readiness dates: AS SEB Pank 21 November 2017 (the scheme's launch day), Swedbank AS 11 September 2018, AS LHV Pank 20 November 2018, Coop Pank AS 9 April 2019, inHouse Pay AS 11 May 2021, Luminor Bank AS 31 August 2021, Bigbank AS 6 March 2023 and Monemon AS 4 March 2024. Two of the eight - inHouse Pay and Monemon - are e-money institutions, not banks.

m-23b71494.t: Eesti Pank describes the plumbing of Estonian instant payments on its website (read 5 October 2026): the largest banks use only EBA Clearing's RT1 system for SEPA instant payments - 'It is used by SEB, Swedbank and LHV, which helped in its development, and also by Coop Pank' - and the banks offering instant payments joined the Eurosystem's TIPS service in 2021. On non-banks it says that indirect participation in RT1 means 'SEPA instant payments can be sent and received by non-bank payment service providers like payment institutions and e-money institutions'.

m-dfe6caca.t: Beneficial-owner filing by an Estonian company, as in force on 5 October 2026 (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act §§ 76-77): an OÜ files, through the commercial register information system, each beneficial owner's name, personal identification code and its country (or date and place of birth and country of residence) and the manner of control; the data must be filed together with the application for entry in the commercial register; changes are filed within 30 days of learning of them; if nothing has changed, the company confirms the data when filing its annual report. The filing duty has applied since 1 September 2018.

m-b1234df4.t: Changes to an Estonian company's beneficial-owner data filed on the e-Business Register portal need neither a signature nor a state fee and are made 'automatically and immediately after submission', per the Centre of Registers' guide 'Modification and approval of beneficial owners' (dated 5 September 2021, read 5 October 2026). They are entered by a person entitled to represent the company after logging in to the portal; the same guide names a notary as the other channel. The portal does not let all beneficial owners be deleted unless new ones are added.

m-8a80f35c.t: Estonia's beneficial-owner register started on 1 September 2018: §§ 76-80 of the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act (adopted 26 October 2017, RT I, 17.11.2017, 2, in force 27 November 2017) entered into force on that later date under § 119(1). Companies file the data through the commercial register information system. On public access the Estonian text has not been narrowed after the Court of Justice judgment of 22 November 2022: § 78(1), in the wording in force since 7 March 2022 and still in the version in force on 5 October 2026, says beneficial-owner data and the notations made on them 'are made public in the commercial register information system'.

m-880cbe0a.t: Estonia's Ministry of Finance announced on 8 June 2026 that beneficial-owner data in the register (TEKSA) 'will no longer be freely accessible to everyone': from 10 July 2026 unauthenticated users were to lose access, and only competent authorities, obliged entities and persons demonstrating a legitimate interest would see the data, free of charge, through the e-Business Register. The Centre of Registers' notice of 4 June 2026 added that the Ministry would decide on access, including to the API, and that beneficial-owner data would stop being published as open data. The Ministry gave the EU's new anti-money-laundering framework and Court of Justice case law as the reason.

m-59e7cda4.t: The restriction of public access to Estonian beneficial-owner data planned for 10 July 2026 did not take effect. The Ministry of Finance's press release of 10 July 2026 says 'the changes planned from 10 July will not be applied and until the new framework enters into force the current access rules apply', and that the date will be announced once the regulation is adopted; per ERR (25 June 2026) the Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs had not approved the draft. On 5 October 2026 a company page on ariregister.rik.ee opened without logging in still showed the beneficial owner's name, personal identification code and manner of control, and no new date had been published.

m-504d22f3.t: Public access to Estonia's beneficial-owner data is unchanged on 5 October 2026, after an announced restriction did not take effect. The Centre of Registers gave notice on 4 June 2026 that 'From July 10, 2026, the access rights to beneficial owners data in the e-Business Register will change' - access only for logged-in persons authorised by the Ministry of Finance, no open-data files. On 10 July 2026 the Ministry said the changes planned from 10 July are not applied and the existing access rules stay until a new regulation is adopted. The Minister of Finance's Regulation No 22 of 6 April 2023, whose § 10(2) makes the data public, stands unamended in Riigi Teataja.

m-42dfb72e.t: If an Estonian company has not filed its beneficial-owner data, the registration department of Tartu County Court notifies it and demands the data, which must then be filed within ten working days of receiving the notice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act § 77²(1)-(2), in force since 7 March 2022; text as of 5 October 2026). The controller of the register of beneficial owners is the Ministry of Finance; the Centre of Registers and Information Systems and the registration department are its processors (§ 76²(2)). The data in that register 'have informative meaning' (§ 76²(4), in force since 15 March 2022).

m-409d52c1.t: Under Estonian law as in force on 5 October 2026 beneficial-owner data are public: § 78(1) of the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act says the data are published in the commercial register information system; they are issued free of charge to obliged entities, government authorities, Finantsinspektsioon and courts (§ 78(3)). The only restriction in the Act is § 79² (in force since 15 March 2022): on a reasoned request the controller limits public access where it would expose the owner to a disproportionate risk of fraud, kidnapping, blackmail, extortion, harassment, violence or intimidation, or where the owner is a minor or lacks full legal capacity.

m-28d474c3.t: Estonian penalty for not filing beneficial-owner data, as in force on 5 October 2026 (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act § 95): a shareholder or member of a private legal person who fails to submit the data, fails to report a change or knowingly submits false data is punished by a fine of up to 300 fine units, and a legal person by a fine of up to EUR 400,000 (amount in force since 1 November 2023, RT I, 17.03.2023, 2) - in both cases only if the act has put an obliged entity in a position where it cannot apply the due-diligence measure of § 20(1) p 3.

m-0592985a.t: While the restriction on Estonian beneficial-owner data is postponed, its machinery is in place. The Centre of Registers' news item (in Estonian, dated 1 July 2026, later updated with the postponement) says applications for assessment of a legitimate interest can still be filed and the beneficial-owner API services taken into use, and that access rights change 'from the entry into force of the regulation'. On 5 October 2026 a public company page on ariregister.rik.ee showed, under the still-visible owner data, a block 'Query for beneficial owners data - Authentication is required to request access', with a paper form to the Ministry of Finance for a person without e-authentication tools.

m-faeb6584.t: Estonian social tax (33%) is due on fees paid to a member of a management or controlling body of a legal person (Social Tax Act § 2(1) 4), § 7(1)), and the Tax and Customs Board applies it to a non-resident board member too: social tax 'is not due on remuneration paid to members of the management body of an Estonian company only if the recipient of such remuneration has been issued in his or her home country a certificate of social security coverage valid in such foreign country on Form A1' (page updated 4 November 2025). The company must also register the paid board member in the employment register.

m-e77c6b9b.t: The Estonian Tax and Customs Board states how it applies Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 (social tax page, updated 20 July 2026): only one state's legislation applies to a person at a time; as a general rule contributions are paid where the work is carried out; for persons working in several countries and for posted workers they are paid in the state whose institution issued an A1 certificate. 'If the A1 certificate has been issued in another Member State, there will be no social tax liability in Estonia and the employee's social security contributions must be paid according to the rules of that Member State.' In Estonia the Social Insurance Board decides the state of affiliation and issues A1.

m-c92ccdb1.t: Under Title II of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 (consolidated version of 31 July 2019, the latest in the EU repository on 5 October 2026) a person is subject to the legislation of one Member State only, and a person pursuing an activity as an employed or self-employed person in a Member State is subject to that state's legislation (Art. 11(1), 11(3)(a)). A person normally active in two or more Member States falls under the state of residence if a substantial part of the activity is pursued there (Art. 13(1)(a), 13(2)(a)). The Regulation has no rule specific to company directors.

m-c5ea6800.t: When another Member State's social security law applies to an employee of an Estonian company, the company carries that state's employer duties: under Art. 21(1) of Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 an employer with its registered office outside the competent Member State 'shall fulfil all the obligations laid down by the legislation applicable to his employees', notably paying contributions, as if established there. Art. 21(2) lets an employer with no place of business there agree with the employee that the employee pays them on its behalf, 'without prejudice to the employer's underlying obligations', with notice to the competent institution. The article speaks of employees, not board members.

m-b9e38479.t: The Estonian Social Insurance Board's guidance on A1 (page updated 11 March 2026) says a person involved with more than one EU state through work must apply for Form A1 to have the applicable legislation determined, and: 'If in addition to another country of employment one only works in Estonia but does not reside here, Form A1 must be applied for at the social security institution of one's country of residence.' It issues A1 'within the next working day' on an electronic application only if listed conditions are met, among them that the employee lives in Estonia; applications with shortcomings or on paper take up to 30 days. The page does not mention members of management boards.

m-85f3ab60.t: The e-Residency programme's guidance on directors' fees (knowledge-base article updated 19 January 2026) sorts a non-resident board member of an Estonian company into three cases for Estonian social tax: a person living and insured in an EU state, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein or Switzerland should obtain an A1 certificate from the home authority 'to avoid having the company pay 33% social tax in Estonia'; a person insured in Canada, Ukraine or Australia may present the certificate under the social security agreement; residents of other third countries 'will not be able to get an exemption'. It adds that nothing obliges an owner to pay himself a salary or fee before dividends are paid.

m-0dd6b786.t: The Estonian Social Tax Act exempts from social tax employee pay (§ 2(1) 1)) and fees under a contract for services (§ 2(1) 6)) that an Estonian resident pays to a non-resident when the place of work is in a foreign state (§ 3 point 7). The exemption does not list § 2(1) 4), the fee of a member of a management or controlling body of a legal person, so a non-resident board member's fee stays within social tax wherever the duties are performed. Estonian text read, version in force 22 May – 31 December 2026 (RT I, 21.05.2026, 19); the version scheduled from 1 January 2027 (RT I, 03.06.2026, 51) has the same points.

m-01b4a99f.t: Until October 2026 an Estonian company paying a fee to a non-resident board member declared it in Annex 2 of form TSD under payment type 156 (income and social tax due) or 157 — a fee 'not taxed with social tax in Estonia if a foreign A1/E101 exists' — naming at code 2060 the state that issued the A1 (Tax and Customs Board instructions, edition from 01.01.2024). Finance Minister Regulation No 21 of 30 September 2026 (RT I, 02.10.2026, 6; in force 5 October 2026) abolished that annex: payments to residents and non-residents are declared in one 'Väljamaksed' part of TSD, with fields for the A1-issuing state and the state of work. Whether numbers 156/157 survive there was not established.

m-e7f8447c.t: The legislative history confirms that Estonia kept its surcharge ban at the PSD2 minimum. The Government's explanatory memorandum to bill 498 SE - the 2017 act transposing PSD2, which added § 725(9) to the Law of Obligations Act - summarises the change as a ban on charging an additional fee for the use of '(most)' card-based payment instruments and states that the ban does not extend to payment cards whose fees are not regulated in Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/751: 'such payment instruments are commercial cards'. The memorandum does not discuss using the Member State option of Article 62(5) of PSD2 to prohibit or limit surcharges more widely.

m-c531a8d8.t: Estonia did not extend the surcharge ban beyond what PSD2 itself requires. For instruments outside § 725(9) of the Law of Obligations Act - in practice commercial cards and three-party schemes - § 725(7) says the contract between the payee and its payment service provider 'may provide for' the right to agree a fee with the payer or offer a discount for a particular payment instrument. Since 15 July 2025 a second sentence caps that fee at the payee's actual cost of using the instrument (added by the act of 18 June 2025, RT I, 08.07.2025, 4). Under § 725(8) a payer not told of the fee before initiating the payment owes nothing.

m-925fac61.t: Estonia did not use the PSD2 option to treat micro-enterprises as consumers. The Law of Obligations Act draws the line at 'consumer': under § 733^14(6) (wording of RT I, 01.03.2023, 3, in force 11 March 2023), where the client 'is not a consumer' the parties may agree that §§ 710^1-711^2 (duty to contract, information), 719^1 (two months' notice of changes), 720 (cancellation), the second sentence of § 724^1(2), § 725(5), §§ 726-727^1, 733^3, 733^4 (burden of proof), 733^6 (refunds) and 733^8 (payer's liability) do not apply in part or in full, and may agree a period other than the 13 months of § 733^7(2) for reporting unauthorised payments. The act has no word for micro-enterprise.

m-534971c6.t: A second Estonian cost cap applies to consumer sales whatever the payment instrument: under § 28-1(2) of the Law of Obligations Act, if a trader charges a consumer a fee for paying a contractual money obligation with a particular means of payment, the fee may not exceed the cost the trader incurs for the use of that means. The Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority may issue a precept against a trader breaching § 28-1 or § 725(9) (Consumer Protection Act § 65(2), wording in force from 1 September 2026). Estonian texts read 5 October 2026.

m-3964de8c.t: Estonia transposed the second Payment Services Directive on the directive's deadline. The Act amending the Payment Institutions and E-money Institutions Act and, in connection with it, other Acts was adopted by the Riigikogu on 15 November 2017, published as RT I, 07.12.2017, 1, and entered into force on 13 January 2018; besides the licensing Act it rewrote the payment-services provisions of the Law of Obligations Act. Payment initiation and account information were added to the list of payment services (§ 3(1) points 7 and 8). Payment institutions already operating had to bring their activity and documents into line with the new wording by 13 July 2018 (§ 132(1)).

m-09559547.t: Estonia's surcharge ban sits in § 725(9) of the Law of Obligations Act (Võlaõigusseadus): a payee may not charge the payer a fee for using a payment instrument where interchange fees are regulated by Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/751, nor for payment services covered by Regulation (EU) No 260/2012 (SEPA credit transfers and direct debits). The provision was inserted by the act published as RT I, 07.12.2017, 1 and has been in force since 13 January 2018; it stood unchanged in the consolidated text in force from 1 September 2026 to 31 December 2026 (RT I, 20.06.2026, 18), read in Estonian on 5 October 2026.

m-07efc368.t: When Estonia banned card surcharges in 2017, the ban was expected to change little in practice. The Government's explanatory memorandum to bill 498 SE (the PSD2 transposition act, in force 13 January 2018) records that, according to the Estonian Banking Association, contracts for the use of card terminals already prohibited charging customers a surcharge to recover card costs, and that the Estonian Chamber of Commerce and Industry assessed the economic effect on traders as minimal 'since surcharging is not customary in Estonia'. The memorandum rates the effect on traders as small.

m-d358c43f.t: AS SEB Pank's page 'Restrictions in executing payments' (read 5 October 2026) states: 'On 1 June 2022, SEB stopped offering payment services in all currencies to Russia and Belarus', its cards cannot be used there, and it 'no longer allows transactions that have a direct or indirect connection with Russia', for example the accounts of a Russian company held in a bank of another country; it 'may refuse' transactions with a link to Belarus. Cross-border payments with Cuba, Crimea/Sevastopol, Iran, North Korea, Sudan, Syria and Venezuela are not enabled. By banking policy the bank does not settle with persons on the US OFAC SDN list or legal entities owned 50% or more by them.

m-ab039f55.t: Besides the countries with which it makes no payments at all, AS SEB Pank publishes a second list of countries and regions where 'there may be restrictions in executing cross-border payments' - on account of sanctions, the risk of their circumvention, or conditions set by correspondent banks or by SEB itself (page 'Restrictions in executing payments', read 5 October 2026). Among the 26 entries are Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Pakistan, Lebanon and Tunisia. The bank calls the list not exhaustive and may refuse or suspend a payment and ask for documents.

m-a5f1d133.t: LHV Pank states in its FAQ 'Account information' (read 5 October 2026): 'We have decided to stop onboarding Russian or Belarusian citizens without a legal basis to live in the European Union', and for companies: 'We have decided to stop onboarding companies whose beneficial owners are Russian or Belarusian citizens without a valid Estonian residence permit.' The test differs: a legal basis to live in the EU for a private person, a valid Estonian residence permit for the beneficial owner of a company. The page gives no date for the decision.

m-8bc3f18c.t: Coop Pank AS publishes its rule on Russian and Belarusian customers in a summary of its risk appetite (last update 28.02.2025): the group does not establish client relationships with, or allow occasional transactions by, Russian or Belarusian citizens without a valid residence permit of an EU or EEA state or Switzerland; the same holds for companies in which such a person holds 50% or more or controls the management or supervisory board as chairman. It performs no transfers to or from Russian or Belarusian banks or their subsidiaries elsewhere, nor, 'in general', to or from Armenian, Azerbaijani, Kazakhstani, Kyrgyzstani, Moldovan, Serbian, Tajikistani, Turkmen and Uzbekistani banks.

m-4fe82302.t: Under § 21 of Estonia's International Sanctions Act (text of 1 July 2026) a 'person with special obligations' - credit and financial institutions and, since 17 June 2024, among others gambling operators, real-estate intermediaries, auditors, accountants, tax advisers, trust and company service providers, notaries and attorneys - checks, when a financial sanction starts, changes or ends, whether a present or prospective customer is sanctioned, applies the due diligence of § 20(1) 1-4 of the AML act, and on finding or suspecting a breach applies the sanction and informs the Financial Intelligence Unit. Omitting it at onboarding costs a legal person up to EUR 400,000 (§ 35^3).

m-4e6fdfde.t: Swedbank AS's page on anti-money-laundering and sanctions (read 5 October 2026) lists 'Prohibited Countries' with which it 'has the obligation and the right not to execute any direct transactions (including cash and non-cash payments, card payments) in any currencies': Afghanistan, Crimea, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, the Republic of Belarus, the Russian Federation, Syria, the non-government-controlled parts of Ukraine's Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, and Venezuela. Indirect transactions are also treated as unacceptable and assessed case by case. The bank says it applies US and UK financial sanctions in addition to those of Estonia, the UN and the EU.

m-45b572a0.t: Estonia's International Sanctions Act (passed 20 February 2019, RT I, 19.03.2019, 11, in force 1 January 2020; text in force 1 July 2026) splits supervision as the AML act does. The Financial Intelligence Unit supervises compliance with financial sanctions by 'persons with special obligations' (§ 30(1)); Finantsinspektsioon supervises the credit and financial institutions under its supervision (§ 30(1^1), added 15 March 2022); the Bar Association and the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs cover attorneys and notaries. Since 17 June 2024 the Tax and Customs Board, the consumer authority, the Transport Board and the Defence Forces supervise other sanction types.

m-fbbd37a3.t: An Estonian company with no business in Estonia may be refused VAT registration. Under § 20(4¹) of the Value-Added Tax Act (in force since 1 March 2014; text as of 5 October 2026) a person must prove, to be registered, that it engages in or is starting business in Estonia; the tax authority may ask for more evidence, decides within five working days of receiving it, and does not register a person who neither engages in nor starts business. The Tax and Customs Board's page for companies founded by e-residents (updated 4 November 2025, read 5 October 2026) says Estonian businesses 'are not automatically deemed value added tax payers'.

m-e3d77562.t: Proposed, not adopted as of 5 October 2026: Government bill 992 SE (Act amending the Value-Added Tax Act, first reading completed 28 September 2026) would end tax periods longer than a calendar month. Point 31 repeals Value-Added Tax Act § 27(4), under which the tax authority may, on a taxable person's reasoned application, set a tax period longer than a month; point 63 adds § 46(29): such decisions made before 31 December 2026 lose validity on 1 January 2027. Neither point is among those deferred to 1 July 2028, so both would start on 1 January 2027. The same bill rewrites § 27(1^5) on showing intra-Community supply data on the VAT return.

m-9e96a314.t: Outline (ii), same café - stage 4, receipts and taxes, as of 5 October 2026. Receipt: every consumer who pays at once gets a document proving the purchase, on paper on demand and by default for most cash purchases; a VAT invoice is not required for a private customer. The tax acts impose no cash register; Alcohol Act § 44 requires one where alcohol is sold. VAT: restaurant and catering services are taxed at the standard 24%; registration is compulsory once turnover passes EUR 40,000 in the calendar year; input VAT on hosting the company's own guests or catering its own employees is not deductible. Income tax: paid by the company on distributed profit - 22% of the amount divided by 0.78.

m-4ab0e5cc.t: Restaurant and catering services carry Estonia's standard VAT rate, 24% of the taxable value as of 5 October 2026: Value-Added Tax Act § 15(1) sets 24% (in force since 1 July 2025) for everything not listed in § 15(1^1)-(4), and those lists - 13% for accommodation or accommodation with breakfast, 9% for books, listed medicines and press publications, 0% for exports and similar - do not mention restaurant or catering services. Their place of supply is Estonia when provided in Estonia (§ 10(2) point 4). Input VAT on goods and services used for receiving guests or for catering or accommodating one's own employees is not deductible (§ 30(1)).

m-3ecce38e.t: VAT registration in Estonia is by application; founding a company does not trigger it. As in force on 5 October 2026 (Value-Added Tax Act § 19(1), wording of 1 January 2025) the duty to register arises on the day a person's turnover arising in Estonia exceeds EUR 40,000 counted from the start of the calendar year; it does not arise if all of the year's turnover is exempt or zero-rated, intra-Community supply of goods excepted. The application is due within three working days and may be filed digitally signed through the commercial register system (§ 20(1)); the tax authority registers within five working days of receipt (§ 20(3)). The text enacted for 1 January 2027 keeps EUR 40,000.

m-35651b8c.t: For an Estonian online shop sending goods to consumers in other EU states, Value-Added Tax Act § 10^1 (wording in force since 1 July 2021; Estonian text read 5 October 2026) keeps Estonia as the place of supply only while three conditions hold: the seller is established in no member state other than Estonia, the buyers are not registered for VAT, and the total of such distance sales and electronically supplied services exceeded EUR 10,000 neither in the previous nor in the current calendar year (§ 10^1(7)). From the supply that passes EUR 10,000 the customer's state is the place of supply (§ 10^1(5), (9)); the seller may choose that treatment earlier, for at least two years (§ 10^1(8)).

m-2c1be6ee.t: Standard VAT in Estonia, by dated versions of § 15(1) of the VAT Act: 20% from 1 July 2009 to 31 December 2023; 22% from 1 January 2024 (RT I, 01.07.2023, 2); 24% from 1 July 2025, introduced by § 21 of the Security Tax Act (RT I, 02.01.2025, 2). That Act also set a return to 22% on 1 January 2029 but was repealed with effect from 18 July 2025; the text in force on 5 October 2026, like the one published for 1 January 2027, states 24% with no end date. Accommodation is 13% since 1 January 2025 (9% before); the 9% rate covers books and educational literature, medicines and some hygiene and disability goods on a ministerial list and, since 1 January 2025, press publications (5% before).

m-c3b778f7.t: Compulsory review (ülevaatus) of annual accounts in Estonia, as in force on 5 October 2026 (Auditors Activities Act § 92(1)-(3)): a review is compulsory where at least two of these are exceeded - sales revenue or income EUR 2,000,000, total assets EUR 1,000,000, average number of employees 24 - or at least one of these - EUR 6,000,000, EUR 3,000,000, 72 employees; a compulsory review may be replaced by an audit. The euro amounts were set by Act RT I, 07.01.2025, 1 (in force 17 January 2025) and apply to reporting periods that began from 1 January 2024. An OÜ below the review thresholds has no statutory audit or review duty unless its articles or another law impose one.

m-b896a781.t: Estonia's audit thresholds in four dated versions of § 91 of the Auditors Activities Act (two-of-three test; one-of-three test). In force 1 January 2015: revenue EUR 2m, assets EUR 1m, 30 employees; EUR 6m, EUR 3m, 90. From 1 January 2016 (RT I, 30.12.2015, 4; for reporting periods beginning from that date, § 184(2¹)): EUR 4m, EUR 2m, 60; EUR 12m, EUR 6m, 180. From 1 July 2017 (RT I, 30.06.2017, 1): the employee figure of the two-of-three test fell from 60 to 50. From 17 January 2025 (RT I, 07.01.2025, 1; applied retroactively to reporting periods begun from 1 January 2024, § 185³(1)): EUR 5m, EUR 2.5m, 50; EUR 15m, EUR 7.5m, 180.

m-aaee498b.t: Estonia redefined its accounting size classes by Act RT I, 07.01.2025, 1, in force 17 January 2025 and applied to reporting periods beginning from 1 January 2024 (Accounting Act § 62(17)). A micro-undertaking is now any accounting entity not exceeding two of: total assets EUR 450,000, income EUR 900,000, 10 employees; a small one, a non-micro entity with two of: EUR 7,500,000, EUR 15,000,000, 50 employees (§ 3 p 14-15). Before, a micro-undertaking was only an OÜ with assets up to EUR 175,000, liabilities not above equity, a sole shareholder who is also a board member and sales up to EUR 50,000; a small one exceeded at most one of EUR 4,000,000 assets, EUR 8,000,000 sales, 50 employees.

m-6bf4052c.t: Compulsory audit of annual accounts in Estonia, as in force on 5 October 2026 (Auditors Activities Act § 91(1)-(2), amounts set by Act RT I, 07.01.2025, 1, in force 17 January 2025): audit is compulsory where at least two of these are exceeded - sales revenue or income EUR 5,000,000, total assets EUR 2,500,000, average number of employees 50 - or at least one of these - EUR 15,000,000, EUR 7,500,000, 180 employees. Under § 185³(1) the new amounts apply retroactively to reporting periods that began on or after 1 January 2024. A private limited company below these lines needs an audit only if its articles or another law require one.

m-563651b8.t: Estonia's review thresholds in three dated versions of § 92 of the Auditors Activities Act (two-of-three test; one-of-three test). In force 1 January 2015: revenue EUR 1m, assets EUR 0.5m, 15 employees; EUR 3m, EUR 1.5m, 45. From 1 January 2016 (RT I, 30.12.2015, 4; for reporting periods beginning from that date, § 184(2¹)): EUR 1.6m, EUR 0.8m, 24; EUR 4.8m, EUR 2.4m, 72. From 17 January 2025 (RT I, 07.01.2025, 1; applied retroactively to reporting periods begun from 1 January 2024, § 185³(1)): EUR 2m, EUR 1m, 24; EUR 6m, EUR 3m, 72 - the employee figures were left unchanged in 2025.

m-1c305a1b.t: Bookkeeping duty in Estonia, as in force on 5 October 2026: every legal person in private or public law registered in Estonia, every sole proprietor and every registered branch of a foreign company is an accounting entity (Accounting Act § 2(2)) and must document and record all its transactions, prepare and file the annual report and keep its accounting documents (§ 4) - source documents for seven years from the end of the financial year (§ 12(1)). The Act does not say who may keep the books: its consolidated text contains no occurrence of the word 'raamatupidaja' (accountant) and no licensing or qualification condition for bookkeeping was found in it.

m-c9fd123c.t: The Estonian Guarantee Fund (Tagatisfond) lists eight credit institutions whose deposits it guarantees (page last edited 04/06/2025): AS Inbank, AS LHV Pank, AS SEB Pank, Bigbank AS, Coop Pank AS, Holm Bank AS, Luminor Bank AS and Swedbank AS. Its FAQ states that 'deposits of both private individuals and businesses are compensated, with the exception of deposits not subject to compensation', and that it does not guarantee deposits in the Estonian branch of a credit institution of another European Economic Area state, which fall under the home state's scheme. A deposit whose disposal the Financial Intelligence Unit has restricted is compensated only after the precept is revoked.

m-b20bd5bb.t: Estonia raised and widened the extra deposit cover for natural persons on 8 April 2022 (RT I, 29.03.2022, 3). Until then § 25(2^1) of the Guarantee Fund Act covered, beyond the EUR 100,000 limit, up to EUR 70,000 of money from the transfer of residential property, for six months from the transfer. Since then it covers up to a further EUR 100,000 credited in the six months before deposits became unavailable from the transfer of residential property, from marriage, divorce, dismissal or redundancy, retirement, disability or the death of a close person, or as insurance indemnity or state or victim compensation. The text in force on 5 October 2026 keeps this.

m-907bbb45.t: Deposits in Estonian banks are guaranteed by the Guarantee Fund. Under § 25(2) of the Guarantee Fund Act (text in force from 21 July 2026) eligible deposits are compensated with accrued interest up to EUR 100,000 per depositor in any one credit institution; a natural person gets up to a further EUR 100,000 for sums credited in the previous six months from a home sale and listed life events (§ 25(2^1)). Payment is completed within seven working days of the date deposits become unavailable; its supervisory board may extend this by up to ten working days in extraordinary circumstances (§ 41(2)). A company's deposit is covered unless the company is one of the excluded entities of § 30.

m-30e30d6c.t: Money that a payment institution or e-money institution keeps in an Estonian bank is outside the Estonian deposit guarantee on 5 October 2026: § 30(1) of the Guarantee Fund Act (in force 21 July 2026) lists 'e-money institution' and 'payment institution' among depositors whose deposits 'shall not be guaranteed or compensated'. The act gives look-through treatment only to one kind of client account: funds of third parties on an account opened for notarial and enforcement agent's acts are handled 'as separate deposits for each person' (§ 25(3^1)). Deposits of persons under international sanctions are not compensated (§ 30(4^1), from 8 April 2022).

m-11f11a8e.t: Estonia's deposit guarantee was last used for Versobank AS. Per the Guarantee Fund's own account (page last edited 03/03/2025) its supervisory board decided on 27 March 2018, a day after the licence was withdrawn, to compensate depositors; payment started on 5 April 2018 through the agent banks Swedbank AS and AS SEB Pank and was disbursed within 17 working days of 26 March 2018; in total EUR 90.2 million went to 2,571 depositors, up to EUR 100,000 each plus interest. The extra cover for money from a home sale was then up to EUR 70,000; it became up to EUR 100,000 on 8 April 2022 (RT I, 29.03.2022, 3). The statutory payout term was seven working days, extendable by ten, in 2018 as now.

m-d9cfa1af.t: SEB Estonia's leaflet 'Interchange fees and scheme fees included in acquiring fee' (in effect from 7 April 2026) gives approximate interchange on domestic cards as 0.20% debit, 0.30% credit and 'up to 2.00%' business cards, for Mastercard and Visa alike, and the same for cards issued elsewhere in the EEA. Scheme fees: Mastercard 0.039% on domestic and 0.114% on other EEA cards; Visa 0.030% debit, 0.035% credit and business. For cards issued outside the EEA it shows 0.20% and 0.30% on consumer debit and credit and marks business-card interchange and all scheme fees 'confidential'. The leaflet says the values are rounded and may not reflect the exact fee.

m-a0b25d60.t: LHV publishes an indicative table of interchange and processing fees for its merchants (read 5 October 2026). For cards issued in the European Economic Area, Mastercard and Visa alike: consumer debit 0.20%, consumer credit 0.30%, cards of legal persons 'up to 2.00%', the same for terminal and e-commerce transactions. For consumer cards issued outside the EEA: 0.20% debit and 0.30% credit at a terminal, 1.15% and 1.50% in e-commerce. The page states the figures are indicative because they come from the price lists of card organisations and processors, which may change at any time independently of AS LHV Pank.

m-9cdc98b5.t: Visa publishes a domestic interchange sheet for Estonia ('Estonia | Domestic Multi-lateral Interchange Fees', April 2025, the version linked on Visa's European fees page on 5 October 2026). Consumer cards: 0.20% for debit and prepaid, 0.30% for credit and deferred debit. Commercial cards are far higher and differ by channel: Visa Business debit 1.30% chip or contactless and 1.65% e-commerce; Platinum Business 1.55% and 1.90%; Infinite Business 1.65% and 2.00%; Corporate and Purchasing 1.55% and 1.90%. Two commercial lines sit at the consumer level: 'Business Credit - Small Market Expense' and 'Corporate - Large Market Enterprise', both 0.30%.

m-715189f7.t: Swedbank Estonia's 'Indicative price components table' (in the bank's terms index effective from 18 January 2021 and 'Effective now' on 5 October 2026) shows the interchange and scheme fees contained in its merchant commission. For Estonian-issued cards: Visa and Mastercard consumer debit and prepaid 0.20%, consumer credit and charge 0.30%, commercial cards 2.00%, the same card-present and card-not-present. Scheme fees shown: EUR 0.002 + 0.035485% for Visa and EUR 0.002 + 0.023066% for Mastercard. 'Estonian cards' are cards issued by payment institutions located in the bank's country of registration. The table calls the fees 'recommended'; the commission itself is agreed per merchant.

m-3362e377.t: Estonia enforces the Interchange Fee Regulation through misdemeanour law. § 113-3 of the Payment Institutions and E-money Institutions Act punishes a breach of Articles 3-5, 8, 10 and 12 of Regulation (EU) 2015/751 with a fine of up to EUR 5,000,000 or up to twice the gain made or loss avoided, and for a legal person alternatively up to 10% of its or its group's turnover (wording in force from 1 November 2023, RT I, 17.03.2023, 2); under § 117(2) the body conducting the proceedings is Finantsinspektsioon. The consumer-side rules - the surcharge ban, cash acceptance, rounding, receipts and price display - sit with the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority.

m-3c9a039f.t: On 5 October 2026 Finantsinspektsioon's register listed 4 Estonian e-money institutions as active: inHouse Pay AS (licence decision 9 September 2019), IPF Digital AS (11 January 2021), Monemon AS (9 October 2023) and Lightspark Payments Europe AS (16 June 2026). The 'Closed' filter of the same register showed no entry in the group of Estonian e-money institutions, only former cross-border providers and their distributors.

m-32423720.t: Paysera opens a business account for an Estonian company in its app. Per its Estonian pages (read 5 October 2026) the head of the company, or a person with a power of attorney e-signed by the head or certified by a notary, first verifies their own identity, then completes a KYC questionnaire; 'one of the required documents is the list of shareholders'. Companies registered in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Bulgaria or Romania use the app; those registered elsewhere file documents in a browser. For a company registered in a SEPA country that is not an 'international company', opening is free and administration EUR 5 a month; an 'international company' pays EUR 100 and EUR 20 a month.

m-4430d796.t: Before a café's first employee starts, the employer enters the start of work in the employment register (Taxation Act, text in force on 5 October 2026): under § 25^2 the person providing work is the obliged person, registers commencement 'no later than the moment the person starts work', and registers suspension and termination within ten days. § 25^1(4) covers, among others, persons working under an employment contract, persons providing services under a contract under the law of obligations (except a sole proprietor and a payer of business income tax), and members of a legal person's management or controlling body, where their work gives rise to a tax liability in Estonia.

m-169b2c01.t: Estonia's employment register, kept by the Tax and Customs Board, as in force on 5 October 2026: the person providing work, resident or non-resident, registers the start of work no later than the moment work starts, and a suspension or termination within ten days (Taxation Act § 25²). Entered are natural persons 'whose working gives rise to a tax liability in Estonia': employees, persons serving under a contract under the law of obligations (except sole proprietors and entrepreneur-account holders) and members of a legal person's management or controlling body (§ 25¹(4) p 1-3). Penalty payments are capped at EUR 3,300 in total - EUR 1,300 the first time, EUR 2,000 the second (§ 25⁸(3)).

m-5b092976.t: Strong customer authentication in Estonian law took effect on 14 September 2019, not with the rest of the PSD2 transposition: § 5(2) of the transposing Act (RT I, 07.12.2017, 1) put the Law of Obligations Act provisions on it (§ 724^4(5) and (8), § 724^5(3), § 724^6, § 727^1(5)) into force 18 months after the Commission's technical standard entered into force, and Finantsinspektsioon's circular of 3 December 2020 dates Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 as in force 14 March 2018 and applied from 14 September 2019. For card payments in e-commerce the circular follows the European Banking Authority: the extra migration period ended on 31 December 2020.
